research:law-standards.angle: Law and technical standards that decide which signatures a government accepts (eIDAS and eIDAS 2, ETSI AdES formats and long-term validation, archiving, national eID signature laws, US federal identity and PKI rules, India IT Act and Aadhaar eSign, Brazil ICP-Brasil), and where DocuSign meets or misses each.

findings.claim: Under eIDAS only a qualified electronic signature (QES) automatically has the legal effect of a handwritten signature and must be recognised in every Member State; DocuSign's default envelope is a simple electronic signature with no signer certificate, so it does not clear the bar wherever a state needs handwriting equivalence.
findings.evidence: eIDAS (Reg. 910/2014) Art. 25(1) says an e-signature cannot be refused only because it is electronic or not qualified; Art. 25(2) gives a QES the equivalent effect of a handwritten signature; Art. 25(3) requires every Member State to recognise a QES based on a qualified certificate from another Member State (text as hosted by legislation.gov.uk; the 2014 text was amended by Reg. 2024/1183). A DocuSign community moderator explains that the EU simple-signature category covers a signature without a digital certificate, and DocuSign's UK blog calls SES the most basic level, needing no specific identity check. DocuSign's own guide says the difference between SES, AES and QES lies mainly in ID checks and where the burden of proof sits (DocuSign pages undated in results; Commission eSignature FAQ last updated 2 Feb 2026).
findings.requirement: Make QES (and AES based on a qualified certificate) a first-class signing level, not an add-on; let a rules table pick the minimum level per jurisdiction and document type; record the level achieved on the signed file and in the evidence report.

findings.claim: When an EU public body asks for an advanced signature for an online service, it only has to accept signatures in the formats named by implementing acts (XAdES, CAdES, PAdES, ASiC). These formats were refreshed on 2 Feb 2026, so a product's output format, not its brand, decides acceptance.
findings.evidence: eIDAS Art. 27 covers public sector bodies that require an AdES for an online service and (per a secondary summary) bars demanding more than a QES cross-border. Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2015/1506 (8 Sep 2015) listed the XAdES, CAdES and PAdES formats plus ASiC containers that public bodies must recognise. Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/248 (adopted 2 Feb 2026, published 3 Feb 2026) repeals 2015/1506, sets updated formats in Annex II, and keeps recognition of the old formats for 24 months after entry into force. I did not retrieve the Annex II list itself.
findings.requirement: Emit signatures in the exact Annex II profiles of Reg. 2026/248 (PAdES baseline for PDF, XAdES or ASiC-E for XML and multi-file bundles, CAdES for binary), and test every output against the Commission's open-source DSS validator.

findings.claim: DocuSign's EU advanced and qualified options exist but are sold as add-ons, and users report that its outputs do not validate cleanly in third-party PDF validators. For a public body that must check signatures from many senders, this is friction.
findings.evidence: A DocuSign employee on the community forum says AES or QES is an add-on in all plans and needs the account team. Forum users report untrusted-chain errors when validating DocuSign AES, and note that Adobe Reader does not show whether a signature is AES or QES, so one user treated the Certificate of Completion as the practical proof. Another thread says DocuSign's platform seal can cause validation errors in third-party PDF validators and that admins can switch the seal off on download (forum posts, undated in results; not official documentation).
findings.requirement: Include AES and QES in base plans used by public bodies; never let a vendor platform seal break the signer's certificate chain (add vendor evidence as a separate document timestamp or ASiC component); pass EU DSS, Adobe AATL and national validators with zero warnings.

findings.claim: Many EU states tie formal dealings with the state to QES or to their own national eID signature, and they provide that signature free. A US workflow product has to plug into those tools rather than replace them.
findings.evidence: Germany: BGB s.126a replaces written form only with a QES, and VwVfG s.3a lets electronic form replace statutory written form in administrative law (consolidated text shows an amendment in BGBl. I Nr. 224 of 22 Jul 2026). France: the arrete of 22 Mar 2019 (in force 1 Apr 2019) requires at least an AdES based on a qualified certificate to sign public procurement contracts. Italy: CAD Art. 65 makes online applications valid if signed with a qualified or digital signature, or if the applicant is identified by SPID, CIE or CNS (text updated 21 Apr 2026). Spain: Ley 39/2015 Art. 10 lists qualified-certificate signatures and Cl@ve Firma, and the state signing app is AutoFirma. Poland: three state-backed options exist, the free podpis zaufany through profil zaufany, the e-ID card podpis osobisty, and the commercial qualified signature. Estonia: ID-card QES in ASiC-E via DigiDoc, and authorities must accept it. Austria: ID Austria has been required for e-government since 5 Dec 2023, and the state runs a PDF signature service. Denmark: MitID handles login, and public bodies sign through NemLog-in3.
findings.requirement: Act as a workflow layer that calls each country's own signing tool (DigiDoc and Smart-ID or ID-card for Estonia, ID Austria, podpis zaufany, SPID and CIE, Cl@ve Firma and AutoFirma, NemLog-in3) and keeps the state's signature intact in the final file; ship a per-country rules table that says which tool a given filing needs.

findings.claim: eIDAS 2 makes the free EU Digital Identity Wallet the default way citizens will produce a QES from late 2026. A product without wallet signing will be outside the main government path; DocuSign has a prototype, not a shipped feature.
findings.evidence: Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 requires each Member State to offer at least one EUDI Wallet by 24 Dec 2026, and the wallet must let natural persons sign with a QES free of charge for non-professional purposes (Garrigues and the German interior ministry's eIDAS2 explainer). Under Art. 5f(2), private relying parties required by law or contract to use strong user authentication must accept the wallet; a commercial blog puts the deadline at 24 Dec 2027. The wallet creates a QES through a remote QSCD run by a QTSP. DocuSign's EU blog says it is building prototypes with Animo through the German SPRIND challenge; I found no announcement of shipped wallet signing as of Nov 2026.
findings.requirement: Register as an EUDI Wallet relying party; accept wallet presentation for signer identity; let the signer create a QES from the wallet through a remote QSCD over the Cloud Signature Consortium API or ETSI TS 119 432; keep the signature free for citizens.

findings.claim: Government records must stay verifiable for decades. ETSI defines four PAdES baseline levels, and only B-LTA (with repeated archive timestamps) survives certificate and timestamp expiry. DocuSign's published EU advanced profile is B-LT, and its forum says validity ends with the last document timestamp.
findings.evidence: ETSI EN 319 142-1 (V1.1.1 2016, V1.2.1 2024, valid from 1 Feb 2024) defines PAdES baseline B-B, B-T, B-LT and B-LTA; LTA needs at least one document timestamp and is the successor of the older LTV profile. ETSI EN 319 102-1 V1.4.1 (2024-06) sets the validation procedures, and the Commission's DSS library (LGPL 2.1) implements them. DocuSign's Standards-Based Signatures data sheet lists PAdES B-LT for the EU Advanced Signature. On the DocuSign forum, an employee says documents completed before DocuSign switched on PAdES-LTV must be downloaded again, and a user notes the file's validity runs to the expiry of the last document timestamp (forum, undated).
findings.requirement: Produce PAdES B-LTA (and XAdES or CAdES LTA) by default, embed all certificates and OCSP or CRL data, run a job that re-timestamps archives before the timestamp authority's certificate expires, and pass the ETSI TS 119 144-4 conformance test suites.

findings.claim: Archiving and preservation are now regulated trust services in the EU, and Germany names a technical guideline for authorities. I found no evidence that DocuSign holds a qualified preservation or archiving status or conforms to TR-ESOR.
findings.evidence: eIDAS Art. 34 sets up qualified preservation services for QES; Implementing Reg. (EU) 2025/1946 cites ETSI TS 119 511 (current V1.2.1, 2025-10). Art. 45j sets up qualified electronic archiving; Implementing Reg. (EU) 2025/2532 cites CEN/TS 18170:2025. BSI TR-03125 (TR-ESOR) describes how signed data stays legally valid over long periods, is treated as state of the art, and mainly applies to federal and state authorities with retention duties. In the US, NARA's e-signature records guidance dates from 18 Oct 2000, and Bulletin 2014-04 with transfer guidance tables (updated Jan 2025) sets acceptable formats for permanent records. The absence of a DocuSign preservation status is an absence of evidence in my searches, not a confirmed gap.
findings.requirement: Convert to PDF/A before signing, keep the evidence inside the archived file, offer a preservation mode built to ETSI TS 119 511 and TR-ESOR (aim for a qualified preservation listing), and export to government records systems in NARA-accepted formats.

findings.claim: In the US, ESIGN and UETA allow e-signatures broadly, but federal agencies choose signature technology by risk and default to PIV-based PKI digital signatures for their own staff. In that model the signer's own government certificate signs the document, not a vendor certificate.
findings.evidence: OMB M-00-10 (25 Apr 2000) implements GPEA and asks agencies to pick e-signature technology through a risk assessment. OMB M-19-17 (21 May 2019) tells agencies to implement NIST SP 800-63-3 and successors and to use PIV as the primary credential. NIST SP 800-63-4 was finalised in July 2025 and supersedes 800-63-3. FIPS 201-3 (Jan 2022) puts a digital signature key on the PIV card with a certificate issued under the Federal PKI Common Policy, and use needs explicit cardholder action. Interior's records policy (RMP-2020-01) makes PIV digital signature the standard and requires approval for alternatives. GSA Digital Signature Policy (Directive 2162.2, signed 5 Feb 2018, expires 29 Feb 2028). The Federal Register requires an X.509 XAdES signature in Word, via PIV or a delegated role certificate on FIPS 140 Level 2 hardware from a Federal PKI CA. DocuSign is not on the Federal PKI Shared Service Provider list (Entrust, WidePoint, Verizon). It says staff can sign with PIV or CAC, but I found no source that this applies the card's own signature key to the PDF.
findings.requirement: Sign with the user's own PIV or CAC signature key (browser or desktop middleware), producing PAdES or XAdES that chains to the Federal Common Policy root; validate against Federal PKI bridge paths; support delegated role certificates; map every flow to an SP 800-63-4 IAL, AAL and FAL and to the agency's GPEA risk assessment.

findings.claim: DocuSign's US cloud authorizations stop at FedRAMP Moderate and DoD IL4, which leaves out high-impact federal systems and IL5 defense data. It is only working toward FedRAMP High.
findings.evidence: DocuSign Federal eSignature got FedRAMP Moderate in Aug 2017. eSignature and CLM hold a DISA provisional IL4 authorization (Apr 2021), with a 22 Oct 2023 condition memo requiring a BCAP connection for IL4 production data. IAM reached FedRAMP Moderate on 15 Sep 2025. DocuSign's government products schedule dated 4 Sep 2026 still describes the Moderate boundary. DocuSign job posts from Feb 2026 and 31 Aug 2026 describe work toward an IL5 environment and FedRAMP High; I found no High authorization.
findings.requirement: Plan for FedRAMP High and DoD IL5 (and GovRAMP High for states) from day one, or offer a self-hosted or agency-cloud deployment that inherits the agency's own authorization.

findings.claim: Federal buyers need signing keys in FIPS 140-3 validated modules. DocuSign's older HSM validations are historical, and its one FIPS 140-3 certificate found was an interim validation with a sunset date that has now passed.
findings.evidence: NIST CMVP lists the DocuSign HSM Appliance (cert 3960, FIPS 140-2 Level 3) and DocuSign Signature Appliance (cert 3141) as historical. Cert 4782 (FIPS 140-3, Level 3) was listed as an active interim validation with a sunset date of 27 Aug 2026, which is before today (20 Nov 2026); its current status needs a direct check. Cert 4441 covers a DocuSign QSCD Appliance (status not checked). FIPS 140-3 replaced 140-2 for new submissions from April 2022.
findings.requirement: Keep all signing and sealing keys in HSMs with active (not historical or sunset) FIPS 140-3 Level 3 certificates, and publish the certificate numbers. For EU remote QES, also use a QSCD certified to CEN EN 419 241-2.

findings.claim: India only treats electronic signature methods listed in the Second Schedule of the IT Act as reliable, and Aadhaar eSign can only be offered by CCA-empanelled eSign Service Providers. DocuSign is not one; it routes Indian signatures through eMudhra.
findings.evidence: IT Act s.3A lets a subscriber sign with a technique that is reliable and listed in the Second Schedule, and the government adds or removes techniques by gazette notification. The First Schedule excludes some documents (sources list negotiable instruments, wills, trusts, powers of attorney; a Sep 2022 change is reported). CCA lists empanelled ESPs, including eMudhra (25 Jun 2015) and Sify (19 Feb 2020); ESPs must pass a CCA-empanelled audit, and Aadhaar keys are created in an HSM and destroyed after one use. Directors filing on MCA21 V3 must register a DSC. A DocuSign community post says that from 22 Jun 2026 DocuSign offers native eMudhra signing under a single DocuSign contract, needing ID Verification or IAM for CX plans.
findings.requirement: Integrate Aadhaar eSign through one or more CCA-empanelled ESPs (or pass the CCA audit to become one), support Class 3 DSC USB tokens for MCA21 and similar portals, block First Schedule document types, and store signed records as CCA guidelines require.

findings.claim: Brazil gives a presumption of truth only to ICP-Brasil signatures, requires them for top-level and real-estate acts, and gives citizens a free state advanced signature through gov.br. DocuSign supports ICP-Brasil only when the signer buys a certificate, and markets itself against gov.br.
findings.evidence: MP 2.200-2/2001 Art. 10 s.1 presumes documents signed with ICP-Brasil certificates to be true; an AGU opinion reads it as equating only ICP-Brasil signatures with handwritten ones. Lei 14.063/2020 (23 Sep 2020) Art. 5 lets each Power set the minimum signature level, makes qualified (ICP-Brasil) signatures mandatory for acts of heads of Powers and ministers and for transfer and registration of real estate, and says qualified signatures prevail when rules conflict; Decreto 10.543/2020 regulates it for the federal executive. ITI says the gov.br advanced signature is free for silver or gold accounts and legally valid under Lei 14.063. DocuSign Brazil says its qualified signature uses an ICP-Brasil A1 or A3 certificate the signer buys from a CA, plus a signing agent install, and has a page comparing DocuSign with gov.br.
findings.requirement: Sign natively with ICP-Brasil certificates (A1, A3 token and cloud A3) using ICP-Brasil signature policies, call the gov.br signature for citizens instead of charging them, and make every output pass the ITI validator (validar.iti.gov.br). The ICP-Brasil policy details (DOC-ICP-15) were not researched here.

findings.claim: China, Canada and Japan also tie government-grade signatures to state-licensed or state-run PKI, so a vendor's own certificate does not qualify.
findings.evidence: China: the Electronic Signature Law gives a reliable e-signature the force of a handwritten signature or seal; certification must come from a provider licensed by MIIT, and foreign certificates count only under an agreement or reciprocity (Hogan Lovells). DocuSign's own China page says that if parties do not use a pre-approved provider, they must prove reliability themselves. Canada: PIPEDA Part 2 requires a secure electronic signature in some federal cases, and SOR/2005-30 only recognises CAs approved by the President of the Treasury Board; only federal CAs cross-certified with the Federal PKI Bridge are recognised. TBS's 2019 guidance uses a four-level assurance model. Japan: the My Number card carries a JPKI signature certificate, e-Gov lists 4,372 procedures (ITU talk, Jun 2026), and company representatives use a separate commercial registration certificate.
findings.requirement: Build a pluggable trust layer so the signing certificate can come from the country's licensed or state CA (MIIT-licensed CAs, GC PKI, JPKI), and map each country's assurance levels (for example Canada's four levels) to the product's signature levels.

findings.claim: Governments and EU institutions often run their own free signing infrastructure, built on open standards and open-source validation. This takes away the core use case a commercial vendor sells to them.
findings.evidence: The European Commission signed its first international agreement (with the World Bank) using its own QES service, EU Sign, in July 2020, and has extended EU Sign to other EU institutions and agencies (EASA and ACER records). The Commission publishes DSS, an LGPL 2.1 Java library for creating and validating AdES signatures against the EU trusted lists, with releases through 2025 and 2026. Other state tools: Estonia's DigiDoc, Austria's PDF signature service, Spain's AutoFirma, Poland's free podpis zaufany, and Brazil's free gov.br signature (see the national findings above).
findings.requirement: Compete on workflow, routing, audit and archiving rather than on the signature itself: be free or near-free for citizens, embed EU DSS for validation, and let public bodies keep their own signing service and keys under the product.

findings.claim: Sovereignty rules in parts of the European public sector can rule out a US-headquartered SaaS signer whatever its EU data residency, because US law can reach the provider.
findings.evidence: Orrick (Jan 2026) reports that France's SecNumCloud requires providers to be immune to third-country authority requests, and that the European Commission's Oct 2025 Cloud Sovereignty Framework sets sovereignty goals for its own buying; it also says there is no general EU ban on non-European providers. DocuSign offers EU data residency, and its law enforcement page says it is subject to the US Stored Communications Act. Advocacy and blog sources argue CLOUD Act exposure remains with EU storage; I treat those as lower authority.
findings.requirement: Offer on-premises or sovereign-operator deployments (for example a SecNumCloud-qualified host), customer-held keys in the customer's own HSM, and a design where the vendor cannot read documents or signing keys.

counter_evidence.claim: The US federal government buys DocuSign across all agencies at a negotiated discount.
counter_evidence.evidence: GSA announced a OneGov agreement with DocuSign on 31 Jul 2025: 70 percent off eSignature Enterprise Pro and 50 percent off Intelligent Agreement Management through 31 Jan 2027, on the GSA Multiple Award Schedule for federal agencies. A later GSA blog lists DocuSign alongside Adobe, AWS and Google among OneGov deals.
counter_evidence.requirement: To compete in US federal sales, a product needs a GSA schedule listing and OneGov-level pricing.

counter_evidence.claim: Large federal agencies run DocuSign at scale, inside FedRAMP Moderate and DoD IL4 boundaries.
counter_evidence.evidence: Veterans Affairs placed a 3-year DocuSign SaaS task order worth about $53.7M (Award 36C10B21F0063, about 2021) through NASA SEWP V, with Regan Technologies as reseller. DocuSign Federal has been FedRAMP Moderate since Aug 2017, and eSignature and CLM have held a DISA provisional IL4 authorization since Apr 2021. DocuSign says it is connected to DISA's BCAP and DISN.
counter_evidence.requirement: FedRAMP Moderate and DoD IL4 are the minimum entry ticket for federal use.

counter_evidence.claim: US states and Australian states have whole-of-government DocuSign agreements.
counter_evidence.evidence: Queensland signed Standing Offer Arrangement SOA-TDS-1022, giving all departments and government-owned corporations access to DocuSign eSignature and CLM (iTnews, 15 Mar 2023). New York has a statewide DocuSign award under its IT umbrella contract (30 Apr 2024). Maine holds master agreements for both Adobe Sign and DocuSign. Arkansas lists DocuSign through a NASPO ValuePoint contract held by Carahsoft (listed expiry 15 Sep 2026). DocuSign holds GovRAMP (formerly StateRAMP) authorization.
counter_evidence.requirement: State-level cooperative contracts (NASPO ValuePoint, state umbrella contracts, Australian standing offers) and GovRAMP are needed to reach this market.

counter_evidence.claim: European central governments have bought DocuSign, including French ministries and UK departments.
counter_evidence.evidence: In 2016 DocuSign announced that French ministries, including the Ministry of Economy, Finance and Industry, chose it for e-signature as part of a 100 percent digital processes drive (vendor press release). In the UK, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero signed a contract with DocuSign UK Limited on 4 Jul 2024, running to Jul 2027, worth GBP 56,717.10. Companies House varied a G-Cloud contract for a DocuSign e-signature system. Resellers list DocuSign on G-Cloud 14, including qualified and advanced signatures. Lambeth Council and the Welsh Government procurement team are named users.
counter_evidence.requirement: A G-Cloud listing in the UK and a French-qualified presence help reach these buyers.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign is itself an EU qualified trust service provider and can issue qualified certificates and timestamps, so it can technically produce QES.
counter_evidence.evidence: DocuSign France SAS is listed as a QTSP on the French trusted list run by ANSSI (DocuSign trust brief; a UK ICO FOI response also reports the listing). DocuSign France acts as CA and RA for qualified certificates with QCP-n-qscd policy identifiers and runs a remote signing device it describes as qualified. DocuSign also says it accepts qualified certificates from any provider on the EU trust list. Its AES certificates come from the Docusign Cloud Signing CA G2, and its Standards-Based Signatures data sheet lists PAdES B-LT, ETSI EN 319 411-2 and EN 319 421. Primary ANSSI list entry not checked directly.
counter_evidence.requirement: A rival needs its own QTSP status or a QTSP partner, and must check the EU trusted list browser for current status.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign meets NIST IAL2 identity proofing through Kantara-accredited partners.
counter_evidence.evidence: DocuSign added an IAL2 option using ID.me and CLEAR, both Kantara-accredited under NIST SP 800-63-3 IAL2 (reported Nov 2025; CLEAR partnership revealed Sep 2025). DocuSign says more than 80 million IAL2-verified ID.me users could verify inside DocuSign as of Apr 2026. One caveat for the premise: NIST SP 800-63-4 replaced 800-63-3 in Jul 2025, so accreditation against rev 4 is the next bar.
counter_evidence.requirement: Offer identity proofing accredited to SP 800-63-4 IAL2 or better.

counter_evidence.claim: Some government bodies explicitly accept signatures made with third-party e-signature software such as DocuSign from the public.
counter_evidence.evidence: In Oct 2023 the IRS made permanent its acceptance of electronic or digital signatures on the forms listed in IRM 10.10.1 exhibits (IRM revised again 12 Aug 2024). Acceptable methods include signatures made with third-party software; Ropes and Gray names DocuSign as an example. The IRM still requires a process to confirm intent, identify and authenticate the signer, and preserve integrity.
counter_evidence.requirement: Keep intent capture, signer authentication and an integrity seal that meet IRM 10.10.1 sections 10.10.1.3 and 10.10.1.6.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign is IRAP assessed at PROTECTED and holds Australian Commonwealth contracts.
counter_evidence.evidence: DocuSign eSignature completed an IRAP assessment at PROTECTED in Sep 2021 (GovTech Review, Nov 2021) and was later reassessed; its first IRAP assessment in 2019 was at OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE. A third-party aggregator lists 10 Commonwealth contracts worth about AUD 539K since 2020 (Future Fund, DTA, Agriculture and others); not checked against AusTender.
counter_evidence.requirement: An IRAP PROTECTED assessment less than 24 months old against the current ISM.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign does support the national PKI signatures in Brazil and India, through certificates and partners.
counter_evidence.evidence: DocuSign Brazil supports qualified signatures with ICP-Brasil A1 and A3 certificates, with no extra DocuSign fee, and cloud certificates through a Safeweb SafeID partnership. In India, a DocuSign community post says that from 22 Jun 2026 eMudhra signing is native in DocuSign under one contract (requires ID Verification or IAM for CX plans).
counter_evidence.requirement: Match this at minimum, then go further by making national PKI signing included and free for signers.

research:law-standards.notes:
Method limits: WebFetch could not reach outside hosts in this session (www.docusign.com and www.fedramp.gov both failed DNS resolution under the session's network rules), so every finding rests on WebSearch result summaries of the cited pages, not full-text reads. To read the primary pages directly (FedRAMP Marketplace entry, DocuSign trust pages, Annex II of Reg. 2026/248, the ANSSI trusted list entry, CMVP status for cert 4782), those hosts would have to be allowed in the session's network settings. Strength ratings reflect this.

Synthesis (my reading of the evidence, not a sourced fact): the premise is overstated. DocuSign is widely used by governments for internal, procurement, HR and low-risk citizen paperwork (GSA OneGov, VA, Queensland, New York, UK departments, French ministries in 2016). What it has not become is the legal signature of the state. In the formal acts where law sets the bar (QES or national eID in the EU, PIV and Federal PKI for US federal staff, Second Schedule methods in India, ICP-Brasil in Brazil, MIIT-licensed CAs in China), the trust comes from a certificate the state or a state-supervised provider issues to the signer, in an ETSI or national format, often free (gov.br, podpis zaufany, ID Austria, the EUDI wallet from Dec 2026). DocuSign's core product is a simple-signature workflow with a vendor seal; its AES, QES and national options are add-ons, partner-dependent, and sometimes do not validate cleanly in third-party validators.

Product requirements in priority order: (1) a jurisdiction rules engine that picks SES, AES, AdES-QC or QES per document type; (2) bring-your-own trust anchor: PIV and CAC, EU national eIDs, EUDI Wallet via CSC API or ETSI TS 119 432, Aadhaar eSign via a CCA ESP, ICP-Brasil and gov.br, JPKI; (3) outputs in the Reg. 2026/248 Annex II formats at PAdES or XAdES B-LTA, validated with the EU DSS library and the ETSI TS 119 144-4 test suites, with no vendor seal breaking the signer chain; (4) PDF/A before signing, re-timestamping, preservation to ETSI TS 119 511 and BSI TR-ESOR, export in NARA formats; (5) FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSMs with active certificates, an EN 419 241-2 QSCD for remote QES; (6) FedRAMP High or IL5, IRAP PROTECTED, GovRAMP, plus self-hosted and sovereign-operator options with customer-held keys; (7) SP 800-63-4 IAL2 accredited proofing; (8) free for citizen signers. Not researched here: ICP-Brasil signature policy documents (DOC-ICP-15), Germany's national eID card signing, Login.gov integration, Korea and the Gulf states.

research:adoption-facts.angle: Facts first: which national and large regional governments use DocuSign and at what scale, what the others use instead (national eID and state signing platforms), and whether the premise that major governments have not widely adopted DocuSign holds, where and how far.

findings.claim: Verdict on the premise: it is only partly true. DocuSign is widely bought as a departmental workflow tool in the US, and at smaller scale in the UK, Australia and Ireland. No national government found uses DocuSign as its national signing system. Where a state issues an eID, the state owns the signing credential, and often the signing workflow too.
findings.evidence: This is a synthesis of the findings below and the counter_evidence. In the US: FedRAMP Moderate since 2017, DoD IL4 since 2021, and a government-wide GSA OneGov discount from July 2025. In the UK, departments buy DocuSign directly, with contracts in the tens of thousands of pounds (2023 to 2025 notices). In Australia: IRAP PROTECTED, plus whole-of-government arrangements in Queensland and NSW. By contrast, citizen and official signing in the EU, Latin America and much of Asia runs on credentials the state issues: EU Sign, Estonia ID-card and Smart-ID, Italy's qualified certificates, Spain's Cl@ve and @firma, gov.br, Aadhaar eSign, Sign with Singpass, UAE PASS, JPKI, e.firma, FirmaGob and PFDR. Several governments also built their own sender-side workflow tools (Singapore's Signify, Argentina's GDE with PFDR, the Commission's EU Sign) or bought domestic vendors (Korea's Modusign, Japan's CloudSign).
findings.requirement: Position the product as the workflow layer that calls the national credential (wallet, eID, state CA), rather than as a replacement for the state's signature. Also offer a deployable or open variant for governments that build their own.

findings.claim: Across the EU, the state-backed EUDI Wallet will give every citizen a free qualified electronic signature (QES) for non-professional use, starting around end of 2026.
findings.evidence: Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 (eIDAS 2, May 2024) requires each Member State to offer a wallet within 24 months of the implementing acts. Sources give different dates: 6 December 2026 (Baker McKenzie, March 2026), 24 December 2026 (Garrigues) and early 2027 (Germany). Wallets must let all natural persons sign with a QES free of charge for non-professional purposes, and Member States may charge for professional use. Using the wallet is voluntary.
findings.requirement: Accept EUDI Wallet identity (PID) and wallet-based remote QES as a signing method. Validate every signature against the EU Trusted Lists. Do not charge citizens per signature where the wallet already makes signing free.

findings.claim: EU institutions use the Commission's own qualified signature service, EU Sign, not DocuSign.
findings.evidence: On 8 July 2020 the Commission said it had signed its first international agreement (with the World Bank) using its own e-signature service. EU Sign is built on the CEF eSignature (DSS) building block, issues qualified signatures recognised across the EU, added cloud-based qualified certificates for staff, and is offered to EU institutions, bodies and agencies (for example ACER, whose data protection notice is dated 9 November 2021). DG DIGIT runs it. A September 2020 DIGIT presentation reported a 7.8x rise in documents signed per month with qualified cloud certificates. No current annual volume was found.
findings.requirement: Produce standard AdES output (PAdES, XAdES, CAdES, ASiC) that the open-source DSS library validates, and accept documents EU Sign has signed and sealed.

findings.claim: Estonia signs at national scale with the state ID-card, Mobile-ID and Smart-ID through DigiDoc. There is no evidence of a role for DocuSign.
findings.evidence: In 2022, RIA (the state information system authority) reported 3 million digital signatures a month, alongside 1.49 million ID-cards in use and 615,000 Smart-ID users. Wikipedia, citing official counts, gives 1,391,704,193 signatures by 7 September 2021. Smart-ID can sign in DigiDoc4 (February 2020). Officials estimate that digital signing saves about a working week per worker a year, roughly 2% of GDP. That figure is an official back-of-envelope estimate with no independent audit, and the OECD notes it is hard to verify.
findings.requirement: Support ID-card, Mobile-ID and Smart-ID signing and the ASiC-E (BDOC) container that DigiDoc produces, and make output verifiable in DigiDoc4.

findings.claim: Italy has one of the largest qualified signature markets in the world, run by domestic qualified trust service providers (QTSPs).
findings.evidence: AgID, the national digital agency, reported on 25 September 2025 that in H1 2025 there were 32.7 million active qualified signature certificates, almost 80% of them remote, over 3.4 billion remote signatures and over 2.5 billion timestamps. H2 2024 had 33.7 million active certificates and H2 2023 had 32.3 million.
findings.requirement: Integrate Italian QTSPs' remote signing (for example through the Cloud Signature Consortium API), support CAdES (.p7m) and PAdES, and accept SPID or CIE for identity.

findings.claim: Spain's central administration uses its own identification and signing stack: Cl@ve, Cl@ve Firma, AutoFirma and the @firma validation platform.
findings.evidence: Official pages describe Cl@ve as the common platform of the state public sector for identification, authentication and e-signature. Cl@ve Firma signs with certificates the administration holds in the cloud, but is available for only a few procedures. AutoFirma is the desktop signing client and @firma is the government's validation platform. A resolution of 14 July 2017 (in force 19 July 2017) sets the rules for non-cryptographic signing with the General State Administration.
findings.requirement: Accept DNIe and FNMT certificates, produce formats AutoFirma can read (XAdES, CAdES, PAdES), and validate through @firma. Cl@ve integration would be needed for citizen flows.

findings.claim: Poland gives citizens free qualified signatures inside the state app mObywatel.
findings.evidence: Since October 2025, a one-year pilot in mObywatel lets adults with an mDowod and a valid e-ID card (NFC phone) make up to five free qualified signatures a month for private matters, choosing among four certified QTSPs (for example Asseco SimplySign and PWPW Sigillum). The Ministry of Digital Affairs publishes the terms. No usage counts were found.
findings.requirement: Accept a QES made in mObywatel and Poland's trusted-profile signature. Pricing must assume citizens already sign for free.

findings.claim: Belgium signs with the state eID card and itsme. The Netherlands has no state-issued signing credential today and points to private QTSPs until the NL Wallet arrives (end 2026).
findings.evidence: The Belgian eID carries separate authentication and signing certificates protected by a PIN. itsme is a QTSP on the EU Trusted List, and Belgian notarial and employment documents need a QES (OneSpan, undated). For the Netherlands, Rijksoverheid explains the three eIDAS levels and sends users to a qualified provider. DigiD is described only as a login tool, and no source shows it signing (inference). A Dutch government presentation (2024) says EUDI wallets with free non-professional QES will reach every citizen from end 2026.
findings.requirement: Support BeID card signing and itsme QES, and get ready for the NL Wallet and the other EUDI wallets.

findings.claim: Finland's public bodies sign with qualified certificates from DVV, the state population data agency, carried on the national ID card.
findings.evidence: Suomi.fi says the Citizen Certificate on the ID card chip is used to log in to public e-services, create electronic signatures and encrypt email. It is the only Finnish eID notified under eIDAS. The Bank of Finland and the Financial Supervisory Authority sign documents with eIDAS-qualified DVV certificates, and DVV runs a PDF validation service (pages current in 2026).
findings.requirement: Validate DVV-signed PDFs and accept Citizen Certificate signing.

findings.claim: In Germany, the state eID is underused and QES is rare. Searches found no DocuSign award by a federal or state (Land) authority.
findings.evidence: A Max Planck study (16 July 2025) found 35% of the adult German-speaking population have activated the eID function. The D21 eGovernment Monitor (reported by Heise, 2024) found 22% of card holders by May 2024. There were 2.9 million eID transactions in February 2025, a monthly record. An IDnow survey (vendor, 2023) said only 6% of Germans had used a QES. Searches of DocuSign pages and German procurement results found no German public-authority DocuSign tender. That is an absence of evidence, not proof of non-use.
findings.requirement: Hold a BSI C5 attestation, offer QES through a German QTSP's remote signing, and support eID (nPA) identification.

findings.claim: France steers sensitive state services to state clouds or SecNumCloud-qualified providers. No DocuSign SecNumCloud qualification was found.
findings.evidence: The 'cloud au centre' doctrine (Circular 6282/SG of 5 July 2021, updated 2023) makes cloud the default for state services and requires sensitive ones to be hosted on the two interministerial state clouds or on a SecNumCloud-qualified offer. A 2024 parliamentary question says many projects still run on derogations. Oodrive is a SecNumCloud provider that offers signature. Searches turned up no SecNumCloud listing for DocuSign. On 10 June 2025, Microsoft France's legal director told the French Senate under oath that he could not guarantee French data would be kept from US authorities (CLOUD Act). This shows why US-owned providers struggle here. (Weak, not checked in this session: SecNumCloud v3.2 is also reported to require protection from non-EU law.)
findings.requirement: Obtain SecNumCloud qualification (in practice EU-controlled hosting and operations), comply with RGS, or offer a version that installs on the state's own clouds.

findings.claim: The UK has no national signing credential. Where the state built a signing service, it built its own: HM Land Registry's Sign your mortgage deed.
findings.evidence: HM Land Registry runs 'Sign your mortgage deed' for remortgages. The homeowner proves identity with GOV.UK One Login (formerly GOV.UK Verify) and signs with a code sent to their phone. Qualifying applications update the register without a caseworker. Separately, DocuSign's data residency page lists five regions (US, Canada, Europe, Australia, Japan) and no UK-specific region.
findings.requirement: Integrate GOV.UK One Login, list on G-Cloud directly, and consider UK data residency for government buyers.

findings.claim: US federal employees, and DoD staff in particular, often sign with their PIV or CAC smart-card certificates, usually in Acrobat, rather than with a cloud e-signature tool.
findings.evidence: A 2012 DoD CAC middleware requirements document says DoD policy requires DoD PKI for digitally signing email, and that HSPD-12 mandates FIPS 201 PIV for federal employees and contractors. Adobe documents DoD PKI test-suite compliance and FIPS 140-2 mode. User forums (2016 to 2020) show routine CAC signing in Acrobat. No current DoD policy document was retrieved.
findings.requirement: Support PKCS#11 signing with PIV and CAC certificates (PAdES), and seek FedRAMP High or DoD IL5 for more sensitive workloads (DocuSign shows only Moderate and IL4).

findings.claim: Canada's federal government has its own internal PKI credential (myKEY) for signing. No federal CanadaBuys award to DocuSign was found.
findings.evidence: Shared Services Canada runs Internal Credential Management (myKEY) for Treasury Board, and departments must use it for internal PKI needs. A PWGSC policy notice says employees can sign contractual documents electronically with their myKEY. The Secure Electronic Signature Regulations recognise a PWGSC medium-assurance signing CA. The Treasury Board published guidance on using e-signatures in 2019. Searches found no federal DocuSign award on CanadaBuys (absence of evidence). The only Canadian award found was a provincial college (NorQuest, Alberta, CAD 161,459).
findings.requirement: Pass a CCCS cloud security assessment (Medium profile, Protected B), keep data in Canada, integrate myKEY and GCKey, and ship a full English and French interface.

findings.claim: India runs signing through the state-regulated Aadhaar eSign and DigiLocker. DocuSign does not support Aadhaar eSign natively.
findings.evidence: eSign is an online signing service under the Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA), offered by empanelled eSign Service Providers. A 2026 industry article citing a Ministry update gives 155.56 crore (1.56 billion) eSigns issued, 44.23 crore by C-DAC. That figure is undated. An older PIB release gave 31.08 crore. A Rajya Sabha reply reported on 12 August 2026 put DigiLocker at 72.43 crore registered users as of 31 July 2026. In a community reply in April 2026, a DocuSign employee said Aadhaar is not directly supported and that DocuSign integrates with eMudhra.
findings.requirement: Become, or integrate natively with, a CCA-empanelled eSign Service Provider (Aadhaar OTP and biometric), and push signed documents to DigiLocker.

findings.claim: Brazil's free gov.br advanced signature handles hundreds of millions of signatures a year. DocuSign markets itself directly against it.
findings.evidence: The 2025 management report of ITI, Brazil's national IT institute, says there were over 214 million gov.br advanced signatures in 2025, the most used gov.br service. That is up from 122 million in 2024 (2024 report) and 95 million in H1 2025 (Agencia Brasil, July 2025). The signature needs a silver or gold gov.br account, and the certificate is issued automatically and free (Law 14.063 of 23 September 2020, Decree 10.543/2020). It is legally 'advanced'. ICP-Brasil certificates are the qualified tier. DocuSign supports ICP-Brasil signing, enabled on request (2021 community post), and publishes a 'Docusign vs gov.br' comparison page.
findings.requirement: Integrate the gov.br advanced signature and ICP-Brasil, validate through ITI's VALIDAR service, and keep citizen signing free.

findings.claim: Singapore's state owns the signature (Sign with Singpass) and built its own internal multi-signer tool (Signify), which over 100 agencies use.
findings.evidence: GovTech launched Sign with Singpass on 4 November 2020 through its subsidiary Assurity Trusted Solutions, the National Certification Authority. Its signatures count as secure electronic signatures under the Electronic Transactions Act. The launch partners included DocuSign, Adobe, iText, Netrust, OneSpan and Dedoco. Signify, built by Open Government Products from a 2023 prototype, collects Singpass signatures on PDFs. Its page says over 100 government agencies and public healthcare institutions use it, and that no new features are planned. A Singpass factsheet dated 30 June 2026 reports 5.5 million users and over 1,400 agencies and organisations.
findings.requirement: Integrate Sign with Singpass, and beat or become the free in-house tool: low or no cost to agencies, and deployable on government cloud.

findings.claim: The UAE signs government documents through the state's UAE PASS. No native DocuSign support for UAE PASS was found.
findings.evidence: The ITU (undated) says UAE PASS gives access to over 5,000 government, semi-government and private entities and that its digital signatures are equivalent to handwritten ones. The Federal Authority for Human Resources (FAHR) applied UAE PASS e-signing to ministries and federal entities for all procedures in the federal HR system. Signing needs a verified (Emirates ID) account level. A DocuSign Community thread asks whether DocuSign supports UAE PASS natively, with no answer shown. Third parties such as emSigner advertise UAE PASS integration.
findings.requirement: Integrate the UAE PASS signing API, require verified accounts for qualified signing, and host data in the UAE.

findings.claim: Saudi Arabia ties e-signatures to state-rooted certificates, used through Nafath and licensed providers.
findings.evidence: The Electronic Transactions Law was amended by a Cabinet decision in October 2023. A signature is linked to a certificate from the National Information Centre (under SDAIA) or from a licensed certification provider. Sources disagree on which body licenses providers (the Digital Government Authority, or formerly the NCDC). emdha's CA, under the Saudi National Root CA, issues certificates for exchanges between government agencies, citizens and residents, and Nafath confirms the signer. A Latham and Watkins guide advises getting written confirmation from a government entity before relying on an e-signature with it.
findings.requirement: Partner with a licensed Saudi certification provider under the National Root CA, verify signers through Nafath, and host data in the Kingdom (in-Kingdom hosting rules not verified in this session).

findings.claim: South Korea opened citizen signing to private certificates in 2020. Civil servants sign with the government PKI (GPKI), and public bodies buy domestic, CSAP-certified e-signature vendors. No DocuSign CSAP certification was found.
findings.evidence: The amended Electronic Signature Act took effect on 10 December 2020 and ended the public certificate's special status. Kakao and PASS signatures were accepted on Government24 and Hometax from 13 January 2021. Joint certificates still handled nearly 90% of 81.07 million year-end tax cases. GPKI authenticates civil servants, and about 650 GPKI certificate files leaked in a breach reported in October 2025. ZDNet (5 May 2026) reports that Modusign's public-sector edition integrates the mobile civil servant ID, GPKI, LDAP and administrative codes, and holds CSAP (the public-sector cloud security certification). Gwangju City and Dangjin City use it, and the Government Employees Pension Service moved about 60,000 documents a year to it (2025).
findings.requirement: Obtain CSAP certification, integrate GPKI and the mobile civil servant ID, sync organisation charts through LDAP, and support Korean administrative standard codes.

findings.claim: Japan's government procurement is gated by ISMAP. DocuSign's ISMAP registration was not found, while Adobe and the domestic CloudSign are registered. JPKI on the My Number Card is the state signing credential.
findings.evidence: Digital Agency pages say the My Number Card chip holds a JPKI signature certificate, and the MyKey platform lets an agency verify signatures for free. Under ISMAP, agencies are in principle required to buy cloud services from the ISMAP list. DocuSign's Japanese ISMAP explainer does not claim registration. Adobe Document Cloud announced ISMAP registration on 6 November 2023. Municipal procurement material for Bengo4's CloudSign says it is ISMAP-certified and used by 20 prefectures (vendor figures). The Local Autonomy Act enforcement regulations were amended on 29 January 2021 to widen which e-signatures municipalities can use for contracts.
findings.requirement: Get on the ISMAP list (or ISMAP-LIU for low-risk use), support JPKI signing, and work inside LGWAN, the closed local-government network.

findings.claim: Indonesia's government signs with certificates from BSrE, a unit of the national cyber agency BSSN.
findings.evidence: BSrE is a technical unit inside BSSN that provides electronic certification for e-government (BSSN Regulation 2 of 2019). An agency must sign a cooperation agreement (PKS) with BSrE, and certificate holders must be its employees (service standard, 2024). data.go.id publishes monthly counts of new government e-signature certificate users since January 2021. The totals were not retrieved.
findings.requirement: Integrate BSrE certificates and its signing API, and fit the PKS model, where the agency, not the vendor, holds the certificate relationship.

findings.claim: Kenya requires government and procuring entities to use certificates from providers licensed by its Communications Authority (CA). The state ICT Authority is the government's own provider.
findings.evidence: The CA licenses Electronic Certification Service Providers (E-CSPs) under the Kenya Information and Communications Act. It accredited the ICT Authority (ICTA) as the Government Certification Authority and E-CSP for the Government of Kenya. Section 59(1) of the Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Regulations 2020 requires certificates from CA-licensed providers. A report (undated) lists four licensed E-CSPs: Geda, eMudhra, TendaWorld and ICTA. On 1 September 2020 the CA invited foreign providers to apply for recognition. A newer rule for critical infrastructure operators is reported only by vendors.
findings.requirement: Obtain foreign E-CSP recognition from the CA, or partner with a licensed E-CSP or ICTA.

findings.claim: Nigeria has no dedicated national trust services authority yet. E-signature recognition is mostly evidentiary.
findings.evidence: The Evidence (Amendment) Act, signed on 12 June 2023, recognises digital signatures for authenticating electronic records, mainly for court purposes. TechCabal (18 November 2025) reports a bill that would let NITDA, the IT development agency, regulate and accredit e-signatures, and warns of fragmentation without an eIDAS-style authority. Whether the bill has been enacted was not confirmed.
findings.requirement: Track NITDA's accreditation regime and be ready to be accredited once it exists. Strong audit trails matter for admissibility in court.

findings.claim: South Africa requires an accredited advanced electronic signature (AES) wherever a law requires a signature without naming the type.
findings.evidence: Under ECTA (sections 13 and 37), an AES must come from a process accredited by the South African Accreditation Authority (SAAA). Where a law requires a signature and does not specify the type, only an AES satisfies it (CMS expert guide). LAWtrust has been accredited for AES since 2012 (ITWeb and the company).
findings.requirement: Obtain SAAA accreditation, or route signatures through an accredited provider such as LAWtrust.

findings.claim: Mexico's government signing runs on e.firma, the advanced signature certificate issued by the tax authority (SAT).
findings.evidence: SAT pages say e.firma is a digital certificate for remote procedures with government. Getting it the first time needs an in-person visit to SAT, it is valid for four years, and it can be renewed online. Secondary sources say it is used in over 400 procedures across 20 agencies, or under agreements with 120 public bodies. The figures conflict and have no clear date. DocuSign publishes a guide to signing in DocuSign with the SAT e.firma.
findings.requirement: Support signing with e.firma (.cer and .key files) and validate against SAT certificates.

findings.claim: Chile's state runs its own advanced-signature platform for public officials, FirmaGob.
findings.evidence: FirmaGob issues advanced electronic signatures (Law 19.799) to authorities and officials through firma.digital.gob.cl, with ClaveUnica login and an institutional 'ministro de fe' role. The Ministry of Finance (Hacienda) reported that over 80% of Chile's municipalities are enabled. The date of that report was not confirmed.
findings.requirement: Integrate the FirmaGob API and ClaveUnica, and respect the institution's 'ministro de fe' enrolment model.

findings.claim: Argentina's state built and runs its own remote signature platform (PFDR), with free certificates, inside its document management system (GDE).
findings.evidence: Decree 892/2017 created the Remote Digital Signature Platform (PFDR) and made its certificates free. Decree 182/2019 regulates Law 25.506 and sets remote signature as the method for any electronic document in GDE, including administrative acts. The certifier, AC MODERNIZACION-PFDR, operates at firmar.gob.ar.
findings.requirement: Integrate PFDR (firmar.gob.ar) and GDE, and accept free state-issued certificates.

findings.claim: Sovereign cloud gates line up with where DocuSign is strong and weak. It holds the US, Australian and German credentials. ISMAP (Japan), CSAP (Korea), SecNumCloud (France) and FedRAMP High were not found.
findings.evidence: DocuSign trust pages and posts claim: FedRAMP Moderate for eSignature and CLM, plus IAM in September 2025; DoD IL4 provisional authorisation (April 2021); IRAP PROTECTED (September 2021, re-assessed); BSI C5 Type II for eSignature; and Canada Protected-B maintained 'per department'. Searches found no DocuSign FedRAMP High, ISMAP, CSAP or SecNumCloud status. This is an absence of evidence, which needs checking on the official lists. DocuSign's data regions are the US, Canada, Europe, Australia and Japan.
findings.requirement: Plan for each jurisdiction's gate from day one: FedRAMP High or IL5, IRAP, a CCCS assessment, ISMAP, CSAP, SecNumCloud and C5, plus in-country hosting. In the EU this probably means hosting and operations run by an EU entity.

counter_evidence.claim: US federal: DocuSign holds the core security authorisations, and GSA struck a government-wide discount deal with it.
counter_evidence.evidence: DocuSign received FedRAMP Moderate in 2017, sponsored by the FCC (Route Fifty, August 2017). eSignature and CLM are listed on the FedRAMP Marketplace, and the IAM platform added FedRAMP Moderate on 15 September 2025. DISA granted a DoD IL4 provisional authorisation in April 2021. On 31 July 2025, GSA's OneGov deal gave federal agencies 70% off eSignature and 50% off IAM through 31 January 2027, bought through the GSA Multiple Award Schedule. The minimums are 50,000 envelopes or 300 seats.
counter_evidence.requirement: To compete in US federal: FedRAMP Moderate at minimum (High for sensitive workloads), DoD IL4 or IL5, a GSA Schedule listing and OneGov-style published discounts.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign says all 15 US cabinet departments and over 5,500 government agencies use it.
counter_evidence.evidence: This appears on DocuSign's federal and government pages (current 2025 to 2026) and in its OneGov blog post, which mentions use in HR, finance and legal. Carahsoft repeats it. No department is named, and no independent source confirms it.
counter_evidence.requirement: Publish named, verifiable government references. Buyers discount unsupported vendor claims.

counter_evidence.claim: US states and localities buy DocuSign widely through cooperative contracts.
counter_evidence.evidence: Carahsoft lists NASPO ValuePoint Cloud Solutions (AR2472) participating agreements for Alabama, Alaska, Colorado, Connecticut, Hawaii, Kansas, Louisiana, Minnesota, Oregon, Utah, Washington and others, most ending 16 September 2026 (renewal status unknown). Arkansas has a statewide contract. Wisconsin has an AR2472 addendum for agencies and universities. New York has umbrella contract PM68140. Maine holds master agreements for both Adobe Sign and DocuSign. The California Department of Technology signed an e-signature enterprise licence for 2024 to 2027 worth USD 1,891,305, and Orange County a contract of about USD 2.86 million. DocuSign reports GovRAMP authorisation for eSignature, IAM and CLM.
counter_evidence.requirement: Hold GovRAMP (formerly StateRAMP) and be listed on NASPO ValuePoint and state IT contracts.

counter_evidence.claim: UK central government bodies buy DocuSign directly, at modest scale.
counter_evidence.evidence: Contracts Finder notices show: DESNZ paying DocuSign UK GBP 56,717.10 for 17 July 2024 to 16 July 2027; a Department for Business and Trade subscription to 30 July 2026; National Audit Office licences for 2023 to 2026 and again for 2026 to 2031; a Homes England direct award (March 2025) running to 28 February 2029; UKRI licences under G-Cloud 13 (2024); a Crown Commercial Service award, CCSO24A06; and an NHS notice (2024) for 7,700 Business Pro envelopes. G-Cloud 14 lists DocuSign through resellers such as Node4 and Glemnet. These details come from search snippets of the notices, not full reads.
counter_evidence.requirement: List on G-Cloud directly, price for small departmental buys, and meet UK government security baselines.

counter_evidence.claim: Australia: DocuSign is IRAP PROTECTED and has whole-of-government arrangements in two large states. Federal spend is small.
counter_evidence.evidence: DocuSign completed its IRAP PROTECTED assessment in September 2021 (GovTechReview) and was later re-assessed. Queensland's standing offer arrangement SOA-TDS-1022 lets all departments and government-owned corporations opt in to the full DocuSign suite (iTnews). NSW has standing offer C8365 through FujiFilm and Amnesium. South Australia's Local Government Association has a DocuSign contract from 1 November 2021. A third-party aggregator puts federal spend at 10 contracts worth about AUD 539K since 2020, the largest buyer being the Future Fund, with about AUD 24K from the DTA. That figure is not checked against AusTender.
counter_evidence.requirement: Hold IRAP PROTECTED, keep data onshore in Australia, and win state standing-offer arrangements.

counter_evidence.claim: Ireland: a national agency tendered specifically for DocuSign, and the central procurement office planned a cloud e-signature buy.
counter_evidence.evidence: TED notice 435634-2026 from the National Transport Authority seeks the DocuSign IAM platform from DocuSign or an authorised reseller only. The Office of Government Procurement published a prior information notice (closing 26 April 2024) for a cloud e-signature solution to sign supplier frameworks and contracts, naming no vendor. No award was found.
counter_evidence.requirement: Be eligible under EU public procurement (TED) and supply EU-hosted eSignature with eIDAS AES and QES.

counter_evidence.claim: In the EU, DocuSign is itself a qualified trust service provider and plugs into national eIDs such as Belgium's itsme.
counter_evidence.evidence: DocuSign's trust brief says DocuSign France SAS is listed as a QTSP on the trusted list ANSSI manages. It says it provides QES, qualified timestamps, AES and advanced seals recognised in all Member States. DocuSign also markets itsme integration for Belgian QES. Both are vendor statements, and the trusted-list entry was not opened in this session.
counter_evidence.requirement: QTSP status, or a partnership with one, in at least one Member State, and integration with national eID and wallet schemes.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign was a launch partner of Singapore's national Sign with Singpass and supports national credentials in Latin America.
counter_evidence.evidence: GovTech's release of 4 November 2020 names DocuSign among the eight launch partners of Sign with Singpass, and DocuSign later offered free accounts for Singpass users (date not shown). DocuSign says it supports ICP-Brasil qualified signatures, enabled on request (2021 community post), and publishes how to sign with Mexico's SAT e.firma.
counter_evidence.requirement: Be a certified integration partner of each national signing scheme from its launch.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign claims government-grade credentials in Germany, Japan and Canada.
counter_evidence.evidence: DocuSign claims BSI C5 Type II for eSignature. On its Japanese blog, it says its 'EU Advanced' and 'Docusign Express' methods meet Article 2(1) of Japan's Electronic Signature Act and can be used for contracts with national and local public entities. It also claims Canada Protected-B status maintained per department. Since 2017 it has run a Canadian data region on Azure. All of this is vendor material with no independent confirmation found.
counter_evidence.requirement: Back each claimed authorisation with an entry on the official registry (BSI, the ISMAP list, CCCS reports).

research:adoption-facts.notes:
Method: I used WebSearch only. WebFetch failed for www.fedramp.gov and www.gsa.gov (the host did not resolve: outside this session's allowed network), so I stopped fetching. Every finding therefore rests on search-engine summaries of the cited pages, not on full reads. The FedRAMP Marketplace agency-reuse count, the Contracts Finder amounts, the AusTender totals and the EU Trusted List entry for DocuSign France all need a direct check. That requires allowing www.fedramp.gov, www.gsa.gov and the other primary hosts in the session's network settings.

Verdict: the premise is overstated for the US, where DocuSign is FedRAMP and IL4 authorised, on a government-wide OneGov discount, and reportedly in all 15 cabinet departments (vendor claim only), plus many states. It is partly true for the UK, Australia and Ireland, where use is real but departmental and small (contracts from tens of thousands of pounds, two Australian state whole-of-government deals). It is largely true for national signing infrastructure, and for the EU, Latin America and most of Asia and Africa. There, the state issues the signing credential (EUDI Wallet from end 2026, EU Sign, Estonia, Italy's 32.7M qualified certificates, Spain's Cl@ve and @firma, Brazil's 214M gov.br signatures in 2025, India's Aadhaar eSign and DigiLocker, Singpass, UAE PASS, JPKI, e.firma, FirmaGob, PFDR). The state often owns the sender-side workflow too (Singapore's Signify in 100+ agencies, Argentina's GDE, EU Sign) or buys domestic, locally certified vendors (Korea's Modusign with CSAP, Japan's CloudSign with ISMAP).

Pattern worth testing in the other angles: DocuSign wins where no state signing credential exists and its US-origin certifications count (US, UK, AU). It is weak where (a) a free state credential exists, (b) sovereign cloud gates apply that it does not appear to hold (ISMAP, CSAP, SecNumCloud, plus no FedRAMP High found), or (c) the state built its own tool. The CLOUD Act sovereignty concern (Microsoft France's Senate testimony, 10 June 2025) is context for (b), not proof about DocuSign. Absence-of-evidence points (no German or Canadian federal DocuSign award, no ISMAP, CSAP or SecNumCloud listing) are labelled as such and should be confirmed on the official registries. No em dashes are used.

research:sovereignty-security.angle: Sovereignty, security and procurement: why US-hosted e-signature SaaS (DocuSign) hits a ceiling with major governments, especially European central governments and sensitive or classified workloads, and what a signing product would need to get past it.

findings.claim: Any US-headquartered signing SaaS, DocuSign included, can be reached by US legal process for customer data stored anywhere in the world. This is the root objection of governments that care about sovereignty.
findings.evidence: The CLOUD Act was enacted on 23 March 2018 as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act 2018. It added 18 U.S.C. 2713, which makes a provider disclose data in its 'possession, custody, or control' whether the data sits inside or outside the United States. The DOJ white paper (April 2019) confirms the Act applies to US providers and can reach data held by a foreign subsidiary when the US entity controls that data. DocuSign, Inc. is a Delaware corporation headquartered in San Francisco (SEC filings), so its EU-hosted data still sits under a US parent. FISA Section 702 is a second route, on the intelligence side, and it is the basis of Schrems II (next finding).
sources: DOJ, 'Promoting Public Safety, Privacy, and the Rule of Law Around the World: The Purpose and Impact of the CLOUD Act', April 2019: https://www.justice.gov/opa/press-release/file/1153446/download
findings.requirement: Offer an operating entity and hosting that are legally domiciled, owned and controlled in the customer's jurisdiction, with no foreign parent that has 'control'. Alternatively, offer a self-hosted edition that the government runs itself. Use customer-held keys (an HSM or hold-your-own-key) so the operator cannot produce plaintext. Publish a legal opinion on extraterritorial exposure, plus a transparency report on government data requests.

findings.claim: Since Schrems II, EU public bodies that use a US processor must justify every transfer. The EDPB has said no technical measure works when the provider needs the data in the clear, which is how hosted e-signature normally works.
findings.evidence: CJEU judgment C-311/18 (16 July 2020) struck down the EU-US Privacy Shield because US surveillance (FISA 702, EO 12333) was not proportionate and gave no effective redress. Standard contractual clauses survive only with a case-by-case assessment and 'supplementary measures'. EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 (final version 2.0, 18 June 2021) address a cloud provider that needs data in the clear in the third country (its Use Case 6): the EDPB cannot see an effective technical measure for that case. A hosted signing service renders, hashes and stores the plaintext document, so it falls into this case. The EU-US Data Privacy Framework (Implementing Decision 2023/1795, 10 July 2023) restored a legal route, and the EU General Court dismissed the Latombe challenge (T-553/23) on 3 September 2025. An appeal to the Court of Justice followed. In January 2025 the US removed the Democratic members of the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board, which is part of the redress structure, and European privacy officers cite this as a weak point. The 2025 items are less firmly sourced than the judgment and the EDPB text.
sources: General Court case T-553/23 Latombe v Commission, judgment 3 September 2025: https://curia.europa.eu/juris/liste.jsf?num=T-553/23
findings.requirement: Process and support in the EU only: no remote access from outside the EU, including by any parent company. Render and hash documents in-region. Offer an end-to-end encrypted envelope mode in which documents are encrypted on the client and the operator only ever handles ciphertext and hashes. Ship a ready-made transfer impact assessment and DPIA pack so a public-sector DPO can approve without a custom legal review.

findings.claim: French law and doctrine require sensitive state data to sit on SecNumCloud-qualified clouds that are immune to non-EU law. A US-owned SaaS cannot meet the ownership rules by design.
findings.evidence: The Prime Minister's circular 6282/SG of 5 July 2021 ('Cloud au centre') made cloud the default for state IT. Its update, circular 6404/SG of 31 May 2023, kept the rule that data of particular sensitivity must go on the state's internal clouds or on a commercial cloud that ANSSI has qualified under SecNumCloud and that is protected against non-EU law. SecNumCloud version 3.2 (March 2022) added immunity criteria: the registered office and central administration must be in the EU, non-EU shareholders are capped at about 24 percent each and 39 percent combined, and no non-EU party may hold control. Law 2024-449 of 21 May 2024 (SREN), Article 31, turned the sensitive-data hosting obligation into statute for state administrations and some public operators.
findings.requirement: For France, either (a) host on a SecNumCloud-qualified IaaS through an operating company that itself meets the 3.2 ownership and control rules, ideally with its own qualification, or (b) ship self-hosted software that can run on the state's internal clouds.

findings.claim: French ministries have actively barred US collaboration SaaS on sovereignty grounds. In 2025 a US vendor admitted under oath that it could not guarantee French data would not reach US authorities.
findings.evidence: In September 2021 DINUM told ministries that Microsoft 365 did not fit the Cloud au centre doctrine and should not be newly rolled out (French trade press). In November 2022 the Education ministry replied to a written question from MP Philippe Latombe that the free Microsoft and Google offers for schools were not compliant. On 10 June 2025, at the French Senate's commission of inquiry on public procurement, Microsoft France's director of public and legal affairs (Anton Carniaux) said under oath that he could not guarantee French public data would never be handed to US authorities without French consent. The same reasoning applies to any US SaaS processor, e-signature included. I could not re-check the exact URLs in this session.
sources: French Senate, commission d'enquete on public procurement (commande publique), hearing of 10 June 2025: https://www.senat.fr
Public Senat coverage of the 10 June 2025 hearing: https://www.publicsenat.fr
Assemblee nationale written question by Philippe Latombe and the Education ministry reply, 2022: https://questions.assemblee-nationale.fr
findings.requirement: Be able to give the guarantee Microsoft could not, and back it in the contract: no legal path for a foreign authority to compel disclosure, a duty to notify the customer and challenge any request, and termination rights plus penalties if this is breached.

findings.claim: Germany requires C5 attestations for external cloud and is building its own open-source administrative stack (openDesk, Deutschland-Stack). A signing product has to fit into that stack.
findings.evidence: BSI's C5 catalogue (Cloud Computing Compliance Criteria Catalogue, current edition C5:2020, revision under way in 2025) is the reference for federal use of external cloud services, and the BSI minimum standard for those services expects a C5 attestation. The Federal Interior Ministry set up ZenDiS (Centre for Digital Sovereignty of Public Administration) in 2022. ZenDiS released openDesk 1.0 in October 2024, an open-source workplace built from Nextcloud, Open-Xchange, Collabora, Element/Matrix, Jitsi, OpenProject, XWiki and Univention. The CDU/CSU-SPD coalition agreement of April 2025 commits to a 'Deutschland-Stack' of interoperable, open and sovereign components for public administration, now run by the new Federal Ministry for Digital and State Modernisation (May 2025). As far as I know openDesk has no signing-workflow module (weak, needs checking).
sources: Coalition agreement 'Verantwortung fuer Deutschland', April 2025: https://www.koalitionsvertrag2025.de/
findings.requirement: Obtain a C5 Type 2 attestation. Release under an open-source licence (EUPL or AGPL) and publish on openCode.de. Deploy with Kubernetes/Helm the way openDesk does. Provide a Nextcloud app and an Open-Xchange integration. Support the German eID card and German QTSPs such as D-Trust (Bundesdruckerei) for qualified signatures.

findings.claim: Since 2024, European public bodies have started removing US software at scale. They are a ready market for a sovereign signing tool, but they will not accept a US-hosted SaaS.
findings.evidence: In April 2024 Schleswig-Holstein's cabinet decided to move about 30,000 state workstations from Microsoft Office to LibreOffice, and then to Linux and Open-Xchange/Thunderbird. In 2025 it reported the mail migration largely complete. In June 2025 Denmark's Minister for Digitalisation, Caroline Stage Olsen, told Politiken that her ministry would move from Microsoft Office to LibreOffice and from Windows to Linux; Copenhagen and Aarhus municipalities also reviewed their Microsoft use. In June 2025 the City of Lyon announced a move to OnlyOffice and Linux. In September 2025 the Austrian Armed Forces said about 16,000 workstations had moved to LibreOffice. In October 2025 the ICC (The Hague) was reported to be moving to openDesk. These are press reports that I could not re-check in this session.
sources: Schleswig-Holstein state government, digital sovereignty pages and press releases (April 2024, 2025): https://www.schleswig-holstein.de
Danish Ministry of Digitalisation: https://digmin.dk/ and Politiken interview, June 2025: https://politiken.dk
Ville de Lyon announcement, June 2025: https://www.lyon.fr
findings.requirement: Work fully on Linux desktops and open-source office suites: accept ODF (ISO/IEC 26300) and PDF/A, with no Windows or Microsoft 365 dependency. Provide plug-ins for Nextcloud, Open-Xchange, Thunderbird and LibreOffice. Keep the core open source so a migrating authority is not just swapping one US dependency for another.

findings.claim: US sanctions law lets Washington force a US vendor to cut off a foreign public body. The 2025 ICC episode turned this 'kill switch' risk into a concrete procurement criterion in Europe.
findings.evidence: Executive Order 14203 (6 February 2025) imposed US sanctions on the International Criminal Court. On 15 May 2025 AP reported that Prosecutor Karim Khan had lost access to his Microsoft email after the sanctions. Microsoft later said it had not suspended services to the ICC as a whole. In October 2025 German press (Handelsblatt) reported that the ICC would move to openDesk. DocuSign's terms require compliance with US export controls and sanctions, so a US e-signature vendor can be legally required to drop a foreign public customer or signer.
sources: Executive Order 14203, 6 February 2025, Federal Register: https://www.federalregister.gov
AP News, 15 May 2025, on the ICC sanctions halting the court's work: https://apnews.com
Handelsblatt, October 2025, ICC moving to openDesk: https://www.handelsblatt.com
findings.requirement: Provide continuity that no single foreign government can switch off. That means a self-hostable edition with source escrow, and signed documents that validate offline with standard tools, without depending on servers or revocation endpoints only the vendor controls. Termination clauses should be governed only by the customer's own law.

findings.claim: The EU has not settled sovereignty in a single cloud certificate, so national schemes decide purchases. The European Commission now scores sovereignty in its own cloud procurement.
findings.evidence: ENISA first published the EUCS candidate scheme under the Cybersecurity Act (Regulation 2019/881) in December 2020. The 2022 and 2023 drafts had 'High+' criteria for immunity from non-EU law, pushed by France and others. Those criteria were dropped from the 2024 drafts after opposition from several member states and US industry, and the scheme had still not been adopted as of my latest information. In October 2025 the Commission published a Cloud Sovereignty Framework with graded sovereignty assurance levels for its own cloud tender (weak, not verified in this session).
sources: European Commission DG DIGIT Cloud Sovereignty Framework, October 2025: https://commission.europa.eu
findings.requirement: Build to the strictest national scheme (SecNumCloud, C5, ENS High, ACN) rather than waiting for EUCS. Document ownership, supply chain, sub-processors, staff locations and key custody in a format that maps onto both the EUCS levels and the Commission's sovereignty criteria.

findings.claim: The data protection regulator for the EU institutions has held a US SaaS deployment unlawful. That decision sets the contractual bar any processor, signing included, must clear.
findings.evidence: On 8 March 2024 the EDPS found that the European Commission's use of Microsoft 365 broke Regulation 2018/1725: purposes were not specified well enough and transfers outside the EEA lacked adequate safeguards. It ordered corrective measures by 9 December 2024. In July 2025 the EDPS closed the case after the Commission and Microsoft changed the contract terms.
findings.requirement: Offer a public-sector DPA that lists purposes exhaustively and bans secondary use of documents and metadata by the vendor (analytics, product improvement, AI training). It should name every sub-processor and its location and grant the controller audit rights.

findings.claim: Using signed documents to train AI is a trust flashpoint for public buyers, and DocuSign has faced criticism over it.
findings.evidence: In February 2024 DocuSign published FAQs on using customer data, with contractual consent, to train its AI models. This drew public criticism and prompted clarifications that only data from customers who agreed is used. This is from tech-press coverage that I could not re-check in this session.
sources: DocuSign trust center, AI and data use pages (not reachable this session): https://www.docusign.com/trust
Tech press coverage, February 2024 (specific article not re-verified)
findings.requirement: Guarantee in the contract and in the technical design that no document, field value or signer data trains any model. Any AI assistant should run on a self-hosted open-weight model inside the customer's boundary, with logs under customer control.

findings.claim: The US federal market requires FedRAMP (Moderate, or High for high-impact data), DoD Impact Levels for defence, FIPS 140-3 cryptography, and increasingly GovRAMP for states. Together these are a multi-year barrier to entry.
findings.evidence: The FedRAMP Authorization Act (Section 5921 of the FY2023 NDAA, signed 23 December 2022) put FedRAMP into law. Rev 5 baselines: Low, Moderate (about 323 controls) and High (about 410 controls). High applies to law-enforcement, emergency-services, financial and health systems. FedRAMP 20x, announced in March 2025, aims to speed up authorizations. The DoD Cloud Computing SRG defines IL2, IL4 (controlled unclassified information), IL5 (more sensitive CUI and national security systems, with separation from non-government tenants) and IL6 (classified). Federal systems must use FIPS 140-3 validated cryptography. StateRAMP, used by many states, rebranded as GovRAMP in 2025. DocuSign markets a FedRAMP Moderate authorized eSignature environment and claims DoD IL4. I could not check FedRAMP High or IL5 status because both the FedRAMP Marketplace and docusign.com were unreachable.
sources: DoD Cloud Computing Security Requirements Guide: https://public.cyber.mil/dccs/
findings.requirement: FedRAMP Moderate is the minimum for selling to US agencies, and High is needed for high-impact data. Offer IL4/IL5 on a US government region (GovCloud type) with operations by US persons only, use FIPS 140-3 modules, and get GovRAMP for states. A realistic path for a startup is a reseller or platform partnership, or the FedRAMP 20x track, because a full authorization takes years.

findings.claim: Australia requires IRAP assessment at PROTECTED, and for sensitive whole-of-government data it also requires hosting certification that can impose ownership and control conditions.
findings.evidence: ASD's IRAP program assesses services against the Information Security Manual, and PROTECTED is the usual bar for agency data. The DTA's Hosting Certification Framework (from 2021) adds 'Certified Strategic' and 'Certified Assured' levels, which let government impose ownership and control conditions on providers that host sensitive whole-of-government data.
findings.requirement: Obtain an IRAP assessment at PROTECTED. Host only in Australia with a Certified Strategic or Certified Assured provider, and accept government ownership and control conditions.

findings.claim: Canada treats in-Canada hosting as the main delivery option for Protected B data and expects a CCCS assessment against the PBMM profile.
findings.evidence: Section 4.4.3.14 of the Treasury Board Policy on Service and Digital says computing facilities inside Canada must be identified and evaluated as the principal delivery option for sensitive data classed Protected B, Protected C or Classified. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security assesses cloud providers against the Protected B, Medium Integrity, Medium Availability (PBMM) profile under ITSM.50.100.
