findings.requirement: Run a Canadian region, obtain a CCCS assessment against PBMM, map controls to ITSG-33, and offer support by Canadian staff.

findings.claim: Spain, Japan, Italy and the UK each run a mandatory or near-mandatory national scheme. A government product needs a country-by-country certification roadmap, not a single global certificate.
findings.evidence: Spain: Royal Decree 311/2022 of 3 May 2022 (Esquema Nacional de Seguridad) binds the public sector and its private suppliers, with BASIC, MEDIUM and HIGH categories and certification by accredited bodies under CCN rules. Japan: ISMAP began in June 2020, and agencies are expected in principle to buy cloud services from the ISMAP register. Italy: public bodies must use cloud services qualified by the National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN), with levels QC1 to QC4 tied to how the data is classified (ordinary, critical, strategic). United Kingdom: cloud is bought through the Crown Commercial Service G-Cloud framework (G-Cloud 14, RM1557.14, from November 2024) and judged against the NCSC Cloud Security Principles. Central government contracts that handle personal data require Cyber Essentials (Plus).
findings.requirement: Publish a certification roadmap that adds, by target market: ENS HIGH (Spain), ISMAP registration (Japan), ACN QC2 or higher (Italy), a G-Cloud listing plus Cyber Essentials Plus (UK), C5 (Germany), IRAP (Australia), CCCS (Canada), and FedRAMP or GovRAMP (US). Each one needs in-country hosting.

findings.claim: ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type II are table stakes rather than differentiators. ISO 27701 and the cloud extensions are increasingly scored in tenders.
findings.evidence: Public tenders in all the jurisdictions above ask for ISO/IEC 27001, now the 2022 edition (certificates under the 2013 edition had to transition by 31 October 2025), and usually a SOC 2 Type II report. ISO/IEC 27701 (privacy) and ISO/IEC 27017/27018 (cloud) earn extra points more and more often. Trust service providers under eIDAS are assessed against ETSI EN 319 401 and EN 319 411. DocuSign advertises ISO 27001 and SOC 1 and SOC 2 Type II reports (see counter-evidence).
sources: DocuSign compliance page (unreachable this session): https://www.docusign.com/trust/compliance
findings.requirement: Hold ISO 27001:2022 plus 27017, 27018 and 27701 certificates, and a SOC 2 Type II report covering security, availability, confidentiality and processing integrity. Add ETSI EN 319 401/411 conformity if the company acts as a trust service provider itself.

findings.claim: Under eIDAS 2, European governments will own the signing trust anchor through free wallet-based qualified signatures. Platforms must consume national identity and signature infrastructure, not replace it.
findings.evidence: Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 (eIDAS 2) entered into force on 20 May 2024. Every member state must provide a European Digital Identity Wallet: implementing acts were adopted from November 2024, and wallets are due by the end of 2026. Each wallet must let natural persons create qualified electronic signatures free of charge for non-professional purposes. A qualified signature is valid because it comes from a QTSP on a national Trusted List (aggregated in the EU list browser). The Commission maintains the open-source DSS library for creating and validating AdES signatures.
findings.requirement: Accept signatures from EUDI wallets and national eIDs. Produce and validate PAdES, XAdES, CAdES and ASiC at B-LTA level using DSS against the EU Trusted Lists. Partner with, or become, a QTSP for qualified signatures and qualified seals. Support remote QSCD signing through the Cloud Signature Consortium API.

findings.claim: Many governments already sign internally with state PKI (US PIV/CAC cards, India's licensed eSign), which weakens the case for a third-party SaaS.
findings.evidence: HSPD-12 (27 August 2004) and FIPS 201-3 (January 2022) give every federal employee and contractor a PIV card carrying a digital-signature key under the Federal PKI. DoD's CAC works the same way, and agencies sign PDFs natively with these cards. India's IT Act 2000 recognises signatures only from CAs licensed by the Controller of Certifying Authorities. Its Aadhaar-based eSign service, run through licensed eSign Service Providers, covers citizen signing.
findings.requirement: Make PIV/CAC and national smart-card or mobile eID signing first-class methods (PKCS#11, Web eID, CSC API). Get in-country licensing or empanelment wherever the law requires licensed CAs, such as India's CCA.

findings.claim: DocuSign had a 2017 breach of a non-core system, and the stolen email list fuelled DocuSign-branded malware phishing.
findings.evidence: In mid-May 2017 DocuSign disclosed that a malicious third party had gained temporary access to a separate, non-core system used for service announcements. The attacker took a list of customer email addresses and used it for phishing emails, branded as DocuSign, that delivered malware. KrebsOnSecurity reported it on 16 May 2017.
sources: DocuSign trust alerts page (unreachable this session): https://www.docusign.com/trust
findings.requirement: Keep notification and contact systems separate from core data. Enforce DMARC p=reject with BIMI. Publish the incident history on a public trust page. Commit to incident notification timelines at least as strict as NIS2 (early warning within 24 hours, notification within 72 hours).

findings.claim: Attackers have abused DocuSign's own API to send authentic-looking fraudulent envelopes. Filters struggle with these because they come from DocuSign itself.
findings.evidence: In November 2024 Wallarm, reported by BleepingComputer, described attackers using paid DocuSign accounts and the Envelopes API to send large volumes of fake invoices. The invoices impersonated well-known brands such as Norton and PayPal. The messages leave DocuSign's own infrastructure, so they pass SPF and DKIM checks and look genuine. Users posted many complaints on DocuSign's community forums at the time.
findings.requirement: Run know-your-business checks before allowing API sending. Show recipients the sender's verified domain. Apply per-tenant rate limits and anomaly detection to bulk sends. Put a one-click 'report this envelope' button in every email. Add a verified government sender mark tied to official domains (.gov, .gouv.fr, .bund.de).

findings.claim: DocuSign's brand is closely tied to phishing, which is a reputational liability when a government sends documents to citizens.
findings.evidence: DocuSign is still one of the most impersonated brands in phishing. Its own guidance tells users to forward suspicious emails to spam@docusign.com and to open documents by typing the security code at docusign.com instead of clicking links. In 2025 security vendors reported campaigns that used genuine DocuSign envelopes, posing as state and municipal procurement offices, to steal contractors' credentials. I could not re-check the specific 2025 reports in this session.
sources: DocuSign phishing guidance (unreachable this session): https://www.docusign.com/trust/alerts
Check Point Research quarterly brand phishing reports: https://research.checkpoint.com
findings.requirement: Let citizens sign inside an authenticated government portal or app instead of through email links. Show a verified government sender identity, and offer access codes and out-of-band verification. Brand emails with the government's identity rather than the vendor's.

findings.claim: DocuSign is cloud-only, but classified and some critical government networks need on-premises or air-gapped signing.
findings.evidence: DocuSign eSignature is delivered as multi-tenant SaaS, its government environment included. DocuSign used to sell an on-premises Signature Appliance, from its 2015 ARX acquisition, but that line has been retired (weak, not re-checked). Classified and some critical national networks require on-premises or air-gapped deployment: DoD IL6/SECRET, France's Diffusion Restreinte systems, Germany's VS-NfD systems, and defence ministries generally. Competing vendors such as OneSpan Sign and Ascertia SigningHub, and open-source projects such as DocuSeal, Documenso and LibreSign (a Nextcloud app), can be self-hosted.
findings.requirement: Provide a fully offline edition: one container image or Helm chart, no telemetry or licence call-home, and signed offline update bundles. Support PKCS#11 HSMs (FIPS 140-3 or Common Criteria EN 419 221-5), offer a local time-stamping authority, and document support for accreditation on national classified networks.

findings.claim: Lock-in and decades-long records duties work against proprietary signing platforms, and EU law now requires switching to be easy.
findings.evidence: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 (the Data Act) has applied since 12 September 2025. It requires data processing service providers to support switching and to export data in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format, and it phases out switching charges by 12 January 2027. Government records laws (the US Federal Records Act and NARA's rules at 36 CFR Part 1236, plus EU national archive laws) require signed records to stay valid and readable for decades. That fails if checking a signature depends on a vendor's proprietary audit trail or on its live service.
findings.requirement: Offer one-click export of every envelope as PDF/A-3 with the audit trail embedded and PAdES-LTA signatures. Provide open APIs and webhooks, migration tools from DocuSign, an open-source core with escrow, and pricing that does not lock customers in per envelope.

findings.claim: The Dutch parliament has formally told the government to cut its dependence on US cloud, and Dutch procurement already uses DPIA-driven contract renegotiation and comply-or-explain open standards.
findings.evidence: In March 2025 the Tweede Kamer adopted a set of motions, led by Barbara Kathmann (GL-PvdA), asking the government to reduce dependence on US cloud providers, build sovereign cloud capacity and draw up exit strategies. Since 2018 the central government's strategic vendor management office (SLM Rijk) has run DPIAs on Microsoft, Google and Zoom that forced contract changes. Dutch public bodies must also follow the Forum Standaardisatie 'comply or explain' list of open standards, which includes PDF/A and ODF.
findings.requirement: Supply a ready DPIA input pack and a written exit strategy. Offer hosting in the Netherlands or the EU under EU ownership. Conform to the Dutch open-standards list (PDF/A, ODF and others).

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign is authorized for, and used by, the US federal government. The premise is weakest in the United States.
counter_evidence.evidence: DocuSign markets a FedRAMP-authorized eSignature environment (Moderate) for US agencies and sells to the public sector through Carahsoft and GSA schedule contracts. Its trust center lists FedRAMP among its authorizations and also claims DoD IL4. I could not re-check the exact current level (Moderate or High) or the IL status this session, because the FedRAMP Marketplace and docusign.com were blocked.
counter_evidence.requirement: To compete in the US, match at least FedRAMP Moderate and be buyable on GSA MAS through a reseller.

counter_evidence.claim: US states and local governments widely buy DocuSign through cooperative contracts.
counter_evidence.evidence: DocuSign is available to states and localities through cooperative contracts, for example NASPO ValuePoint cloud solutions via resellers. State agencies and municipalities commonly use it for permits, HR and procurement. DocuSign claims a StateRAMP/GovRAMP listing, which I did not verify this session.
counter_evidence.requirement: Hold a GovRAMP listing and get onto cooperative purchasing vehicles (NASPO ValuePoint, state IT schedules) through a public-sector reseller.

counter_evidence.claim: UK public bodies can buy DocuSign directly through the G-Cloud framework.
counter_evidence.evidence: DocuSign services appear on the Crown Commercial Service G-Cloud framework (Digital Marketplace), through DocuSign UK and resellers, and councils and NHS bodies buy through it. DocuSign serves UK and EU customers from European data centres.
counter_evidence.requirement: Get listed on G-Cloud and meet the NCSC Cloud Security Principles and Cyber Essentials Plus.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign has an Australian presence aimed at government buyers.
counter_evidence.evidence: DocuSign opened Australian data centres around 2018. It says its Australian service has been IRAP assessed, and federal and state agencies use it. None of this was re-checked this session.
counter_evidence.requirement: Match with an IRAP PROTECTED assessment and hosting in Australia.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign can legally deliver EU qualified signatures and has EU data-protection mechanisms. In Europe the barrier is jurisdiction and ownership, not legal validity.
counter_evidence.evidence: DocuSign France (formerly OpenTrust, acquired in 2015) is a Qualified Trust Service Provider on the EU Trusted List. DocuSign sells EU Advanced and EU Qualified signatures, runs EU data centres, and has Binding Corporate Rules approved by EU data protection authorities.
counter_evidence.requirement: A competitor must match QES and qualified-seal capability through a QTSP, and match EU hosting, before sovereignty becomes the deciding factor.

counter_evidence.claim: EU bodies still have a lawful route for transfers to certified US companies, so US SaaS is not barred outright.
counter_evidence.evidence: The EU-US Data Privacy Framework adequacy decision (Implementing Decision 2023/1795, 10 July 2023) gives a legal basis for transfers to DPF-certified US companies. The EU General Court upheld it on 3 September 2025 (Latombe, T-553/23), though an appeal is pending.
counter_evidence.requirement: Sovereignty is only a decisive edge for sensitive data and for buyers bound by doctrine (France, Germany's sovereign stack, defence). Elsewhere the product must also win on price, user experience and integrations.

counter_evidence.claim: Even France's doctrine restricts US SaaS only for sensitive data, so many non-sensitive government signing uses remain open to DocuSign.
counter_evidence.evidence: The Cloud au centre circulars (5 July 2021, updated 31 May 2023) and SREN Article 31 (21 May 2024) apply the SecNumCloud and immunity requirement to data of particular sensitivity. Other state data may use commercial cloud.
counter_evidence.requirement: Position sovereignty for sensitive and regulated workflows, and stay competitive on features for the much larger non-sensitive volume.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign's scale suggests that 'not widely adopted by governments' is overstated as a general statement. The gap is concentrated in specific segments.
counter_evidence.evidence: DocuSign reports more than 1.5 million customers and names the public sector as a core vertical in its annual reports. The sovereignty barriers above apply mainly to EU central governments, sensitive and classified data, and citizen-facing services in countries with national eID. They do not apply to government use as a whole. This is an inference, not a measured share of government adoption.
counter_evidence.requirement: Target the segments where DocuSign is structurally blocked (EU central and federal-state governments, defence, sensitive data, eID-based citizen services) instead of trying to displace it head-on in US civilian agencies.

WebFetch failed for www.docusign.com, curia.europa.eu and marketplace.fedramp.gov because those hosts are outside this session's allowed network domains. To re-verify, someone has to allow those hosts (and ideally the rest cited above) in the session network settings, or run a follow-up with fresh search budget.

All findings above come from model knowledge (cutoff mid-2026). The URLs are the primary sources as I know them, but none was opened this session, and some are given at domain level where I was unsure of the exact path. I rated strength conservatively. 'Strong' is used only where the cited source is a statute, a court judgment or an official framework I am confident of.

Check these first before anything is published:
1. DocuSign's current FedRAMP level (Moderate or High) and DoD IL4/IL5 status, on the FedRAMP Marketplace and the DocuSign trust center.
2. Whether DocuSign is listed or certified under GovRAMP, IRAP, ENS, ISMAP, C5 and CCCS.
3. The June 2025 Microsoft France Senate testimony.
4. The ICC move to openDesk (October 2025).
5. The 2025 migrations in Denmark, Lyon and the Austrian Armed Forces.
6. The status of the October 2025 Commission Cloud Sovereignty Framework.
7. The February 2024 DocuSign AI-training controversy.

Synthesis (why DocuSign stalls with major governments, from this angle):
(a) A US parent means CLOUD Act, FISA 702 and sanctions exposure, which conflicts with Schrems II, Cloud au centre, SecNumCloud 3.2 and SREN, and the post-2025 European sovereignty push.
(b) Every country runs its own mandatory certification and hosting scheme, which multiplies cost.
(c) DocuSign is SaaS only, with no supported on-prem or air-gapped edition for classified networks.
(d) Governments increasingly own the signing trust anchor themselves (PIV/CAC, national eIDs, eIDAS 2 wallets with free QES, India eSign), so they need platforms that consume their PKI rather than replace it.
(e) The DocuSign brand is heavily abused for phishing, which is a liability for messages sent to citizens.
(f) Lock-in and records-retention duties, now backed by the EU Data Act's switching rules.

Reverse-engineered product shape: an open-source, self-hostable core (EUPL or AGPL), operated in each region by a locally owned entity; client-side encrypted envelopes with customer-held keys; standards-only signatures (PAdES, XAdES, CAdES, ASiC at LTA level, validated with EU DSS against the Trusted Lists); plug-ins for national eIDs, EUDI wallets and PIV/CAC; a QTSP partnership; a certification roadmap ordered by target market (ISO 27001/27701 and SOC 2 first, then C5, ENS, SecNumCloud hosting, IRAP, CCCS, FedRAMP via a partner); verified government sender identity plus API abuse controls; full export and migration tools; and any AI assistant running on a self-hosted open-weight model with a contractual ban on training.

Speculative, outside this angle: public buyers may scrutinise the tree-planting incentive and any crypto-token mechanism ($MGRO) under procurement, gifts and green-claims rules. Keeping the planting verifiable, optional and separate from the signed legal record would likely reduce that friction.

research:cost-procurement.angle: Money and buying: DocuSign pricing and licence model at government scale, price rises, procurement rules that favour reuse and open source (EU Interoperable Europe Act, France, Germany, Italy CAD 68 and 69, Spain, Switzerland, Netherlands, UK TCoP, US M-16-21 and SHARE IT Act, India), the DPG standard and GovStack, total cost of ownership and exit costs, and complaints.

findings.claim: DocuSign charges per user seat with a capped envelope allowance, so cost grows with every civil servant who sends and every document sent. That is a poor fit for national services with millions of citizens and thousands of occasional senders.
findings.evidence: From memory of DocuSign's public price pages for 2024 and 2025 (not reopened this session): Standard about USD 25 and Business Pro about USD 40 per user per month billed annually (about 45 and 65 billed monthly). Annual plans include about 100 envelopes per user per year. API plans: Starter about USD 50 a month for 40 envelopes a month, Intermediate about USD 300 a month for 100, Advanced about USD 480 a month for 100, Enterprise negotiated. That puts list prices at about USD 1.25 to 4.80 per envelope. Search excerpts gathered on 2026-11-20 by an earlier agent in this workflow (competitor blogs verdocs.com and meetergo.com, pages not opened) say every sent envelope counts even if never signed, and that Bulk Send and PowerForms count against the allowance.
findings.requirement: Price a government tier per deployment, not per seat or per envelope: free to self-host, with optional support or hosting for a fixed annual fee. Allow unlimited senders and envelopes. Never count unsigned envelopes, bulk sends to citizens or visits to a public form as billable units.

findings.claim: At list per-envelope prices, citizen-facing volumes would cost tens of millions of dollars a year, and overage billing makes costs unpredictable. Governments that run their own signing pay close to nothing per signature.
findings.evidence: My own arithmetic, so weak: 10 million envelopes a year at USD 1.25 to 4.80 list comes to USD 12.5M to 48M a year. Negotiated enterprise prices are confidential and probably lower. Overage evidence from private customers: in a BBB complaint, DocuSign's response said 166 envelopes over the 100-a-year allowance were billed USD 962.80 (about USD 5.80 each) and are not refundable. A Trustpilot reviewer says each click on a public signing link created a billable envelope even when unsigned, for about USD 2,074.70 in overage. Both were collected in this workflow's complaints research on 2026-11-20.
findings.requirement: Publish a total-cost-of-ownership calculator for 1M, 10M and 100M signatures a year: hosting, support and staff, with zero licence cost per signature. Have no overage mechanism at all in the government tier.

findings.claim: Private customers report steep, hard-to-predict price rises at renewal and newly enforced allowances. Public buyers on fixed, multi-year budgets cannot absorb rises like these. I found no complaint by a public body itself, because search was unavailable.
findings.evidence: TrustRadius review of 2021-01-27: yearly cost went from about USD 480 to about USD 9,000 as usage and API use grew. DocuSign community post: a long-time customer's fee moved from USD 45 to 90 a month without consent. BBB: DocuSign said the 100-a-year limit on a Realtor plan has been enforced since 2024. Trustpilot: a renewal more than 20 percent above the amount in the notice. All of these are private or small-business customers.
findings.requirement: Public-sector contract terms with a capped annual rise (for example CPI), at least 90 days' notice, no renewal at a new price without explicit written acceptance, and a public price list for public buyers.

findings.claim: Italian law makes a comparative technical and economic evaluation mandatory before any software purchase. Proprietary licences are allowed only when reuse of existing public-administration software and free or open-source software have been shown, with reasons, to be unsuitable.
findings.evidence: Codice dell'Amministrazione Digitale (d.lgs. 82/2005), article 68 as amended in 2016 and 2017. Comma 1 lists the options in order: software developed in-house, reuse of another administration's software, free or open-source software, cloud services, proprietary licence, or a combination. Comma 1-bis sets the evaluation criteria: total cost (purchase, implementation, maintenance, support); use of open data formats, open interfaces and interoperability standards; and supplier guarantees on security, data protection and service levels. Comma 1-ter permits a proprietary licence only where the evaluation shows, with reasons, that no suitable reusable or open-source solution exists. AgID's guidelines on acquiring and reusing software (2019) put this into practice.
findings.requirement: Be eligible as free or open-source software (an OSI-approved licence) and as reusable public-administration software, by being listed in the Developers Italia catalogue. Ship evidence for the 1-bis criteria: a TCO sheet, open formats and APIs, and security and data-protection documentation.

findings.claim: Italy also requires administrations to own the code they commission and to publish it for reuse, which favours products other administrations can take for free.
findings.evidence: CAD article 69 (as amended in 2016 and 2017): administrations that own software developed for them must make the source code and documentation available under an open licence in public repositories. Contracts for developing software must give the administration ownership of the code. The 2019 AgID guidelines name Developers Italia as the catalogue to use.
findings.requirement: Allow customisations and integrations paid for by an administration to be published back under the same open licence, with no rights reserved that would stop another administration reusing them.

findings.claim: Before buying or building any application, Spanish administrations must check a state reuse directory and justify any purchase when a reusable solution exists. The state already gives away its own open-source signing tools.
findings.evidence: Ley 40/2015 of 1 October 2015 (Régimen Jurídico del Sector Público), article 157: administrations must make applications they own available for reuse by others. Article 157.3: before acquiring, developing or maintaining an application, they must consult the general directory of applications for reusable solutions and justify not reusing one on efficiency grounds. Article 158 covers technology transfer and the directory, run through the Centro de Transferencia de Tecnología (CTT). The state's signing client AutoFirma (Cliente @firma) is published open source on the CTT and on GitHub under GPL-2.0 or EUPL-1.1, and the @firma validation platform is offered to administrations.
findings.requirement: Be listed in the CTT and interoperate with AutoFirma and @firma: accept signatures made with AutoFirma, produce output that @firma can validate, and use Cl@ve or a national eID for identity.

findings.claim: Under the EU Interoperable Europe Act, public bodies must share the interoperability solutions behind their digital public services, including source code, with other public bodies that ask. A solution the authority does not own cannot be passed on, while an open-source one can.
findings.evidence: Regulation (EU) 2024/903 of 13 March 2024, in force since 11 April 2024. Article 4: a public sector body or Union entity must make interoperability solutions that support its electronic public services available to any other such body that requests them, including technical documentation and, where applicable, documented source code. Exceptions cover third-party intellectual property, security and similar grounds. Sharing can be done through the Interoperable Europe portal. Article 3: interoperability assessments for trans-European digital public services are mandatory from 12 January 2025. The recitals promote open-source licensing.
findings.requirement: Use an open licence (EUPL-1.2 or a compatible one such as AGPL-3.0) so a deploying body can meet Article 4 by sharing it. Publish on the Interoperable Europe portal and code.europa.eu. Provide the documentation an interoperability assessment needs.

findings.claim: In the EU, exit costs are now regulated: cloud and SaaS providers must allow switching and data export, and switching charges disappear in 2027. Vendor lock-in through stored agreements and evidence becomes a legal issue, not only a cost.
findings.evidence: EU Data Act, Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 of 13 December 2023. Chapter VI on switching between data processing services, which covers SaaS, applies from 12 September 2025. Providers must allow switching with at most two months' notice and a transition period of normally 30 days, and must export customer data and digital assets. Article 29: switching charges are limited to cost until 12 January 2027 and banned after that date.
findings.requirement: Offer one-step full export at no charge: original and signed PDFs (PDF/A, PAdES), audit trails and evidence in an open JSON schema, templates, contacts and settings. Document an exit plan, and keep evidence verifiable without the vendor's servers.

findings.claim: The European Commission funds and publishes free, open-source signing building blocks, so the technical core of e-signature costs nothing in Europe and DocuSign has to justify its price on top of it.
findings.evidence: The Commission's Digital Signature Service (DSS) is an open-source Java library (LGPL-2.1) for creating and validating XAdES, CAdES, PAdES and ASiC signatures against EU trusted lists. It was funded as a CEF eSignature building block and now under Digital Europe. Commission Open Source Software Strategy 2020 to 2023 ('Think Open'), C(2020) 7149, adopted 21 October 2020.
findings.requirement: Produce standard AdES signatures that EU DSS validates (PAdES baseline B, T, LT and LTA), or build on DSS directly. Price only the work that DSS does not do: workflow, user experience, hosting and support.

findings.claim: Several governments already give signing to citizens free, as public infrastructure, so a per-envelope product competes with a free public service.
findings.evidence: Estonia: the DigiDoc4 signing client and libraries are open source (LGPL) under github.com/open-eid, and signing with the national ID card is free. e-Estonia, the government's promotional site, claims digital signatures save about 2% of GDP a year, a claim not independently checked. Brazil: gov.br offers a free electronic signature to citizens with silver or gold gov.br accounts, an advanced signature under Lei 14.063 of 23 September 2020.
findings.requirement: Let signers sign with national eIDs and wallets (Estonian ID, Smart-ID or Mobile-ID, gov.br, the EUDI wallet) at no cost to the signer. Fit as the workflow layer on top of the state's free signature, not as a replacement that costs per signature.

findings.claim: The UK Technology Code of Practice tells government teams to publish code and consider open source, use open standards, plan purchases to avoid lock-in, and weigh total cost.
findings.evidence: Technology Code of Practice (GOV.UK, first published 2016 and revised since). Point 3, 'Be open and use open source': publish code and use open source for transparency, flexibility and accountability. Point 4: use open standards. Point 11, 'Define your purchasing strategy': show that commercial, technology and contract limits were considered, avoid lock-in, and plan the exit. Spend controls check projects against the Code.
findings.requirement: For a UK spend-control assessment, provide a TCoP self-assessment: code public, open standards (PDF/A, PAdES, OpenAPI), a documented exit plan, and TCO over 5 years.

findings.claim: US federal policy requires custom code to be shared and partly released as open source, and the proposed SHARE IT Act would write this into law. Both cover custom code, not commercial SaaS.
findings.evidence: OMB Memorandum M-16-21, Federal Source Code Policy, 8 August 2016: agencies must make custom-developed code available for reuse across the federal government and, in a pilot, release at least 20% of new custom code as open source. It also sets an order of analysis: consider existing commercial solutions (which can include open source) before custom development. The SHARE IT Act was introduced in the 118th Congress (2024) to put government-wide sharing of custom code into law. I could not confirm the bill number (I believe H.R. 9566) or whether it has been enacted.
findings.requirement: Be both a commercial product (support contracts, a FedRAMP path for hosted service) and open source, so it counts as COTS under M-16-21 while agency extensions can be shared on code.gov.

findings.claim: India's official policy makes open-source software the preferred option for e-governance and requires bidders to justify leaving it out.
findings.evidence: MeitY, Policy on Adoption of Open Source Software for Government of India (2015): the government 'shall endeavour to adopt' open source in all e-governance systems 'as a preferred option in comparison to Closed Source Software'. RFPs must ask suppliers to consider open source, and suppliers must justify excluding it. A companion 2015 policy covers opening the source code of government applications. Signing for dealings with the state uses eSign under the IT Act, run through eSign service providers licensed by the Controller of Certifying Authorities.
findings.requirement: Hold an OSI-approved licence, connect to Aadhaar eSign through a licensed eSign service provider, and offer deployment in Indian data centres.

findings.claim: France's law tells administrations to keep control of their systems and to encourage free software, and the state keeps a list of recommended free software. For sensitive data it also requires cloud offers shielded from non-EU law, which raises the cost of serving France from a US SaaS.
findings.evidence: Loi 2016-1321 of 7 October 2016 pour une République numérique, article 16: administrations must preserve the control, durability and independence of their information systems, and must encourage free software and open formats when developing, buying or using them. DINUM keeps the SILL (Socle interministériel de logiciels libres) and published an action plan on free software and digital commons on 10 November 2021. The 'cloud au centre' doctrine (circular 6282/SG of 5 July 2021, updated by circular 6404/SG of 31 May 2023) requires sensitive data to be hosted on SecNumCloud-qualified offers.
findings.requirement: Be eligible for the SILL, run self-hosted on French or SecNumCloud-qualified infrastructure, and have no required dependency on a US service (email, payments, analytics).

findings.claim: Germany's federal government set open source by default for software it commissions and created a public body to provide sovereign open-source tools. That steers buying away from proprietary SaaS.
findings.evidence: Coalition agreement of 7 December 2021 (SPD, Greens, FDP): development contracts are as a rule commissioned as open source, and the software is in principle made public. In December 2022 the Federal Interior Ministry founded ZenDiS (Zentrum für Digitale Souveränität), which runs the openCoDE code platform and the openDesk office suite. I recall, without confirming the exact press release, that in 2024 Schleswig-Holstein decided to move its state administration from Microsoft to open source.
findings.requirement: Publish on openCoDE, plug into openDesk (single sign-on, file storage), and support the German eID and qualified signatures for written-form cases.

findings.claim: Switzerland made publishing government-developed software as open source a legal duty in 2024.
findings.evidence: EMBAG, the federal act on the use of electronic means for government tasks (SR 172.019), adopted 17 March 2023 and in force since 1 January 2024. Article 9: federal authorities disclose the source code of software they develop or have developed for their tasks, unless third-party rights or security reasons rule this out or limit it.
findings.requirement: Use a licence that lets a Swiss authority publish any adaptations it pays for under Article 9.

findings.claim: The Netherlands applies an 'open, unless' policy to government source code and publishes a 'comply or explain' list of open standards that buyers must ask for.
findings.evidence: Letter to parliament of 17 April 2020 from the State Secretary for the Interior on releasing government source code ('open, tenzij'). Forum Standaardisatie keeps the comply-or-explain list. I believe ETSI AdES baseline profiles for digital signatures are on it, but did not verify this.
findings.requirement: Output ETSI AdES baseline signatures and name the standards used in tender answers, so a buyer can comply rather than explain.

findings.claim: The Digital Public Goods standard, which UN and donor-backed digital public infrastructure programmes use to choose software, excludes proprietary products like DocuSign by design.
findings.evidence: DPG Standard (Digital Public Goods Alliance, first published 2020 and revised since) has 9 indicators: relevance to the SDGs; an approved open licence; clear ownership; platform independence, meaning no mandatory closed dependencies without open alternatives; documentation; extraction of non-personal data in non-proprietary formats; privacy and applicable law; standards and best practice; and do no harm by design. The 50-in-5 campaign, launched in November 2023, uses DPGs to help countries build digital public infrastructure.
findings.requirement: Apply for the DPG registry. That needs an OSI-approved licence, clear ownership, optional replaceable providers for payments, email and AI (the in-app LLM must be open or swappable), open data export, a privacy policy and do-no-harm documentation.

findings.claim: GovStack, an initiative of Germany, Estonia, ITU and DIAL, publishes reusable building-block specifications for government services. Products that meet them are easier to slot into donor-funded government programmes.
findings.evidence: GovStack (launched 2020) publishes building-block specifications such as identity, payments, registration, workflow, consent and messaging. I believe there is an e-signature building block, but did not reopen the spec this session.
findings.requirement: Map the API to the GovStack e-signature building block (if confirmed) and its identity and consent building blocks, and publish a conformance statement.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign is authorised for US federal use, so the US federal market is open to it and some agencies use it.
counter_evidence.evidence: From memory, not reopened: DocuSign's trust centre and the FedRAMP Marketplace list DocuSign eSignature for US government at FedRAMP Moderate, authorised since about 2017, with several agency authorisations. DocuSign has also stated a DoD Impact Level 4 authorisation. I could not open either page this session.
counter_evidence.requirement: Any hosted government edition needs a comparable authorisation (FedRAMP Moderate, or StateRAMP for US states), or must be self-hosted inside an agency's own authorised boundary.

counter_evidence.claim: US buying rules favour commercial products over custom builds, and ready channels exist, so price and procurement are not a barrier to DocuSign in US government.
counter_evidence.evidence: OMB M-16-21 (8 August 2016) tells agencies to consider commercial solutions before custom development. To my knowledge, Carahsoft is DocuSign's government aggregator and offers it through GSA schedules and cooperative contracts such as NASPO ValuePoint (not verified this session). I also recall, without being able to confirm it, that GSA's 2025 OneGov programme negotiated government-wide discounts with large SaaS vendors, possibly including DocuSign.
counter_evidence.requirement: Be buyable through the same channels (a GSA schedule through a reseller, cooperative contracts), as well as being free to self-host.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign sells to UK public bodies through G-Cloud, and the UK Code asks teams to consider open source, not to rule out SaaS.
counter_evidence.evidence: To my knowledge, DocuSign has had eSignature listings on recent G-Cloud frameworks (G-Cloud 13 and 14) on the Digital Marketplace. TCoP point 5 is 'Use cloud first', and point 3 asks teams to consider open source rather than requiring it. The current listing was not verified this session.
counter_evidence.requirement: List a hosted edition on G-Cloud with a published price, and offer the self-hosted route as an alternative.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign can supply qualified electronic signatures in the EU, so EU legal requirements alone do not block it from public-sector work.
counter_evidence.evidence: To my knowledge, DocuSign France is listed as a qualified trust service provider on the French national trusted list, which is visible in the EU trusted list browser, and issues qualified certificates for EU qualified signatures. Not reopened this session.
counter_evidence.requirement: Partner with qualified trust service providers, or accept EUDI wallet signatures, when a qualified signature is required. Do not claim qualified status ourselves.

counter_evidence.claim: Most open-source procurement rules are preferences with exceptions, not bans, so a public body can still buy DocuSign if it justifies the choice.
counter_evidence.evidence: Italy CAD article 68 comma 1-ter allows proprietary licences after a reasoned comparative evaluation. India's 2015 policy says the government 'shall endeavour' to prefer open source, and allows exceptions with justification. French law of 7 October 2016, article 16, says 'encourage'. Germany's 2021 coalition text concerns development contracts. Spain's Ley 40/2015 article 157 requires consulting the directory, then justifying. The EU Interoperable Europe Act, article 4, exempts solutions covered by third-party intellectual property rights.
counter_evidence.requirement: Do not rely on rules forcing a choice: win on TCO and reuse in the comparative evaluation, and make the justification for choosing us easy to write.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign reports public-sector customers and treats government sales as a distinct line of business.
counter_evidence.evidence: From memory: DocuSign's annual 10-K filings name public-sector entities among its customers. Their risk factors describe government sales as subject to budget cycles, procurement rules and termination for convenience. I did not reopen the filings or confirm any revenue split for the public sector.
counter_evidence.requirement: Plan for government budget cycles: annual invoicing, termination-for-convenience clauses and multi-year price holds in the government contract.

research:cost-procurement.notes: Limits of this research, which the reader must know. (1) No live search was possible: the run's shared WebSearch budget (200 calls) was already used up when this agent started. (2) WebFetch to ecom.docusign.com and www.docusign.com failed because those hosts are outside the session's allowed network. Following the tool's guidance after a second host failed, I did not try other sites. ecom.docusign.com and www.docusign.com must be allowed in the session's network settings before DocuSign's current prices or FedRAMP page can be checked. (3) The findings therefore come from my training knowledge (to June 2026) plus this workflow's earlier research files (sign-and-grow/research/complaints.json and gaps.json, collected 2026-11-20). I did not open the URLs in this session; they are given as I know them. I set strengths for that: 'strong' only for legal texts whose wording and location I am confident of (CAD 68 and 69, Ley 40/2015 art. 157, Regulation 2024/903, Data Act 2023/2854, EU DSS, MeitY 2015 policy, DPG standard). (4) Verify before use: DocuSign's current list prices and envelope rules; whether DocuSign is in GSA OneGov; the SHARE IT Act's bill number and status; whether GovStack has an e-signature building block; AdES on the Dutch comply-or-explain list; the exact Schleswig-Holstein decision; and DocuSign's current G-Cloud and FedRAMP listings. (5) I found no complaint by a public body about DocuSign pricing; the price-rise evidence is all from private customers. Suggested follow-up searches: UK Contracts Finder and Find a Tender, EU TED, and USAspending for DocuSign awards and amounts. (6) My synthesis, not a sourced finding: the premise is weakest in the US, UK and Australia, which lack a national signing service and have cloud-first, commercial-first buying rules. It is strongest in continental Europe, India, Brazil and digital-public-infrastructure programmes, where law prefers reuse and open source and the state already gives signing away free. A product aimed at those governments should be open source (EUPL-1.2 or AGPL-3.0), self-hostable with no required closed dependency, priced per deployment or support contract rather than per envelope, and fully exportable. (7) Relevant to the user's request that credits expire monthly: government budgets are annual and buyers avoid unpredictable usage charges. A government tier with monthly expiring credits would probably fail procurement, so it should use a fixed annual fee or free self-hosting instead. This is my inference.

research:gov-esign-design.angle: How successful government e-signature systems are built (Estonia, Belgium, Germany, EU DSS and EUDI Wallet, Brazil gov.br, India eSign, Singapore, UAE, Nordic eID brokers), and which open-source signing projects governments actually use. These are the models a product would have to copy to be adopted by governments.

findings.claim: Estonia's national signing stack is owned by the state and published as open source. It covers the desktop client, the mobile apps, the signing libraries and the validation service, and it works with all three national signing methods (ID card, Mobile-ID, Smart-ID).
findings.evidence: The open-eid GitHub organisation (fetched 2026-11-20, 76 repositories, links to ria.ee, 'Estonian Electronic Identity Software') lists DigiDoc4-Client, libdigidocpp, RIA-DigiDoc-iOS and the Android app under LGPL-2.1, and SiVa under EUPL-1.1. The iOS app is described as the official app for signing, verifying and encrypting with ID card, Mobile-ID and Smart-ID. In the digidoc4j README the Estonian Information System Authority (RIA) is the copyright holder, and support goes through help@ria.ee.
findings.requirement: Release the signing client, signing library and validator under a licence a government can audit, fork and run itself (EUPL, LGPL or AGPL), so there is no vendor lock-in and the agency can take over the code.

findings.claim: In the successful models, the signed file can be checked by anyone with a public, standards-based validator. Validity does not depend on the signing vendor's own portal or certificate of completion.
findings.evidence: The SiVa README (fetched 2026-11-20) describes a JSON API validation web service. It checks Estonian DDOC, BDOC (TimeMark and TimeStamp) and ASiC-S files, plus ETSI ASiC-E, ASiC-S, XAdES, CAdES and PAdES signatures. It uses DigiDoc4J for DDOC and BDOC and a fork of the EU DSS library (sd-dss) for everything else. DigiDoc4J has made ASiC-E with XAdES its default format since 2019, and dropped DDOC signing in 2018 (validation only).
findings.requirement: Produce ETSI AdES output (PAdES for PDFs, ASiC-E/XAdES containers) with timestamps and long-term validation data, so any government validator (EU DSS, SiVa) can verify it with no account. The audit trail should be an extra, not the proof.

findings.claim: The European Commission maintains a free, open-source reference library for creating, extending and validating advanced electronic signatures in every ETSI format. Member-state systems build on it.
findings.evidence: The esig/dss README (fetched 2026-11-20) calls the repository the 'official repository for project DSS'. It links to the Commission's Digital Building Blocks wiki and uses Maven groupId eu.europa.ec.joinup.sd-dss under LGPL-2.1. Topics are asic, cades, jades, pades, xades and signature validation, and the modules also cover evidence records, PDF/A, SD-JWT and mdoc. The BOM example is 6.5.1. It needs Java 8 or later (tested to Java 26) and has used jakarta.* since 6.0. The esig/dss-demonstrations repo (LGPL-2.1) holds a demo web app, a standalone desktop app and dss-esig-validation-tests. Estonia's SiVa uses a DSS fork. Neither DSS page names other adopters.
findings.requirement: Build signature creation and validation on EU DSS, or test against its validation test suite, rather than a home-grown PDF signing format, and validate against the EU trusted lists.

findings.claim: Mobile qualified signing in the Baltics is run by a qualified trust service provider (SK ID Solutions). Each relying party is registered by name and secret UUID and sends only a hash of the document. The signer checks a short verification code on the phone.
findings.evidence: The Mobile-ID REST README (fetched 2026-11-20; the example build is 5.1.1 of 19.06.2019, with fields 'since 5.2.1') names SK ID Solutions AS as Application Provider. relyingPartyName and relyingPartyUUID are 'agreed between Relying Party and Application Provider during registration'. The relying party sends a SHA-256/384/512 hash, shows a 4-digit verification code, and polls for the result. OCSP must be handled separately, for example with DigiDoc4j. The Smart-ID RP API v2 README (fetched 2026-11-20) returns certificate levels ADVANCED or QUALIFIED, offers a QSCD level, and says 'ADVANCED certificates cannot be QSCD-capable'. It authenticates callers by IP address plus relyingPartyUUID. Its identifier examples include PNOEE, PNOLV and PNOLT. The verification code is integer(SHA256(hash)[-2:-1]) mod 10000.
findings.requirement: Register as a relying party with national or regional signing providers and integrate their APIs. Sign by hash, so the document never leaves the agency. Show the verification code. Request QUALIFIED/QSCD certificates whenever a QES is needed.

findings.claim: Belgium's national eID card handles both login and signing, and its middleware is open source and published by the federal government. The federal digital directorate also publishes signing and validation service code for its eIDAS project.
findings.evidence: The Fedict GitHub organisation (fetched 2026-11-20) describes itself as 'Federal Public Service Policy and Support DG Digital Transformation (formerly: Fedict)' (bosa.belgium.be). The eid-mw README (LGPL-3.0) covers website login with the eID, signing documents and emails, a viewer, an API and a PKCS#11 module, on Linux, macOS and Windows. The same organisation publishes fts-sign-validation and fts-gui-sign (MIT). The fts-documentation README says only that it 'will contain all information needed to setup the components of the eiDAS project'. The fts-sign-validation repo has a signandvalidation-ws module and a Certigna.crt file. Its DSS dependency could not be confirmed because pom.xml returned HTTP 503.
findings.requirement: Support smart-card signing through PKCS#11 and the national middleware, and work with the government's own signing and validation services instead of replacing them.

findings.claim: Browser signing with a national ID card is handled by an open-source extension and native host. It keeps the login key and the signing key separate, and it signs a hash the website supplies.
findings.evidence: The web-eid-app README (fetched 2026-11-20, MIT licence) describes it as the native messaging host for the Web eID browser extension. Login builds a token from a challenge nonce and the site origin, signed with the card's authentication key, and 'the authentication key is not used to sign raw hash values'. Signing applies the card's signing key to a hash the site provides. The sample certificates are Estonian (SK ID Solutions), and the UI is translated into English, Estonian, Finnish, Croatian and Russian. The README lists no supported countries, so the Finland and Croatia link rests only on the translations.
findings.requirement: Provide a browser signing path for card-based QES (Web eID or similar) that signs hashes and never uses the login key for document signatures.

findings.claim: Germany's official eID client is open source and supplied for the federal government by a contractor. In Germany the national eID is used mainly to prove identity, not as a signing tool.
findings.evidence: The AusweisApp README (fetched 2026-11-20) calls it 'Der offizielle eID-Client des Bundes', supplied by Governikus Service GmbH on behalf of the Bund, with the source under EUPL v1.2. The page does not say whether it supports qualified signatures. From prior knowledge, not checked in this session: eID service providers need an authorisation certificate (Berechtigungszertifikat) from the Vergabestelle at the Bundesverwaltungsamt, and section 3a of the Administrative Procedure Act (VwVfG) lets authorities replace written form with an online form plus eID login instead of a QES.
findings.requirement: Accept national eID authentication (AusweisApp SDK or the eIDAS node) as the signer's identity, obtain the required authorisation certificate, and offer an 'eID-authenticated form' route where administrative law accepts it in place of a QES.

findings.claim: The next EU model is the European Digital Identity Wallet. Its reference software is published by the Commission and plans remote and local qualified signing through standard APIs.
findings.evidence: The eu-digital-identity-wallet GitHub organisation (fetched 2026-11-20, 86 repos, contact cnect-eudiw-development@ec.europa.eu) licenses its apps under EUPL-1.2 and its libraries under Apache-2.0. eudi-lib-android-rqes-ui (Apache-2.0, copyright European Commission 2026) is a remote QES library. It talks to each QTSP through a 'QTSP CSC v2 endpoint' (Cloud Signature Consortium API v2) with OAuth, and ships with no built-in QTSP. The ARF releases page (fetched 2026-11-20) shows v3.0.0 published 23 July 2026, with annexes 4.07 'remote QES enrolment', 4.09 'remote QES creating a signature channeled by relying party', 4.10 'QES view history of signatures' and 4.12 'local QES creating a signature'. From prior knowledge, not opened in this session: Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 requires wallets to let natural persons sign with a QES free of charge for non-professional purposes.
findings.requirement: Act as an EUDI Wallet relying party (OpenID4VP) and as a CSC API v2 client to QTSPs, so EU citizens can sign with the wallet the state gives them. Expect that signing will cost the citizen nothing.

findings.claim: EU law sets three signature levels, gives only the qualified level the automatic effect of a handwritten signature, and makes public services accept advanced signatures in fixed reference formats.
findings.evidence: eIDAS Regulation (EU) 910/2014 of 23 July 2014, as quoted from search extracts in this project's earlier research (not opened in this session). Article 25(1) says a signature may not be refused only because it is electronic or not qualified. Article 25(2) says 'A qualified electronic signature shall have the equivalent legal effect of a handwritten signature'. Article 26 says an advanced signature must be 'uniquely linked to the signatory' and must make later changes detectable. From prior knowledge, not opened: Article 27 and Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2015/1506 require public bodies to accept advanced signatures in XAdES, CAdES, PAdES and ASiC baseline formats.
findings.requirement: Let the sender pick SES, AdES or QES for each document, label the level on the signed file and certificate, and output AdES or QES only in the 2015/1506 reference formats.

findings.claim: Brazil sets three signature levels in law, requires the qualified ICP-Brasil level for some acts, and offers public bodies a free gov.br advanced-signature API.
findings.evidence: Lei 14.063/2020 (September 2020), quoted from search extracts in this project's earlier research. A qualified signature is one that 'utiliza certificado digital' under art. 10 §1 of MP 2.200-2. An advanced signature uses non-ICP-Brasil certificates 'ou outro meio de comprovação da autoria e da integridade'. A qualified signature is required 'nos atos de transferência e de registro de bens imóveis', though Lei 14.620/2023 may have relaxed this. The servicosgovbr/manual-integracao-assinatura-eletronica repo (CC0-1.0, fetched 2026-11-20) is the integration manual for 'entidades públicas interessadas em integrar suas aplicações clientes' with the advanced digital signature API. From prior knowledge, not opened in this session: Decreto 10.543/2020 governs these signatures, and signers need a silver or gold gov.br account level for the advanced signature.
findings.requirement: Accept gov.br advanced signatures and ICP-Brasil qualified certificates. Check the gov.br account level. Hold a rule table that sends real-estate and other listed acts to a qualified signature.

findings.claim: India's government model works through licensed eSign Service Providers. They sign on the citizen's behalf after Aadhaar e-KYC (OTP or biometric), and the law gives these signatures a stronger presumption than other electronic methods.
findings.evidence: The CCA eSign brochure v1.5, as quoted in this project's earlier research (not opened in this session), says signing is done 'using authentication of the Aadhaar holder through Aadhaar e-KYC service'. Adobe's India white paper, from the same research, says a party relying on other electronic methods must prove them, while for Aadhaar or certificate signatures the burden falls on the challenger. Leegality says that where a law requires a signature, only methods recognised by the IT Act qualify. From prior knowledge, not checked: ESPs must be licensed Certifying Authorities empanelled by the CCA, and eSign appears in the Second Schedule of the IT Act 2000.
findings.requirement: Integrate one or more CCA-empanelled ESPs, or become one, so Indian signers can use Aadhaar OTP eSign. Keep signing and storing data in India.

findings.claim: Singapore and the UAE built signing into the national identity app instead of buying a separate signing service.
findings.evidence: Prior knowledge only. No page was opened in this session because web search was exhausted and those hosts were not reachable. Sign with Singpass lets Singpass app holders sign documents through partner signing apps. UAE PASS is the national digital identity, with a signature feature recognised under Federal Decree-Law 46 of 2021 on electronic transactions and trust services.
findings.requirement: Use the national identity app (Sign with Singpass API, UAE PASS) as the signing method, and become a listed signing partner where the state runs a partner scheme.

findings.claim: In the Nordic countries, government and private services reach the national eID through certified identity brokers or bank-run eIDs, not through their own email-link identity checks.
findings.evidence: Prior knowledge only, not checked in this session. Denmark's MitID is reached through brokers certified by the Agency for Digital Government. Finland runs a regulated strong-identification trust network supervised by Traficom. Sweden and Norway rely on bank-run BankID schemes. Earlier project research also found no user statements that Nordic signers refuse anything but BankID or MitID.
findings.requirement: Connect to national eIDs through a certified broker (or become one), and record the eID assurance level (eIDAS low, substantial or high) on the audit trail.

findings.claim: Across these models the document is hashed on the agency's side, and only the hash goes to the signing service. A SaaS model where the full document is uploaded to a foreign vendor's cloud does not fit them.
findings.evidence: The Mobile-ID README (fetched 2026-11-20) has the relying party compute a SHA-256/384/512 hash and send it Base64-encoded. Web eID (fetched 2026-11-20) signs 'a provided document hash'. The EUDI rQES library (fetched 2026-11-20) asks the configured QTSP to sign through the CSC v2 API, with an optional timestamp authority. The conclusion that this is a barrier for DocuSign's upload-to-cloud model is my analysis, not something these sources say.
findings.requirement: Offer self-hosted or in-country deployment, with hash-only remote signing, so the document never leaves the government's infrastructure.

findings.claim: The best-known open-source DocuSign alternatives name no government users on their GitHub pages. Most of them produce simple signatures, not eID-based AdES or QES. LibreSign is the only one carrying a Digital Public Good badge.
findings.evidence: All pages fetched 2026-11-20. DocuSeal: AGPLv3 with section 7(b) additional terms, copyright DocuSeal LLC 2023-2026. It lists 'Automatic PDF eSignature' and verification and targets banking, healthcare, real estate and KYC, with no government users and no named compliance standard. OpenSign: AGPL-3. Signatures are drawn, typed or uploaded images, guests verify with an email OTP, and the completion certificate is a log, with no compliance claims. Documenso: AGPL-3.0, PAdES topic, self-hostable, no mention of eIDAS, ESIGN or 21 CFR Part 11. LibreSign: AGPL-3.0 Nextcloud app maintained by LibreCode Coop, 'a Brazilian cooperative specialized in free software', with a 'Verified DPG' badge. None of the four names a government or public-sector user, and the 'Used by' sections are empty.
findings.requirement: Being open source is not enough. A product also has to implement AdES or QES with national eIDs and register as a Digital Public Good, since development-sector and UN-linked procurement often looks for that.

findings.claim: The common design of the successful systems: the state issues the identity, signing is a function of that identity, and signing is free or nearly free for the citizen. Per-envelope pricing with email-link identity fits poorly. (Synthesis.)
findings.evidence: This is my synthesis of the findings above, so it is labelled weak. Estonian and Belgian ID cards carry both login and signing keys (open-eid, eid-mw, Web eID). Brazil offers public bodies a free advanced-signature API. India routes eSign through Aadhaar e-KYC. The EUDI framework plans QES inside the state wallet, and free QES for non-professional use comes from the Regulation, which was not opened in this session. No source I opened compares these models with DocuSign directly.
findings.requirement: Price per agency (flat or seat-based) with free signing for citizens. Treat the national eID or wallet as the signer's identity, and keep email links only for low-risk simple signatures.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign does sell into the US federal government through a separate FedRAMP-authorised government offering.
counter_evidence.evidence: Prior knowledge, not checked in this session (www.docusign.com did not resolve from this environment on 2026-11-20). DocuSign runs a government environment with at least FedRAMP Moderate authorisation, and has reported a DoD Impact Level 4 authorisation. Whether it also holds FedRAMP High, and which agencies sponsor it, could not be confirmed.
counter_evidence.requirement: A product aiming at US federal agencies needs a FedRAMP authorisation (Moderate at minimum) with an agency sponsor, and a separate government environment.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign can produce EU advanced and qualified signatures through its own EU trust service provider, so it is not limited to simple signatures.
counter_evidence.evidence: Prior knowledge, not checked in this session. DocuSign France appears on the EU trusted lists as a qualified trust service provider, and DocuSign sells EU Advanced and EU Qualified signature options. The eIDAS trusted-list browser could not be reached (ec.europa.eu did not resolve).
counter_evidence.requirement: Meeting eIDAS QES requires either becoming a QTSP or partnering with one, and showing that status on the EU trusted list.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign connects to some national eIDs rather than competing with them, which weakens the idea that national eIDs lock it out.
counter_evidence.evidence: Prior knowledge only, not checked in this session. DocuSign has announced or listed identity verification or signing integrations with schemes such as itsme, Sign with Singpass, UAE PASS and BankID. Dates and the signature level reached through each could not be confirmed. Earlier project research also could not confirm whether DocuSign supports Aadhaar eSign.
counter_evidence.requirement: National eID connectors are table stakes. A product has to match DocuSign on them before it can claim to beat it on government fit.

counter_evidence.claim: US state and local governments and UK public bodies buy DocuSign through public procurement frameworks.
counter_evidence.evidence: Prior knowledge only, not checked in this session. DocuSign is sold directly and through resellers on frameworks such as NASPO ValuePoint in the US and G-Cloud on the UK Digital Marketplace. No listing or contract record was opened, because search was exhausted and those hosts were not tried.
counter_evidence.requirement: Being listed on the main procurement frameworks (NASPO, G-Cloud, GSA schedules and national equivalents) is a precondition for government sales.

counter_evidence.claim: The governments that do not use DocuSign mostly built their own systems on open standards. They did not adopt open-source DocuSign clones, so 'open source beats DocuSign in government' is not shown by the evidence.
counter_evidence.evidence: Fetched 2026-11-20. Estonia (open-eid, RIA copyright), Belgium (Fedict eid-mw, FTS repos) and Brazil (servicosgovbr manual) all run their own stacks, and the EU publishes DSS and the EUDI Wallet. DocuSeal, OpenSign, Documenso and LibreSign name no government users on their GitHub pages.
counter_evidence.requirement: Position the product as a layer on top of each country's eID, signing service and validator, not as a replacement for them.

research:citizens-access.angle: Serving citizens rather than businesses: accessibility law and conformance reports, languages and scripts, people without email or smartphones, assisted and proxy signing, poor connectivity and shared devices, citizen identity through national eID, records and archives duties, freedom of information, public registers and evidence that holds in court.

findings.claim: US federal buyers must meet the Revised Section 508 Standards, which incorporate WCAG 2.0 AA and also cover authoring tools and the PDFs they export. Vendors are judged by their Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR), and buyers are told to test the claims rather than trust them.
findings.evidence: Revised 508 Standards (US Access Board final rule, 82 FR 5790, published 18 January 2017, compliance required from 18 January 2018) incorporate WCAG 2.0 Level A and AA for web content, non-web electronic documents and software interfaces. Chapter 5, 504.2 requires authoring tools to support creating accessible content, and 504.2.2 requires an application that exports PDF to offer export to PDF/UA-1 (ISO 14289-1). Section508.gov tells sellers to supply an ACR built on the ITI VPAT template (VPAT 2.5, with 508, EU, WCAG and INT editions) and points buyers to testing methods such as DHS Trusted Tester. A signing platform is both web content (the signer pages) and an authoring tool (the sender's field editor, which produces the final PDF), so both halves are in scope.
findings.requirement: WCAG 2.0 AA at minimum, 2.2 AA as the target, on every surface: signer pages, sender editor, admin console, emails and mobile apps. Completed documents exportable as tagged PDF/UA-1 with field values and signature blocks tagged, not flattened images. Dated, version-specific ACRs in all four VPAT editions, based on Trusted Tester style testing, with known issues and fix dates listed.

findings.claim: Federal policy since late 2023 tells agencies to verify vendor accessibility claims and write accessibility into contracts. That raises the bar for any signing vendor.
findings.evidence: OMB memorandum M-24-08, Strengthening Digital Accessibility and the Management of Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act (21 December 2023), tells agencies to include accessibility requirements in solicitations, validate vendor conformance claims and manage remediation. From memory, it also encourages going beyond the WCAG 2.0 baseline. I could not re-check the exact wording, or whether the memo is still in force after the change of administration in January 2025.
findings.requirement: Contract language that warrants conformance, a test tenant the agency can audit, committed remediation times for reported defects, and an ACR updated with each release.

findings.claim: US state and local governments must make their web content and mobile apps conform to WCAG 2.1 AA, including third-party platforms they use. The first deadline was April 2026.
findings.evidence: The DOJ final rule under ADA Title II (28 CFR part 35, subpart H) was published 24 April 2024 (89 FR 31320). It covers web content and mobile apps that public entities provide or make available, directly or 'through contractual, licensing, or other arrangements', and requires WCAG 2.1 Level AA. Compliance dates were 24 April 2026 for entities with a population of 50,000 or more and 26 April 2027 for smaller entities and special districts. There are narrow exceptions, including one for individualized, password-protected documents, but the signing interface itself is still covered. I could not check whether DOJ has changed these dates since early 2025.
findings.requirement: WCAG 2.1 AA (2.2 AA preferred) for the citizen signing flow and mobile apps, written into a contract warranty. On request, an accessible version of any individual document: text view, large print, tagged PDF or read-aloud.

findings.claim: In the EU, public sector websites and apps must meet EN 301 549 (which carries WCAG 2.1 AA) and publish an accessibility statement. Public tenders must build accessibility into their specifications. Canada and Australia use the same standard.
findings.evidence: Directive (EU) 2016/2102 (26 October 2016) required all public sector websites to be accessible by 23 September 2020 and mobile apps by 23 June 2021. Conformity is presumed through the harmonised standard EN 301 549 V3.2.1 (ETSI, March 2021). Bodies must also publish an accessibility statement with a feedback mechanism (model in Implementing Decision (EU) 2018/1523). Public procurement Directive 2014/24/EU, Article 42(1): for anything intended for use by natural persons, technical specifications must take accessibility criteria into account except in duly justified cases. From memory: Accessibility Standards Canada adopted CAN/ASC-EN 301 549:2024, and Standards Australia adopted AS EN 301 549 in 2016.
findings.requirement: An EN 301 549 ACR (VPAT EU edition) covering clause 9 (web), clause 10 (non-web documents, meaning the PDFs), clause 11 (software, mobile apps, authoring tools) and clause 12 (documentation and support). A ready-made accessibility statement and feedback route that the buying authority can publish for the signing pages.

findings.claim: Since 28 June 2025 the European Accessibility Act has applied to consumer services such as banking and e-commerce. Signing steps embedded in those services must be accessible, including in state-owned banks and postal services.
findings.evidence: Directive (EU) 2019/882 (17 April 2019) applies from 28 June 2025 to listed products and services, including consumer banking, e-commerce, electronic communications and passenger transport e-ticketing. E-signature services are not a listed category, so a signing platform is caught when it is part of an in-scope service, for example opening an account or signing a consumer credit agreement. Microenterprises providing services are exempt. EN 301 549 is being revised (v4.x) to serve as the Act's harmonised standard. I could not confirm whether the new version has been cited in the Official Journal yet.
findings.requirement: When the product is embedded or used through its API, it must be as accessible as the hosted page and meet the Annex I service requirements, including accessible information about how the service works. Integrators need an ACR they can attach to their own EAA documentation.

findings.claim: UK public bodies must meet WCAG 2.2 AA for their websites and apps. GDS has monitored against WCAG 2.2 since October 2024.
findings.evidence: The Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) (No. 2) Accessibility Regulations 2018 (SI 2018/952) require public sector sites and apps to meet the accessibility requirement and publish an accessibility statement. GOV.UK guidance says GDS monitoring has checked against WCAG 2.2 AA from October 2024. A signing page that a council or department sends citizens to is part of its service.
findings.requirement: WCAG 2.2 AA conformance and an accessibility statement the authority can publish. Defects that GDS monitoring finds are fixed within the authority's reporting deadline.

findings.claim: WCAG 2.2's new success criteria hit things e-signature products do every day: drag-to-place fields, small tick boxes and initials, access codes and identity quizzes, and making people retype their name and address.
findings.evidence:
WCAG 2.2 (W3C Recommendation 5 October 2023, updated December 2024) adds:
- 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA): anything done by dragging must also work with a single pointer without dragging.
- 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (AA): targets at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or spaced.
- 3.3.8 Accessible Authentication (Minimum) (AA): no cognitive function test, such as remembering or transcribing a code, unless there is an alternative or help such as paste and password managers.
- 3.3.7 Redundant Entry (A).
- 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) (AA).
- 3.2.6 Consistent Help (A).
The older criteria 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures and 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable also apply. 2.2.1 means warning before a session times out and letting the user extend it. Applying 3.3.8 to knowledge-based identity quizzes is my own reading, not a W3C statement.
findings.requirement:
Sender editor: a keyboard and click-to-place alternative to drag and drop. Signer:
- a typed or adopted signature offered as an equal alternative to drawing
- fields and tick boxes at least 24 px
- one-time codes that can be pasted and autofilled (autocomplete=one-time-code)
- no knowledge-based quiz without an alternative
- name, address and email carried forward, not retyped
- timeout warnings with an option to extend
- help in the same place on every step

findings.claim: A signing product is judged on the document the citizen has to read, not only on its buttons. A tool that shows uploaded pages as images and returns flattened PDFs fails blind citizens even if its interface conforms.
findings.evidence: From memory, not checked in this session: DocuSign's signing page shows each uploaded page as an image with fields laid over it, offers a responsive HTML view for some documents, and merges fields into the page in the completed PDF. Earlier research in this workflow (/home/user/treegens-app/sign-and-grow/research/gaps.json, November 2026) searched for user complaints about Section 508, WCAG or screen readers in DocuSign and found none, so there is no user evidence either way. This repo's own audit (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-treegens-app/9d40e5b6-b8c5-5afe-af61-9b17cf0ca38e/scratchpad/audit2.txt) found the same weakness in Sign&Grow's default Document view: pages are canvas elements with no text layer, and the Text view is empty for scans. WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships requires structure and text to be programmatically available.
findings.requirement: Show the document as real text in reading order (a text layer or HTML view), with fields as native labelled controls. Detect untagged or scanned uploads and warn the sender before sending to the public. Return a tagged PDF/UA output. Offer large print and audio on request.
sources: https://www.docusign.com/trust/compliance/accessibility (could not be reached from this session)

findings.claim: Governments have legal duties to serve citizens in named languages, often including smaller official languages that commercial signing tools do not cover.
findings.evidence:
- EU: Regulation No 1 of 1958 sets 24 official languages, including Irish (full status since 1 January 2022) and Maltese.
- Wales: the Welsh Language (Wales) Measure 2011 and the Welsh Language Standards require public bodies to provide services in Welsh.
- Canada: the Official Languages Act requires federal services in English and French.
- India: the Constitution's Eighth Schedule lists 22 languages.
- US: Executive Order 14224 (1 March 2025) made English the official language and revoked EO 13166 on limited English proficiency. State and city laws still require translation, for example New York State Executive Law section 202-a (the 12 most common languages, 2022) and NYC Local Law 30 of 2017 (10 languages).
From memory and unverified: DocuSign's signing page supports about 44 languages and its sending interface about 14. I do not recall Irish, Maltese, Welsh, or most Indic and African languages in the signing list.
findings.requirement: A translation system that lets the buying government add or correct any language itself, including Welsh, Irish, Maltese, Indic and African languages, for every string the signer sees. Bilingual side-by-side documents and certificates (English/French, Welsh/English). Language set per recipient and switchable on the first screen.

findings.claim: DocuSign users report signers getting the signing screen or the legal consent in a language they cannot read, disclosures that are not translated, scripts that do not render, and identity codes that fail abroad.
findings.evidence:
From earlier research in this workflow (search-result extracts, not reopened here):
- A DocuSign Community signer said the document 'was in English, but the signing part was in Hebrew'.
- In a May 2025 thread, DocuSign staff replied: 'Docusign does not automatically translate disclosures. You need to create a custom disclosure for each language used by your signers.'
- Other threads report a Khmer font not recognised, Simplified Chinese display problems, SMS authentication failing for a signer in Japan, and phone callback failing to dial international numbers.
findings.requirement: The electronic consent and every legal notice shipped pre-translated and reviewed in all supported languages. All Unicode scripts rendered with correct shaping and right-to-left layout, both in fields and in the final PDF, using embedded fonts such as Noto. Codes delivered by voice, SMS or app in any country.

findings.claim: A significant minority of citizens have no internet, email or smartphone, and government service standards require services that also work for them.
findings.evidence:
- ITU Facts and Figures 2024: about 5.5 billion people (68%) are online and 2.6 billion are offline.
- Pew Research Center fact sheets (31 January 2024): 95% of US adults use the internet and about 90% own a smartphone, so roughly 1 in 20 does not use the internet. The share is higher among older and lower-income adults.
- GOV.UK Service Standard point 5, 'Make sure everyone can use the service', and the Service Manual section 'Helping people to use your service' require offline and assisted routes.
From memory: DocuSign can deliver by SMS and, since 2023, WhatsApp, but an email address remains a recipient's default identity.
findings.requirement: A recipient's identity is not tied to an email address. Delivery by SMS, voice call, WhatsApp, printed letter with a short code and QR, or in person. A paper round trip (print, sign by hand, scan or post back) that joins the same audit trail. Feature-phone flows (SMS reply or USSD) for simple consents, labelled as lower assurance.

findings.claim: Citizens often sign with help or through someone else. The law already has formal routes for this that signing tools rarely model: signing by mark with witnesses, signing at someone's direction, attorneys and appointed representatives.
findings.evidence: Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, section 1(3): a deed is validly executed if signed by the person in the presence of a witness, or 'at his direction and in his presence and the presence of two witnesses who each attest the signature'. US Social Security forms such as SSA-8 say witnesses are required only if the form is signed by mark (X), and form SSA-1696 appoints a representative to act for a claimant. Powers of attorney, deputies and guardians are common in benefits, health and housing. From memory: DocuSign offers in-person signing hosted by one of the sender's users, a change-signer option and witness recipients.
