I could not confirm whether it records the legal capacity (attorney, guardian, at direction) and the helper's identity separately from the signer.
findings.requirement: An explicit 'signing for someone else' role that records the capacity and attaches the authority document. Signature by mark with two witnesses. The helper's or counter clerk's identity recorded separately from the signer. A 'read to me' step logged in the audit trail. A counter mode for staff-assisted signing on an agency device, with the citizen's own confirmation by a code to their phone or by eID.

findings.claim: The consent to do business electronically, which signing tools show first, is usually long English legal text. The law requires meaningful consent, and government standards require plain language.
findings.evidence: ESIGN Act, 15 U.S.C. 7001(c)(1): before giving consumers legally required information electronically, they must affirmatively consent after a clear disclosure, in a way that 'reasonably demonstrates' they can access the electronic form. The Plain Writing Act of 2010 (Public Law 111-274) requires federal agencies to use plain language in documents the public uses. GOV.UK content guidance writes for a reading age of about 9. DocuSign staff said in May 2025 that disclosures are not translated automatically (earlier workflow research). From memory: DocuSign's default Electronic Record and Signature Disclosure is several screens of legal English.
findings.requirement: Consent and step text in plain language at about reading age 9, in every supported language, with optional audio. One idea per screen. A short summary of what the citizen is agreeing to, shown above the document. The record notes which language and version of the consent was shown.

findings.claim: Government service standards expect services to keep working on slow connections, old browsers and shared computers, which favours light, resilient signing pages.
findings.evidence: The GOV.UK Service Manual page on progressive enhancement tells teams to build so that the core service still works when JavaScript or CSS fail to load. WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable requires a warning and a way to extend before a timeout. Public libraries and community centres provide shared computers for people with no device of their own. From memory and unverified: DocuSign's browser signing is a JavaScript application, and its offline signing is limited to in-person signing in the mobile app.
findings.requirement: A small first load that works on 2G and old Android browsers. The signer resumes where they left off after a dropped connection. Offline signing with secure queueing. A shared-device mode that keeps nothing in the browser, signs out on finish and clears downloaded PDFs. No dependence on third-party cookies.

findings.claim: In the EU, citizen identity for public services is meant to come from national eID schemes and, from about the end of 2026, the European Digital Identity Wallet. The wallet also gives citizens free qualified signatures. Email-link signing does not fit this model.
findings.evidence: eIDAS Regulation (EU) 910/2014, Article 6 (applied from 29 September 2018): where national law requires electronic identification at substantial or high assurance for an online public service, the body must recognise notified eID means from other member states. Article 25(2): a qualified electronic signature has the equivalent legal effect of a handwritten one (also confirmed in earlier workflow research). Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 (eIDAS 2, in force 20 May 2024) requires every member state to offer a European Digital Identity Wallet. Implementing acts adopted from late 2024 put the wallets in place around the end of 2026. The wallets must let natural persons create qualified signatures, free of charge for non-professional purposes (my recollection of Article 5a), and public bodies that rely on eID must accept them.
findings.requirement: Act as a relying party for national eIDs (through eIDAS nodes or national brokers) and for the EUDI Wallet (OpenID4VP presentation and wallet-based qualified signatures). Record the assurance level (low, substantial or high) on the certificate. Produce advanced and qualified (PAdES) signatures through a qualified trust service provider.

findings.claim: In several large countries the state itself gives citizens free signing tied to national ID. A commercial email-based tool is competing with a free government service that carries more legal weight.
findings.evidence:
- Germany: VwVfG section 3a lets written form in administrative procedures be replaced only by a qualified electronic signature or by specified state channels, such as online forms with eID card authentication.
- Estonia: ID-card, Mobile-ID and Smart-ID signatures have been legally equal to handwritten ones for over two decades and are free to citizens.
- Brazil: Decreto 10.543/2020 (13 November 2020) sets simple, advanced and qualified signature levels for dealings with federal bodies, and the gov.br signer gives citizens a free advanced signature.
- India: Aadhaar eSign is offered through licensed eSign Service Providers under the Controller of Certifying Authorities (earlier workflow research).
findings.requirement: Do not compete with national signing; orchestrate it. Let the citizen sign inside the workflow with the national tool (gov.br, Smart-ID, Aadhaar eSign, an ID card or the EUDI Wallet). Keep the product's own value in the workflow, accessibility, records and evidence layers.

findings.claim: US federal services increasingly expect identity through Login.gov or other credentials proofed to NIST SP 800-63, not through an email link, and auditors check assurance claims.
findings.evidence: NIST SP 800-63 Digital Identity Guidelines define identity assurance (IAL) and authenticator assurance (AAL) levels. Revision 4 was finalised in 2025 (date from memory). GSA runs Login.gov for public sign-in and identity verification. GSA's Office of Inspector General (report JE23-003, 7 March 2023) found GSA had misled customer agencies about Login.gov meeting IAL2, which shows that assurance claims get audited. An email-link signature is at most an unproofed credential.
findings.requirement: Accept Login.gov (OIDC) for the public and PIV/CAC cards for staff. Record IAL and AAL on the certificate. Do not build its own selfie-biometric proofing. Use knowledge-based questions only as a fallback, with an accessible alternative.

findings.claim: US federal records rules require agencies to keep signed records, their signature evidence and metadata trustworthy for the whole retention period. Since mid-2024, permanent records go to NARA only in electronic form.
findings.evidence: NARA's 'Records Management Guidance for Agencies Implementing Electronic Signature Technologies' (18 October 2000) says agencies must decide what signature information to keep with the record so it stays trustworthy for as long as the record is kept: typically the signer's name, the date and time, and the meaning of the signature. 36 CFR Part 1236 sets electronic records management requirements. 36 CFR 1222.32 makes records that contractors create or hold for an agency into federal records, which contracts must cover. OMB/NARA memoranda M-19-21 (28 June 2019) and M-23-07 (23 December 2022) set 30 June 2024 as the date after which NARA accepts permanent records only electronically, with metadata.
findings.requirement: Retention controlled by the agency: schedules per record series mapped to NARA schedules or the GRS, legal holds, logged disposition and no automatic purge by the vendor. Bulk export of each record as PDF/A with embedded signature validation data, plus the audit trail and metadata in open formats (XML, JSON, CSV), packaged for NARA transfer. Signatures that can be validated without the vendor's service.

findings.claim: UK public records rules require authorities to keep records authentic and usable for decades, and to transfer selected records to The National Archives at 20 years.
findings.evidence: The Public Records Act 1958, as amended by the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010, moved the transfer point from 30 to 20 years, phased in from 2013 to 2022. The Lord Chancellor's Code of Practice on the management of records under section 46 of FOIA (revised July 2021) expects authorities to keep records authentic, reliable and accessible for as long as they are needed, including digital continuity and contract controls over third-party systems. The National Archives' PRONOM registry is the reference for file formats.
findings.requirement: Output ready for preservation: PDF/A-2 or PDF/A-3 with long-term validation (PAdES B-LTA), audit trails in open formats, and an exit plan that hands every record and its evidence to the authority in formats PRONOM can identify.

findings.claim: Records held in a vendor's cloud still belong to the authority for freedom of information purposes, so the signing system must support search, export and redaction within statutory deadlines.
findings.evidence: UK Freedom of Information Act 2000, section 3(2)(b): information counts as held by a public authority if another person holds it on the authority's behalf. Section 10 sets 20 working days to respond. US FOIA, 5 U.S.C. 552(f)(2)(B), added by the OPEN Government Act of 2007: a record includes information maintained for an agency by a government contractor for records management purposes.
findings.requirement: Admin search across all envelopes, including drafts, voided and declined ones. Export with audit logs. A redaction tool for personal data. An access log, so the authority can answer FOI and subject access requests within deadline.

findings.claim: Courts accept electronic signatures in principle, but email-link signatures can fail when the relying party cannot prove who signed, while qualified signatures carry a legal presumption. Governments need evidence that stands up without the vendor in the room.
findings.evidence:
- California Court of Appeal, Fabian v. Renovate America, Inc. (2019) 42 Cal.App.5th 1062: the company failed to authenticate an electronic signature (reported as made through DocuSign) because it gave no evidence of how the signer was verified, so it could not enforce the arbitration clause. Case details are from memory.
- Germany: Arbeitsgericht Berlin, 28 September 2021, 36 Ca 15296/20, as reported by law firms in earlier workflow research, held void a fixed-term clause signed through DocuSign with a non-qualified signature, because statutory written form needs a qualified signature (BGB section 126a).
- EU: eIDAS Article 25(2) gives only a qualified signature the effect of a handwritten one.
- England and Wales: the Law Commission report 'Electronic execution of documents' (Law Com No 386, September 2019) confirmed e-signatures can meet statutory signature requirements, subject to evidence of identity and intent.
findings.requirement: Signature level (simple, advanced or qualified) chosen per document type from a rules table per country. Each signed PDF carries a PAdES signature and an RFC 3161 timestamp from a qualified timestamp authority, so anyone can validate it with the EU DSS tool or Adobe. An evidence report that explains the identity steps taken. A standard custodian declaration for court.
sources: Fabian v. Renovate America, Inc. (2019) 42 Cal.App.5th 1062 (California Court of Appeal)

findings.claim: Governments increasingly have to publish what they sign, so a signing product needs a public, privacy-safe way to prove that a document is authentic and to publish contracts.
findings.evidence: The UK Procurement Act 2023 (in force 24 February 2025) requires contract details notices and, from memory of section 94, publication of a copy of the contract for public contracts over 5 million pounds. Many governments publish procurement data using the Open Contracting Data Standard. Ukraine's Prozorro procurement system runs on qualified e-signatures. Estonia uses KSI hash-chain timestamps to prove the integrity of state records. Applying these to the design of a signing product is my own inference.
findings.requirement: A public verification page where anyone can check a document's hash, date, signer role and assurance level without seeing personal data. Redaction before publication. Export in OCDS format. Optionally, anchoring hashes in a public append-only log (for example the Treegens chain), described as an extra and not a legal requirement.

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign is authorised for US federal use, so the premise that governments do not adopt it is overstated, at least for US federal back-office work.
counter_evidence.evidence: From memory, not re-checked: DocuSign eSignature has held a FedRAMP Moderate authorisation since about 2017, is listed on the FedRAMP Marketplace, and DocuSign markets a government offering and reports public sector as a customer segment. DocuSign's trust pages could not be reached from this session, and I could not look up agency contracts on USAspending or SAM.gov.
counter_evidence.requirement: FedRAMP Moderate (High for some agencies), and StateRAMP/GovRAMP for US states, are the entry ticket. A new product needs them, or must run on a platform that already has them.
sources: https://www.docusign.com/trust/compliance/fedramp (could not be reached from this session)

counter_evidence.claim: DocuSign can produce EU qualified signatures and connect to some national eIDs, so it is not locked out of EU public-sector use.
counter_evidence.evidence: From memory, not verified in this session: DocuSign France, the former OpenTrust business acquired in 2015, is a qualified trust service provider on the EU Trusted List. DocuSign offers 'EU Advanced' and 'EU Qualified' signature types, with identity checks that include some national eIDs such as Swedish and Norwegian BankID and Belgian itsme.
counter_evidence.requirement: Qualified trust service provider status, or a partnership with one, plus national eID connectors. These are what let a vendor into EU public-sector deals that need advanced or qualified signatures.
sources: https://www.docusign.com/trust/compliance/eidas (could not be reached from this session)

counter_evidence.claim: On paper, DocuSign already covers several citizen needs: accessibility reports, many signing languages, SMS and WhatsApp delivery, and in-person signing.
counter_evidence.evidence: DocuSign announced WhatsApp delivery in 2023 (DocuSign press release and developer blog, and a TechRadar report, found by earlier workflow research). From memory and unverified: DocuSign says its signing experience is designed to meet WCAG 2.1 AA and Section 508 and publishes ACRs, and it supports about 44 signing languages, SMS delivery and host-led in-person signing.
counter_evidence.requirement: Matching these features is the minimum. A competitor has to win on depth: an accessible sender editor, tagged PDF output, languages the government can add itself, and assisted-signing roles with recorded capacity.
sources: https://www.docusign.com/trust/compliance/accessibility (could not be reached from this session)

counter_evidence.claim: UK government bodies accept signatures made on commercial e-signature platforms for some high-value transactions.
counter_evidence.evidence: HM Land Registry has accepted electronically signed deeds made through e-signature platforms since 27 July 2020. The conveyancer runs the process and the signer receives a one-time password (HM Land Registry blog of that date and Practice Guide 8, found by earlier workflow research).
counter_evidence.requirement: The registry's specific rules (one-time-password second factor, conveyancer certification, witness rules) as configurable policies per document type.

counter_evidence.claim: US law and policy have pushed agencies to accept electronic signatures for decades, and agencies buy commercial tools for it.
counter_evidence.evidence: The Government Paperwork Elimination Act of 1998 (Public Law 105-277, Title XVII) required agencies to allow electronic submission and electronic signatures where practicable, and OMB M-00-10 (25 April 2000) implemented it. OMB M-23-22, Delivering a Digital-First Public Experience (22 September 2023), tells agencies to digitise forms and accept electronic signatures (wording from memory). I could not look up specific agency DocuSign contracts in this session, so the claim that agencies buy DocuSign in particular is not verified.
counter_evidence.requirement: Documented alignment with the GPEA and M-00-10 risk-based choice of signature method, so that agencies can justify the level used for each form.

**What the evidence suggests (my analysis, moderate confidence):** the premise needs narrowing. DocuSign is used in government back offices and business-to-government work, notably in the US federal government through FedRAMP. Its weak spot is high-assurance services aimed at citizens. Five reasons:
1. Its identity is an email link, while governments identify citizens through national eID: eIDAS and the EUDI Wallet, Login.gov, GOV.UK One Login, BankID, Aadhaar, gov.br.
2. In several large countries the state itself gives citizens free signing with more legal weight: Estonia, Brazil, India, Germany through qualified signatures.
3. Records, FOI and archives duties need retention controlled by the agency, open-format export and signatures that can be checked without the vendor.
4. Accessibility is judged on the whole surface. That includes the sender editor, the document the citizen reads and the output PDF (PDF/UA under 508 rule 504.2.2), not only the signing buttons.
5. Languages, assisted signing and offline routes are thin for the citizens who need them most.

**What a product needs to be adopted:**
- connect to national eIDs and record the assurance level
- orchestrate national signing tools rather than replace them
- audited ACRs (508, EN 301 549, WCAG 2.2) for every surface, and tagged output
- languages the government can add itself, and plain-language consent
- non-email channels, a paper round trip, and assisted or proxy roles with recorded capacity
- archive-grade PAdES-LTA output, with exports and retention the agency controls
- FOI search and redaction, and a public verification register

synthesis.premise_verdict: Partly true, and overstated as a blanket claim. FALSE for the US federal and state market. DocuSign has been FedRAMP Moderate since August 2017 and has held a DoD IL4 provisional authorisation since April 2021. GSA struck a government-wide OneGov deal on 31 July 2025: 70% off eSignature and 50% off IAM through 31 January 2027. VA placed a roughly USD 53.7M three-year task order. DocuSign also holds GovRAMP and appears on NASPO ValuePoint contracts for many states, plus statewide awards in New York, California, Maine and Arkansas. This is the strongest counter-evidence. DocuSign's claim that all 15 cabinet departments use it is unverified vendor material. PARTLY TRUE for the UK, Australia and Ireland. Use is real but departmental and modest: UK Contracts Finder awards in the tens of thousands of pounds, and an NHS buy of 7,700 envelopes. In Australia, DocuSign is IRAP PROTECTED with whole-of-government arrangements in Queensland and NSW, but federal spend is only about AUD 539K since 2020 (unverified aggregator figure). Ireland's National Transport Authority tendered for it in 2026. LARGELY TRUE for national signing infrastructure and for formal acts of state. No national government found uses DocuSign as its national signature system. In the EU, Latin America, India and much of Asia, the state, or a provider it licenses, issues the signing credential, often free. Examples: the EUDI Wallet with free QES from about December 2026, EU Sign for EU institutions, Estonia's 3M signatures a month, Italy's 32.7M qualified certificates and 3.4B remote signatures in H1 2025, Brazil's 214M free gov.br signatures in 2025, about 1.56B Aadhaar eSigns, and Singpass, UAE PASS, JPKI, e.firma, FirmaGob and PFDR. US federal staff sign with PIV/CAC under Federal PKI. Many states also own the sender-side workflow (EU Sign, Singapore's Signify in 100+ agencies, Argentina's GDE) or buy domestic, locally certified vendors (Modusign with CSAP in Korea, CloudSign with ISMAP in Japan). No DocuSign award was found at German or Canadian federal level, and no ISMAP, CSAP, SecNumCloud or FedRAMP High status was found. These are absences of evidence, not proof. The accurate premise is: DocuSign is widely bought as a departmental workflow tool where no state credential exists and US certifications count, but it has not become the legal signature of any major state. Caveat: most findings rest on search summaries rather than full reads of primary pages. The FedRAMP Marketplace, the EU Trusted List entry for DocuSign France, CMVP certificate 4782, the Reg. 2026/248 Annex II and the registry absences all need a direct check before publication.

reasons.reason: 1. The state owns the signing credential and gives it to citizens free, so a per-envelope vendor competes with free public infrastructure
reasons.explanation: Wherever a state issues an eID or a state-rooted certificate, legal trust comes from that credential, not from the workflow vendor. Free examples include gov.br (214M advanced signatures in 2025), EUDI Wallet QES (required free for non-professional use under Reg. 2024/1183), Poland's mObywatel (5 free QES a month), Estonia's ID-card and Smart-ID, Argentina's PFDR (free certificates under Decree 892/2017), Aadhaar eSign, Sign with Singpass and UAE PASS. DocuSign at best plugs into these, through eMudhra, ICP-Brasil on request, or as a Singpass launch partner. Some it does not support natively, such as Aadhaar and UAE PASS. It markets itself directly against gov.br. This is the most consistent pattern across all four research angles.
reasons.where: EU member states, Brazil, India, Singapore, UAE, Japan, Argentina, Chile, Mexico, Indonesia; weak in US, UK, Australia where no national signing credential exists

reasons.reason: 2. The law sets a signature bar for formal acts that DocuSign's default product does not meet
reasons.explanation: Under eIDAS Art. 25, only a QES is automatically equivalent to handwriting and recognised across the EU. Germany (BGB s.126a), France (public procurement requires an AdES on a qualified certificate), Italy (CAD Art. 65) and Spain (Ley 39/2015 Art. 10) tie formal dealings with the state to a QES or to national tools. In Brazil, only ICP-Brasil signatures carry a presumption of truth, and they are mandatory for acts of heads of Powers and for real estate (Lei 14.063/2020). India recognises only Second Schedule methods from CCA-licensed providers. China requires MIIT-licensed CAs. Canada requires Treasury Board-recognised CAs. US federal staff default to PIV keys under Federal PKI (FIPS 201-3, M-19-17), and DocuSign is not a Federal PKI shared service provider. DocuSign's default envelope is a simple signature with no signer certificate. AES and QES are add-ons, and forum users report validation warnings. Counter-evidence: DocuSign France is a listed QTSP, and the IRS accepts third-party e-signatures on many forms.
reasons.where: EU, Brazil, India, China, Canada, US federal staff signing; not a barrier for low-risk internal, HR and procurement paperwork

reasons.reason: 3. Governments build or own the signing tools themselves, often as open source, which removes the core use case
reasons.explanation: The Commission runs EU Sign, built on its own LGPL DSS library, and offers it to EU agencies. Spain publishes AutoFirma under GPL/EUPL and runs @firma. Estonia's DigiDoc is LGPL. Singapore built Signify (100+ agencies). Argentina embeds PFDR in GDE. Chile runs FirmaGob for officials. Austria runs a state PDF signature service. Germany's ZenDiS ships openDesk, and the 2025 coalition plans a Deutschland-Stack. HM Land Registry built Sign your mortgage deed on GOV.UK One Login. The free technical core forces a vendor to justify its price on workflow alone.
reasons.where: EU institutions, Spain, Estonia, Austria, Germany, Singapore, Argentina, Chile, UK (Land Registry)

reasons.reason: 4. Sovereignty: a US parent company is exposed to the CLOUD Act, FISA 702 and US sanctions, which European doctrine on sensitive data rules out
reasons.explanation: 18 U.S.C. 2713 (CLOUD Act, 2018) reaches data a US provider controls anywhere in the world. Schrems II (C-311/18) and EDPB Recommendations 01/2020 Use Case 6 find no effective technical measure where the provider needs plaintext, and hosted signing does. France's Cloud au centre circulars (2021, 2023), SecNumCloud 3.2 immunity and ownership caps, and SREN Art. 31 (2024) require sensitive state data on immune clouds. On 10 June 2025, Microsoft France testified under oath that it could not guarantee French data would be kept from US authorities. In 2025, sanctions under EO 14203 were reported to cut the ICC prosecutor's Microsoft email, and the ICC reportedly moved to openDesk. Counter-evidence: the EU-US Data Privacy Framework was upheld by the General Court on 3 September 2025 (appeal pending), and French doctrine binds only sensitive data, so non-sensitive use stays open to DocuSign. The 2025 press items were not re-verified.
reasons.where: France and EU central governments for sensitive data, defence, Germany's sovereign stack, Netherlands (2025 parliamentary motions), Denmark; weaker for non-sensitive EU use

reasons.reason: 5. Every country runs its own mandatory cloud certification and hosting gate, and DocuSign appears to lack several
reasons.explanation: Japan expects agencies to buy from the ISMAP list, where Adobe and CloudSign are registered and DocuSign was not found. Korea requires CSAP, which Modusign holds and DocuSign was not found to. France requires SecNumCloud, not found for DocuSign. US high-impact and defence data needs FedRAMP High and IL5, which DocuSign is only working toward. Other gates: Spain's ENS, Italy's ACN QC levels, Germany's C5 (DocuSign claims it), Canada's CCCS PBMM with in-Canada hosting, Australia's IRAP plus Hosting Certification Framework, and the UK's G-Cloud plus Cyber Essentials Plus. EUCS did not settle sovereignty at EU level, so national schemes decide. DocuSign data regions cover only the US, Canada, Europe, Australia and Japan, with no UK, Korea, India or Gulf region. The missing listings are absence of evidence and need registry checks.
reasons.where: Japan, South Korea, France, US high-impact and defence, Spain, Italy, Canada federal, Australia, UK, India, UAE, Saudi Arabia

reasons.reason: 6. Procurement law prefers reuse and open source and makes buyers justify proprietary licences
reasons.explanation: Several laws make buyers justify a proprietary choice. Italy's CAD Art. 68 orders the options (reuse, then open source, then proprietary) and requires a reasoned comparative evaluation, and Art. 69 requires administrations to own and publish commissioned code. Spain's Ley 40/2015 Art. 157 requires checking the CTT reuse directory and justifying non-reuse. The EU Interoperable Europe Act Art. 4 (in force 11 April 2024) requires sharing interoperability solutions, which a third-party IP product cannot satisfy. Other levers: India's 2015 OSS policy (open source preferred, exclusion must be justified), France's 2016 Loi numérique Art. 16 and the SILL, Germany's open-source-by-default for commissioned software, Switzerland's EMBAG Art. 9, the UK TCoP, US M-16-21, and the Digital Public Goods standard used by donor-funded DPI programmes, which proprietary products cannot meet. Counter-evidence: these are mostly preferences with exceptions, not bans.
reasons.where: Italy, Spain, EU, India, France, Germany, Switzerland, UK, low and middle income countries via DPG and GovStack programmes

reasons.reason: 7. Long-term validity, archiving and lock-in: decades-long record duties clash with a vendor-dependent evidence model
reasons.explanation: Government records must stay verifiable for decades, and only PAdES B-LTA with re-timestamping survives certificate expiry. DocuSign's published EU advanced profile is B-LT. Its forum says validity ends with the last document timestamp and that pre-LTV documents had to be downloaded again. Preservation and archiving are now qualified eIDAS trust services (Implementing Regs. 2025/1946 and 2025/2532), and Germany applies TR-ESOR to authorities. No DocuSign preservation status was found. The EU Data Act has required switching and export since 12 September 2025 and bans switching charges from 12 January 2027. NARA and the Federal Records Act need durable formats.
reasons.where: EU, Germany, US federal records, any archive-bound public body

reasons.reason: 8. Per-seat and per-envelope pricing does not fit citizen-scale volumes or fixed public budgets
reasons.explanation: List prices work out to about USD 1.25 to 4.80 per envelope, with roughly 100 envelopes per seat a year. Unsigned envelopes, bulk sends and PowerForm visits count against the allowance. At 10M envelopes a year that would be USD 12.5M to 48M at list price, an estimate of my own; negotiated prices are confidential and likely lower. Private customers report overage at about USD 5.80 per envelope, unconsented doubling of fees, and renewal rises above 20%. Fixed multi-year public budgets cannot absorb this. No complaint from a public body itself was found, and the US OneGov discount partly answers this objection.
reasons.where: Citizen-facing national services everywhere; less so in US federal under OneGov

reasons.reason: 9. The brand is abused for phishing, and its API has been abused to send genuine-looking fraud
reasons.explanation: In 2017 a breach of a non-core system leaked customer emails that fuelled DocuSign-branded malware. In November 2024, Wallarm and BleepingComputer reported attackers using paid accounts and the Envelopes API to send fake invoices that pass SPF and DKIM. DocuSign is one of the most impersonated brands in phishing. For a government sending documents to millions of citizens, emails branded as DocuSign are a liability.

reasons.reason: 10. Cloud only: there is no supported on-premises or air-gapped edition for classified and critical networks
reasons.explanation: DocuSign eSignature is multi-tenant SaaS, its government environment included, and the old on-prem Signature Appliance line appears retired (weak, not re-checked). Several networks need on-prem or air-gapped deployment: DoD IL6/SECRET, France's Diffusion Restreinte, Germany's VS-NfD and defence ministries generally. Self-hostable rivals exist: OneSpan, Ascertia, DocuSeal, Documenso and LibreSign.
reasons.where: Defence and classified networks in the US, France, Germany and elsewhere

reasons.reason: 11. Data-use and contract trust: secondary use and AI training are flashpoints for public buyers
reasons.explanation: In March 2024 the EDPS found the Commission's Microsoft 365 use unlawful for unspecified purposes and inadequate transfer safeguards. That sets the contract bar for any SaaS processor. DocuSign's February 2024 FAQ on training AI on customer data (with consent) drew public criticism. This is press coverage that was not re-verified.
reasons.where: EU institutions and data-protection-led buyers globally

requirements.requirement: Build a jurisdiction rules engine that sets the minimum signature level (SES, AES, AdES on a qualified certificate, QES, or a named national tool) for each country and document type. It must block excluded document types, such as India's First Schedule (wills, negotiable instruments, powers of attorney), and force QES where the law requires it, such as German written form, Brazilian real estate and acts of heads of Powers. Record the level achieved on the signed file and in the evidence report.
requirements.why: Acceptance depends on the legal level for each act (eIDAS Art. 25, BGB 126a, Lei 14.063 Art. 5, IT Act Second Schedule), not on the brand.
requirements.who_needs_it: All markets; essential in EU, Brazil, India

requirements.requirement: Output standard AdES at B-LTA by default: PAdES for PDF, XAdES or ASiC-E for XML and bundles, CAdES (.p7m) for binary. Profiles must match Annex II of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/248, keeping the old 2015/1506 formats during the 24-month transition. Embed all certificates and OCSP/CRL data.
requirements.why: EU public bodies only have to accept the listed formats (eIDAS Art. 27), and only B-LTA survives certificate and timestamp expiry. DocuSign publishes only B-LT.
requirements.who_needs_it: EU/EEA public bodies, any archive-bound government

requirements.requirement: Validate every incoming and outgoing signature with the Commission's open-source DSS library against the EU Trusted Lists. Pass with zero warnings in Adobe (AATL), DigiDoc4, Spain's @firma, Brazil's ITI VALIDAR, Finland's DVV validator and Japan's MyKey platform.
requirements.why: Users report DocuSign outputs raising untrusted-chain warnings. A public body receiving files from many senders needs clean validation.
requirements.who_needs_it: EU, Estonia, Spain, Brazil, Finland, Japan

requirements.requirement: Never let a vendor platform seal break the signer's certificate chain. Add vendor evidence only as a separate document timestamp or ASiC component.
requirements.why: Forum reports say DocuSign's platform seal causes third-party validation errors.

requirements.requirement: Add a long-term preservation pipeline: convert to PDF/A before signing, export PDF/A-3 with the audit trail embedded, re-timestamp archives on a schedule before TSA certificates expire, and offer a preservation mode built to ETSI TS 119 511, BSI TR-ESOR and CEN/TS 18170. Export in NARA-accepted formats.
requirements.why: Decades-long records duties; qualified preservation and archiving under eIDAS Arts. 34 and 45j; TR-ESOR for German authorities; 36 CFR 1236.

requirements.requirement: Build a pluggable bring-your-own-trust-anchor layer. The signing certificate can come from the user's smart card (PKCS#11, Web eID), a remote QSCD over the Cloud Signature Consortium API or ETSI TS 119 432, or a national or state CA. The product orchestrates the workflow and never replaces the state's signature.
requirements.why: The state owns the credential in most major governments. The product must be the workflow layer that calls it.
requirements.who_needs_it: All non-US markets and US federal staff

requirements.requirement: Act as an EUDI Wallet relying party: accept PID presentation for signer identity, and let the signer create a QES from the wallet through a QTSP's remote QSCD, free to the citizen. Prepare for the NL Wallet and the German wallet.
requirements.why: Reg. 2024/1183 makes free wallet QES the default citizen path from about December 2026. DocuSign has only a prototype.

requirements.requirement: Build EU national connectors: Estonia ID-card, Mobile-ID and Smart-ID (ASiC-E/BDOC); Belgian BeID and itsme; ID Austria; Poland's podpis zaufany, podpis osobisty and mObywatel QES; Italy's SPID/CIE identity plus remote signing from Italian QTSPs; Spain's Cl@ve, Cl@ve Firma, DNIe and FNMT certificates, with output AutoFirma can read; Germany's nPA eID plus a German QTSP such as D-Trust; Finland's DVV Citizen Certificate; Denmark's MitID and NemLog-in3.
requirements.why: Each state ties formal dealings to its own tool and gives it free. Citizens will not buy a second credential.
requirements.who_needs_it: Estonia, Belgium, Austria, Poland, Italy, Spain, Germany, Finland, Denmark

requirements.requirement: Support US federal signing with the user's own PIV or CAC signature key, producing PAdES or XAdES chained to the Federal Common Policy root. Validate Federal PKI bridge paths, support delegated role certificates, and map each flow to NIST SP 800-63-4 IAL, AAL and FAL levels and to the agency's GPEA risk assessment.
requirements.why: Federal staff default to PIV signatures (FIPS 201-3, M-19-17, the Interior and GSA policies). Federal Register submissions require PIV-based XAdES.

requirements.requirement: Build Americas connectors: gov.br advanced signature for citizens (free), and ICP-Brasil A1, A3 token and cloud A3 under ICP-Brasil signature policies; Mexico's SAT e.firma (.cer/.key); Chile's FirmaGob API with ClaveUnica and the institutional ministro de fe enrolment; Argentina's PFDR (firmar.gob.ar) and GDE; Canada's myKEY and GCKey.
requirements.why: These are the state signature systems in each country. ICP-Brasil alone carries a presumption of truth, and gov.br is free.

requirements.requirement: Build Asia, Middle East and Africa connectors: India's Aadhaar eSign through a CCA-empanelled ESP, Class 3 DSC USB tokens for MCA21-type portals, and push to DigiLocker; Sign with Singpass; UAE PASS signing with verified-account enforcement; Saudi Nafath with a licensed provider under the National Root CA; Japan's JPKI on the My Number Card; Korea's GPKI and mobile civil servant ID, LDAP org-chart sync and administrative standard codes; Indonesia's BSrE API under the agency-held PKS model; certificates from Kenya's ICTA and E-CSPs; South Africa SAAA-accredited AES; China MIIT-licensed CAs.
requirements.why: Every one of these states roots signatures in a state or state-licensed PKI. DocuSign lacks native Aadhaar and UAE PASS support.
requirements.who_needs_it: India, Singapore, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Japan, South Korea, Indonesia, Kenya, South Africa, China

requirements.requirement: Integrate GOV.UK One Login for UK citizen identity, with a code-to-phone signing step modelled on HM Land Registry's Sign your mortgage deed.
requirements.why: The UK has no national signing credential, and the state's own signing service uses One Login.

requirements.requirement: Offer an end-to-end encrypted envelope mode: documents are encrypted on the client, the operator handles only ciphertext and hashes, and keys are customer-held (hold-your-own-key in the customer's HSM). The vendor must be technically unable to read documents or signing keys.
requirements.why: EDPB Use Case 6 sees no effective measure when the provider sees plaintext. Customer-held keys answer CLOUD Act exposure.
requirements.who_needs_it: EU public bodies, France, Germany, defence

requirements.requirement: Ship a self-hosted and air-gapped edition: one container image or Helm chart deployable like openDesk, no telemetry or licence call-home, signed offline update bundles, PKCS#11 HSM support, and a local time-stamping authority. It must run on state internal clouds and in Japan's LGWAN.
requirements.why: Classified networks (IL6, Diffusion Restreinte, VS-NfD), France's state clouds, and governments that build their own all need it. DocuSign is SaaS only.
requirements.who_needs_it: Defence ministries, France, Germany, Japan local government, any government wanting to own the stack

requirements.requirement: Make signed documents verifiable offline with standard tools, with no dependence on vendor servers or vendor-only revocation endpoints.
requirements.why: Continuity against sanctions kill switches (the 2025 ICC case) and decades-long record validity.

requirements.requirement: Offer one-click full export and migration at no charge: original and signed PDFs (PDF/A, PAdES), audit trails in an open JSON schema, templates, contacts and settings. Include an import tool from DocuSign, open APIs and webhooks.
requirements.why: EU Data Act switching rules apply from 12 September 2025, switching fees are banned from 12 January 2027, and UK TCoP point 11 requires an exit plan.

requirements.requirement: Build anti-abuse controls: know-your-business checks before API or bulk sending, a verified sender domain mark for official domains (.gov, .gouv.fr, .bund.de), per-tenant rate limits with anomaly detection, a one-click report button in every email, and DMARC p=reject with BIMI.
requirements.why: DocuSign's API was abused in 2024 to send fake invoices that pass SPF and DKIM, and the brand is heavily phished.

requirements.requirement: Let citizens sign inside the government's own authenticated portal or app, with the government's branding rather than the vendor's. Offer access codes and out-of-band verification, and do not rely on email links.
requirements.why: This reduces phishing risk and matches how states already deliver services (gov.br, Singpass, mObywatel).

requirements.requirement: Work fully on Linux and open office suites: accept ODF (ISO/IEC 26300) and PDF/A, with no Windows or Microsoft 365 dependency. Ship plug-ins for Nextcloud, Open-Xchange, Thunderbird, LibreOffice and openDesk, with single sign-on and file storage.
requirements.why: Schleswig-Holstein, the Danish ministry, Lyon, the Austrian Armed Forces and the ICC are migrating off US software, and the Dutch comply-or-explain list includes ODF and PDF/A.
requirements.who_needs_it: Germany, Denmark, France, Austria, Netherlands, international organisations

requirements.requirement: Keep the AI help assistant on a self-hosted open-weight model inside the customer's boundary. It must be swappable or switchable off per tenant, its logs must stay under customer control, and no document, field value or signer data may be used for training.
requirements.why: Training on customer data is a trust flashpoint (DocuSign's 2024 controversy, EDPS ruling on Microsoft 365). DPG platform independence requires replaceable components.

requirements.requirement: Keep the tree-planting impact feature and any token mechanic optional and switchable off per tenant, kept out of the signed legal record and the evidence report, and independently verifiable.
requirements.why: Speculative, not researched: public buyers may test incentives against procurement, gift and green-claims rules. A signed record must contain only the agreement and its evidence.
requirements.who_needs_it: Government tenants; especially EU public bodies

requirements.requirement: Provide a full localised interface, at minimum English and French for Canada and the official languages of each target market.
requirements.why: Canadian federal requirement; the same applies to multilingual EU states.

requirements.requirement: Build a public total-cost-of-ownership calculator for 1M, 10M and 100M signatures a year, covering hosting, support and staff, with zero licence cost per signature.
requirements.why: Italy's CAD Art. 68 comma 1-bis and the UK TCoP require total-cost evaluation, and per-envelope cost at citizen scale is DocuSign's weak point.
requirements.who_needs_it: Italy, UK, all buyers running comparative evaluations

requirements.requirement: Host data and processing in each target market: EU, UK, Canada, Australia, Japan, Korea, India, UAE, Saudi Arabia (in-Kingdom rules not verified) and Brazil. Render and hash documents in-region, with no remote access from outside the region, including by a parent company.
requirements.why: Canadian Protected B policy (Policy on Service and Digital 4.4.3.14), Australia's Hosting Certification Framework, Schrems II, and national schemes that require in-country hosting. DocuSign has no UK, Korea, India or Gulf region.

requirements.requirement: For France, run on a SecNumCloud-qualified IaaS through an operator that itself meets the SecNumCloud 3.2 ownership and control rules, or on the state's interministerial clouds.
requirements.why: Cloud au centre circulars 6282/SG and 6404/SG, plus SREN Art. 31, for sensitive data.

requirements.requirement: For the US, run on a government region (GovCloud type) operated by US persons only, at IL4 and IL5 separation, with GovRAMP-ready hosting for states.
requirements.why: DoD Cloud SRG and FedRAMP High baselines. DocuSign stops at Moderate and IL4.

requirements.requirement: Keep all signing and sealing keys in HSMs with active (not historical or sunset) FIPS 140-3 Level 3 certificates, and publish the certificate numbers. Use a QSCD certified to EN 419 241-2 for remote QES, and HSMs to EN 419 221-5.
requirements.why: Federal FIPS 140-3 rules and eIDAS remote QES. DocuSign's HSM validations are historical, and its interim 140-3 certificate passed its sunset date on 27 August 2026.

requirements.requirement: In Australia, host only with a DTA Certified Strategic or Certified Assured provider.
requirements.why: The Hosting Certification Framework for sensitive whole-of-government data.

requirements.requirement: Run notification and contact systems separately from core document data, and publish a public trust page with the incident history.
requirements.why: The 2017 DocuSign breach of a non-core system leaked customer emails used for phishing.

requirements.requirement: Hold ISO/IEC 27001:2022, 27017, 27018 and 27701 certificates, and a SOC 2 Type II report covering security, availability, confidentiality and processing integrity.
requirements.why: Baseline requirements in tenders across all researched jurisdictions.

requirements.requirement: US path: FedRAMP Moderate, then High, through FedRAMP 20x or a platform partner, plus DoD IL4 and IL5 and GovRAMP. Alternatively, a self-hosted edition that inherits the agency's own ATO.
requirements.why: FedRAMP Authorization Act (FY2023 NDAA). Moderate is the entry ticket, and High and IL5 are unoccupied ground DocuSign has not reached.

requirements.requirement: National cloud certifications, ordered by target market: C5 Type 2 (Germany), ENS HIGH (Spain), ACN QC2 or higher (Italy), SecNumCloud (France), ISMAP or ISMAP-LIU (Japan), CSAP (Korea), IRAP PROTECTED renewed within 24 months against the current ISM (Australia), CCCS PBMM under ITSM.50.100 (Canada), and Cyber Essentials Plus with the NCSC Cloud Security Principles (UK).
requirements.why: Each country gates purchases on its own scheme, and EUCS has not replaced them. DocuSign appears to lack ISMAP, CSAP and SecNumCloud.
requirements.who_needs_it: Germany, Spain, Italy, France, Japan, Korea, Australia, Canada, UK

requirements.requirement: Obtain QTSP status in at least one EU Member State (ETSI EN 319 401 and 411), or partner with QTSPs, for qualified certificates, seals and timestamps. Aim later for a qualified preservation listing. Do not claim qualified status without a Trusted List entry.
requirements.why: QES requires a QTSP on a national Trusted List. DocuSign France is a QTSP, so a rival must match it.

requirements.requirement: National signature licensing: become a CCA-empanelled eSign Service Provider or integrate one (India); obtain SAAA AES accreditation or route through LAWtrust (South Africa); get foreign E-CSP recognition from the Communications Authority or partner with ICTA (Kenya); use a licensed provider under the Saudi National Root CA; use MIIT-licensed CAs (China); work with ICP-Brasil accredited CAs (Brazil); and be ready for NITDA accreditation once it exists (Nigeria).
requirements.why: These states recognise only signatures from licensed or accredited providers.
requirements.who_needs_it: India, South Africa, Kenya, Saudi Arabia, China, Brazil, Nigeria

requirements.requirement: Offer identity proofing accredited to NIST SP 800-63-4 IAL2 or higher (for example through Kantara-accredited providers).
requirements.why: SP 800-63-4 superseded 800-63-3 in July 2025. DocuSign offers IAL2 through ID.me and CLEAR under rev 3.

requirements.requirement: Pass the ETSI TS 119 144-4 signature conformance test suites, and back every claimed authorisation with an entry on the official registry (FedRAMP Marketplace, BSI, ISMAP list, CCCS, CMVP, EU Trusted List).
requirements.why: Buyers discount vendor claims that a registry cannot confirm. Many of DocuSign's claims are vendor-only.

requirements.requirement: Apply for the Digital Public Goods registry: OSI-approved licence, clear ownership, replaceable providers for email, payments and AI, open data export, a privacy policy and do-no-harm documentation. Publish a GovStack building-block conformance statement (whether an e-signature building block exists is unconfirmed).
requirements.why: UN and donor-backed DPI programmes such as 50-in-5 select from DPGs, which excludes proprietary products by design.
requirements.who_needs_it: Low and middle income country governments, donor programmes

requirements.requirement: License the core under an OSI-approved copyleft licence (EUPL-1.2 or AGPL-3.0), with no reserved rights that stop an administration publishing or sharing the customisations it paid for.
requirements.why: Interoperable Europe Act Art. 4 sharing, Italy's CAD Art. 68 and 69, Switzerland's EMBAG Art. 9, Spain's Ley 40/2015 Art. 157, India's OSS policy, France's 2016 law Art. 16, and the DPG standard.
requirements.who_needs_it: EU, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, India, France, Germany

requirements.requirement: Offer a public-sector DPA: an exhaustive list of purposes, a ban on secondary use of documents and metadata (analytics, product improvement, AI training), every sub-processor and its location named, and controller audit rights. Ship a ready DPIA and transfer impact assessment pack.
requirements.why: The EDPS March 2024 ruling on the Commission's Microsoft 365 use, Schrems II, and the Dutch SLM Rijk DPIA practice.
requirements.who_needs_it: EU institutions, EU public bodies, Netherlands

requirements.requirement: Contractual sovereignty guarantee: no legal path for a foreign authority to compel disclosure, a duty to notify the customer of and challenge any request, termination rights and penalties on breach, the customer's own law governing termination, a published legal opinion on extraterritorial exposure, and a transparency report.
requirements.why: Microsoft France could not give this guarantee under oath in June 2025, and US vendors remain bound by the CLOUD Act and sanctions.

requirements.requirement: Put the source code in escrow and guarantee continuity in the contract, so no single foreign government can switch the service off.
requirements.why: Sanctions risk shown by the 2025 ICC episode.

requirements.requirement: Price the government tier per deployment, not per seat or envelope: free to self-host, with a fixed annual fee for support or hosting, unlimited senders and envelopes, and no overage. Unsigned envelopes, bulk citizen sends and public form visits are never billable, and citizen signers never pay. Keep monthly-expiring consumer credits out of the government tier (an inference from the fixed-budget findings).
requirements.why: Per-envelope cost at citizen scale, overage complaints, and states that already give signatures away free (gov.br, the EUDI Wallet, mObywatel).

requirements.requirement: Government contract terms: annual rises capped (for example at CPI), at least 90 days' notice, no renewal at a new price without explicit written acceptance, a public price list, multi-year price holds, annual invoicing, and termination for convenience.
requirements.why: Renewal price-rise complaints, and government budget cycles flagged in DocuSign's own 10-K risk factors.

requirements.requirement: Commit to incident notification at least as strict as NIS2: early warning within 24 hours, notification within 72 hours.
requirements.why: NIS2 baseline, and a public-sector trust expectation after the 2017 breach.

requirements.requirement: Capture intent, authenticate the signer and seal integrity in line with IRS IRM 10.10.1 sections 10.10.1.3 and 10.10.1.6, and keep audit trails strong enough for evidentiary admissibility.
requirements.why: The IRS accepts third-party e-signatures under these conditions, and Nigeria's recognition is evidentiary (Evidence Amendment Act 2023).
requirements.who_needs_it: US IRS filings, Nigeria, courts generally

requirements.requirement: Set up a locally domiciled, locally owned and controlled operating entity for each sovereign region, starting with an EU entity. It must meet SecNumCloud 3.2 caps (about 24% per non-EU shareholder, 39% combined, no non-EU control) and have no foreign parent with control over the data.
requirements.why: CLOUD Act control test, SecNumCloud immunity, Australian ownership conditions.

requirements.requirement: Get onto procurement vehicles: GSA MAS through a reseller with OneGov-style published discounts, NASPO ValuePoint and state umbrella contracts, a direct G-Cloud listing with a published price, Australian state standing offers, TED eligibility for EU tenders, and CanadaBuys.
requirements.why: DocuSign reaches government through exactly these channels, and buyers rarely buy outside them.

requirements.requirement: List in public reuse catalogues: Developers Italia, Spain's CTT, France's SILL, Germany's openCoDE, code.europa.eu and the Interoperable Europe portal, and code.gov.
requirements.why: Reuse laws require buyers to check these catalogues first.
requirements.who_needs_it: Italy, Spain, France, Germany, EU, US

requirements.requirement: Be a certified integration partner of each national signing scheme from its launch: EUDI Wallet pilots, Singpass, UAE PASS, Nafath, a CCA ESP, and QTSPs in Italy, Germany and Poland.
requirements.why: DocuSign won Singapore access as a Sign with Singpass launch partner, and states favour early certified partners.
requirements.who_needs_it: EU, Singapore, UAE, Saudi Arabia, India

requirements.requirement: Provide in-country support staff where required (Canadian staff, US-persons-only operations for IL5, EU-only staff for EU tenants), and publish a staff-location statement.
requirements.why: CCCS and Protected B expectations, the DoD SRG, and EU no-remote-access requirements.

requirements.requirement: Publish named, verifiable government references, and a certification roadmap ordered by target market: ISO and SOC 2 first, then C5, ENS, SecNumCloud hosting, IRAP, CCCS, ISMAP, CSAP, and FedRAMP through a partner.
requirements.why: Buyers discount unsupported vendor claims, and each gate takes months to years.

requirements.requirement: Position the product as the workflow, routing, audit and archiving layer on top of the state's own free signature, and target the segments where DocuSign is structurally blocked: EU central and German state governments, defence, sensitive data, eID-based citizen services and donor-funded DPI. Do not attack US civilian agencies head-on.
requirements.why: DocuSign is entrenched in US federal (OneGov, FedRAMP, IL4) but is not the legal signature of any major state.

requirements.requirement: Track regulatory change continuously: eIDAS 2 implementing acts and wallet dates, the Reg. 2026/248 transition, the outcome of the Latombe appeal on the Data Privacy Framework, SHARE IT Act status, Nigeria's NITDA bill, and Saudi in-Kingdom hosting rules. Re-verify unconfirmed items (DocuSign FedRAMP High, ISMAP and CSAP status, CMVP certificate 4782) on the official registries.
requirements.why: Several findings rest on search summaries or carry conflicting dates, and the rules are moving.

status.evidence: src/lib/paperwork.ts: a check before sending reads the subject, document names and text for words that usually mean a will, power of attorney, land sale, long lease, fixed-term employment contract or a deed needing a witness or notary (English, German, Spanish, Portuguese, French). It warns, never blocks, and writes the warning to the audit trail. /help#outside-us has dated country notes with sources. Missing: there is only one signature level (simple electronic), no per-country or per-document minimum level, no blocking, and no level recorded on the signed file.

README 'What is not in it': 'PDFs are not cryptographically signed with a PKI certificate (PAdES)'. src/server/pdf.ts stamps values with pdf-lib and appends a certificate page; there is no CMS signature, no timestamp, no XAdES, ASiC or CAdES output.
/verify (POST /public/verify in src/server/routes-account.ts) only compares the SHA-256 of a whole file with completed files stored here. No signature validation, no trust lists, no DSS.

There is no platform seal yet, so nothing breaks a chain today, but worse: flatPages() in src/server/pdf.ts copies every uploaded page into a new document, so any digital signature already in an uploaded PDF is silently destroyed in the signed output.

GET /api/export ZIP (signed PDFs, audit trails, CSV index), the evidence pack with the audit trail as JSON and how to recompute its chain (src/server/evidence.ts), and the SHA-256 kept a year after deletion (FINGERPRINT_KEPT_DAYS in src/lib/evidence.ts). Missing: PDF/A, audit trail embedded as a PDF/A-3 attachment, re-timestamping, retention schedules, a preservation mode, NARA formats.
No certificate handling of any kind: no PKCS#11, Web eID, CSC API or national CA support.
No OpenID4VP, PID or wallet code.
Only Google and Microsoft OpenID Connect with fixed endpoints (provider() in src/server/oidc.ts). The code flow with PKCE and hand-written ID token checks is a reusable base.

No PIV/CAC, no X.509 signing, no Federal PKI path validation, no IAL/AAL/FAL recorded. CHECK_PROVES in src/lib/checks.ts honestly says what each existing check (link, access code, email or SMS code) proves.
No gov.br, ICP-Brasil, e.firma, FirmaGob, PFDR or GCKey integration.
No Aadhaar eSign, DSC token, Singpass, UAE PASS, Nafath, JPKI, GPKI, BSrE or licensed-CA integration.
No GOV.UK One Login. A one-time code by text message to the signer's phone exists (src/server/signercode.ts), which resembles the Land Registry code step but involves no identity proofing.

FILE_ENCRYPTION_KEY encrypts stored files with AES-256-GCM (src/server/filecrypt.ts), but the key sits in server settings, the server processes plaintext, and the database is not encrypted (README 'Encrypting stored files', 'What is not protected'). The operator can read everything.

One Node process, SQLite through node:sqlite (src/server/db.ts), files on disk, fonts and pdf.js bundled locally, an internal 15-minute timer (src/instrumentation.ts), and every outside service off unless configured (SMTP, Stripe, Twilio, Google, Microsoft). Missing: container image or Helm chart, an outbound allowlist, Next.js build telemetry switched off, HSM, a time-stamping authority, signed offline update bundles, LGWAN testing.

The SHA-256 of the signed PDF is in every completion email and the chain head is on the certificate, and the evidence pack lets anyone recompute the audit chain offline. But there is no embedded signature a standard PDF reader can check, and /verify is the vendor's own server.

A free export ZIP on every plan, also after cancelling (GET /api/export in src/server/routes-trust.ts), the evidence pack, the full JSON API and webhooks. Missing: templates, contacts, groups and settings in the export, a published JSON schema, any import, a DocuSign import.

Daily limits on newly emailed people for untrusted accounts, a fake payment notice filter (src/server/fakenotice.ts), reports with an automatic pause (ABUSE_SUSPEND_AFTER), a security code in every email checkable on /check, a report link in every signing email, and bounce and complaint handling. Missing: business checks before API or bulk use, a verified official sender domain mark, per-tenant API rate limits and anomaly alerts. DMARC and BIMI are DNS work for the operator.

Embedded signing links (POST /envelopes/{id}/recipient-view, redirect only; framing is refused by X-Frame-Options SAMEORIGIN in next.config.mjs), account logo and colour on emails and the signing page, access codes, email and SMS codes, and 'I will send the link myself'. The vendor name stays in emails (footer in src/server/mail.ts), and a portal cannot assert who the signer is.

Browser only, runs on Linux, no Windows or Microsoft 365 dependency. Uploads are PDF, PNG and JPEG only (README: Word or Google Docs upload not built, so no ODF). No Nextcloud, LibreOffice, Thunderbird or openDesk plug-ins, and no SAML or generic OIDC single sign-on.

The helper is not built yet. The brief (research/briefs.json, 'chat') defaults to hosted Kimi K3 through OpenRouter or Moonshot. It allows SUPPORT_CHAT_BASE_URL (any OpenAI-compatible host, so a self-hosted endpoint is possible) and stores nothing beyond limits and hand-overs. No per-tenant switch is planned.

Every certificate of completion prints the paper, water and CO2e saved and 'Every dollar paid to Sign&Grow plants 10 mangrove trees with Treegens' (src/server/pdf.ts, around line 470), and so does the email footer (src/server/mail.ts line 100). There is no per-tenant switch, and the impact brief adds a '10 mangroves' line to the signing page and the request email.

English only (LANGUAGE_NOTE in src/lib/policy.ts, <html lang="en"> in src/app/layout.tsx). The groundwork is good: the PDF prints many scripts, right-to-left ordering works (src/server/bidi.ts), and date and number formats are per account.
No calculator. Pricing is per signature (PRICING in src/lib/impact.ts).

One region per deployment by design (README: 'one region for everything, because storage is one disk'), stated on /security from DATA_REGION and DATA_HOST. Any region works by running a separate instance. Nothing runs in any of the listed markets today.
No hosting arrangement exists.
No hosting arrangement exists.
No HSM and no signing keys. APP_SECRET and FILE_ENCRYPTION_KEY live in environment settings or DATA_DIR.
No hosting arrangement exists.

/security is a public trust page that lists what the code does and does not do. Mail goes through a separately configured SMTP provider. There is no incident history, and contacts and emails sit in the same SQLite file as the documents.
/security says: 'No security certification. We have not been audited against a security standard'.
None held or started.
None held or started.
No QTSP status and no QTSP partner.
No national licences or partners.
No identity proofing. README 'What is not in it': ID verification not built.
No conformance tests have been run, and no claims are made either (the honest starting point).
package.json is "private": true and there is no LICENSE file, so the code is not open source and cannot apply.
No licence.

WHO_CAN_SEE and KEPT_AFTER_DELETION in src/lib/policy.ts, and sub-processors listed from settings (src/lib/dataplace.ts). No signed DPA, no contractual ban on secondary use, no DPIA or transfer impact assessment pack.

But the price is per signature (US$1, PRICING in src/lib/impact.ts), bulk sends pay per signer, there is no price per deployment, and monthly expiry is being added now (the 'expiry' brief).

batches.title: Honesty guard and tenant switches: no false certification claims, trees and AI kept out of the legal record
batches.needs_from_operator: Owner decision 8: take the impact block off every certificate (recommended) or only off government tenants' certificates.
batches.brief:
Goal: before any public buyer sees the product, make it impossible for the product to claim a certification it does not hold, and make the tree and AI features optional per tenant and absent from the signed legal record.

Build:
1. src/lib/claims.ts: one registry of every certification, accreditation and legal status a public buyer may ask about: ISO/IEC 27001, 27017, 27018 and 27701, SOC 2 Type II, FedRAMP Moderate and High, DoD IL4 and IL5, GovRAMP, BSI C5, ENS, ACN QC, SecNumCloud, ISMAP, CSAP, IRAP, CCCS PBMM, Cyber Essentials Plus, G-Cloud listing, eIDAS QTSP, qualified seal, QES, FIPS 140-3 validated module, a third-party WCAG 2.2 AA or EN 301 549 audit, Section 508 ACR, HIPAA BAA, Digital Public Goods registry, CCA ESP, ICP-Brasil. Each entry has id, name, status ('not_held' | 'in_progress' | 'held'), and for 'held': the official registry URL, certificate or listing number, scope, issued and expiry dates, and who checked it and when. All start as 'not_held'. A 'held' entry past its expiry date reads as not held. claimText(id) returns the only sentence any page may print about it, for example 'We do not hold an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate.'
2. A public page /security/certifications, built only from the registry, that lists every entry in plain words. Link it from /security, where the existing 'No security certification' point stays and quotes the registry.
3. tests/claims.test.ts: scan src/**, README.md, .env.example, public/ and docs/ for each name and its common spellings (FedRAMP, ISO 27001, SOC 2, SecNumCloud, IRAP, ISMAP, C5, FIPS, '508', 'VPAT') and for the risky words 'qualified electronic signature', 'advanced electronic signature', 'QES', 'legally binding', 'compliant', 'certified', 'FIPS validated', 'eIDAS compliant'. A hit fails unless the line, or the line above it, carries a marker comment 'claims-ok: <id> <reason>' and the sentence agrees with the entry's status. Existing honest sentences (for example the README line that the product does not make advanced or qualified signatures) get markers. The test prints each hit with file and line.
4. src/server/tenantpolicy.ts with a db.ts migration adding to accounts: impact_display ('on'|'off', default 'on'), ai_helper ('on'|'off', default 'on'), white_label (0/1, default 0, used by G17). DEPLOYMENT_PROFILE=government makes new accounts start with impact off and the AI helper off. Owners and admins change these under Settings, Account, each change goes into the account's history, and API keys cannot change them. tenantPolicy(accountId) is the one reader. batches.title: Sovereign single container: any cloud, on premises or air-gapped, no call home, outbound allowlist, backups
files_touched: src/app/api/[...path]/route.ts or a new health route file
batches.needs_from_operator: Owner decision on the signing key for offline update bundles (who holds it). No licence is needed to build, but publishing the image waits for decision 1.
batches.brief:
Goal: a public body can run the whole product itself, as one container, on any cloud, on its own servers or on a network with no internet, with nothing calling home and every outside service optional.

Read first: node_modules/next/dist/docs (AGENTS.md: this Next.js version differs from what you know), especially standalone output.

Build:
1. Dockerfile, multi-stage, on a pinned base image digest with Node 22 LTS. The build runs npm ci (fonts are built then by scripts/copy-assets.mjs, so the runtime needs no network), next build with NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 set in both build and runtime, and Next's standalone output if this version supports it, otherwise a pruned node_modules. Run as a non-root user with a read-only root filesystem and one writable volume at DATA_DIR. Add a HEALTHCHECK against a new GET /api/health that answers 200 only when the database opens, DATA_DIR is writable, the file store is not stopped (fileStoreWarning) and the internal timer ticked within 30 minutes, and otherwise says which of these failed. It gives out nothing about tenants.
2. deploy/compose.yaml (the app, a volume, an env file) and a Helm chart deploy/helm/growsigning: replicas fixed at 1 with strategy Recreate (SQLite has one writer, so say why in values.yaml), a PVC, a Secret for APP_SECRET and FILE_ENCRYPTION_KEY, and a NetworkPolicy whose egress is denied by default, with a list to allow.
3. src/server/outbound.ts, installed from src/instrumentation.ts before anything else runs. On start, compute the outside hosts the configuration implies: the SMTP host, api.stripe.com when Stripe keys are set, Twilio or the SMS webhook host, Google or Microsoft when configured, and later the TSA, OCSP and AI hosts. Log that list once and show it on /security as 'This server connects to: ...', with what each is for. With SOVEREIGN_MODE=1, wrap globalThis.fetch so any host outside that list plus OUTBOUND_ALLOW (comma separated) is refused with an error naming the host and the setting. Check the SMTP host the same way at start. Webhook targets are tenant-chosen: in sovereign mode they must match WEBHOOK_ALLOW_HOSTS. Log a refused host once an hour, not per call.
4. Air-gapped use: document and test that the server starts and works with no network. Payments, Google, Microsoft and SMS stay off, mail goes through an internal relay or is recorded as 'Not emailed', and signing links come from the API (recipient-view) or 'I will send the link myself'. scripts/release-bundle.mjs writes a release bundle: the image tarball (docker save), the SBOM from G03, SHA256SUMS, and a detached signature with an offline key (minisign or cosign key mode, per the owner's decision). scripts/verify-bundle.mjs checks it before docker load and refuses a bundle that does not verify.
5. Backups: scripts/backup.mjs makes a consistent copy of sign.db while the server runs. Use node:sqlite's backup function if this Node version has it (check: it is newer than 22.13), otherwise VACUUM INTO. It copies DATA_DIR/blobs with a manifest of SHA-256 sums and never copies FILE_ENCRYPTION_KEY or APP_SECRET; say where those must be kept instead. scripts/restore.mjs checks the manifest and refuses a partial backup.
6. Reproducible build notes for source escrow: the lockfile, the pinned base digest, and the exact commands, so an escrow agent can rebuild the same image.
7. README section 'Running it yourself': one container, the volume, the settings that matter, what each outside service does and that each is optional, what works with no network, backups and restore, and why there is one replica. No claim of 'air-gap certified'. Say exactly what was tested ('started and completed an envelope with docker run --network none on <date>').

Tests (tests/sovereign.test.ts, no network): the computed host list for several configurations; sovereign mode refuses an unlisted host and allows a listed one; a webhook to an unlisted host is refused at save and at delivery; /api/health in each failure state; backup then restore gives a byte-identical database and blobs; a backup without its manifest is refused. Add scripts/container-smoke.sh, run by hand where Docker exists: build, run with --network none, create an envelope through the API, sign it through recipient-view, download the signed PDF, and check /verify matches.

Settings: SOVEREIGN_MODE, OUTBOUND_ALLOW, WEBHOOK_ALLOW_HOSTS. Add them to .env.example and the README table.

Leave out: Postgres and more than one replica (G26), HSM (G21), timestamping (G05).

batches.brief:
Goal: give a procurement officer every document they normally ask for on day one, true to the code, dated, and clear about what is self-assessed.

Build:
1. scripts/sbom.mjs, run as npm run sbom: writes docs/procurement/sbom.cdx.json in CycloneDX (npm sbom --sbom-format cyclonedx; npm 10.9 has it) and docs/procurement/third-party-licences.md (every package and font with its licence: pdf-lib MIT, Noto OFL-1.1, DejaVu, and so on). It fails on a package with no licence. Once the owner picks the product licence (decision 1), it also fails on a licence that cannot be combined with it.
2. docs/procurement/security-whitepaper.md: architecture (one process, SQLite, the file store, the internal timer), data flows with a diagram, a data inventory (from README 'What is not protected'), a crypto inventory (scrypt passwords, AES-256-GCM with HKDF-SHA256 for files, HMAC-SHA256 links and codes, TOTP HMAC-SHA1, the SHA-256 audit chain, TLS left to the reverse proxy), sessions, two-step login, rate limits, logging, backups, encryption at rest and its limits, and what is not done. Every statement names the file it rests on. Dated.
3. docs/procurement/controls-self-mapping.md: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A and NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 Moderate, family by family, each control marked 'done by the software (file)', 'the operator's job' or 'not done'. The title says 'Self-assessment. Not audited by anyone.'
4. docs/procurement/data-processing-terms-template.md, marked 'Template for a lawyer. Not legal advice. Not a contract until signed': an exhaustive list of purposes; a ban on secondary use (analytics, product improvement, AI training), which the software can stand behind because it stores no analytics; sub-processors with locations taken from settings; audit rights; deletion; notification within 24 and 72 hours; return of data. Next to each clause, note which code makes it true or that it is a promise only.
5. docs/procurement/dpia-pack.md and transfer-impact-assessment-template.md: data categories (from the inventory), risks, the mitigations the code has, and the operator's choices left open.
6. docs/procurement/exit-plan.md (UK TCoP point 11): what the export holds and its formats, steps, timing, and what is lost (point to G19 for the full export).
7. docs/procurement/incident-response.md: what the software logs and alerts on today, what an operator must staff to meet 24 and 72 hours, and the template notices.
8. /security/subprocessors, built from src/lib/dataplace.ts settings (only switched-on providers, with country and purpose). /security/disclosure, plus public/.well-known/security.txt (RFC 9116) from SECURITY_CONTACT, with Expires set a year ahead at build. Without SECURITY_CONTACT, no security.txt exists and the page says who to ask instead.
9. /procurement, a public page listing each document with its date and a download link. A 'Certifications' line comes from the G01 registry, and 'Accessibility conformance report' links to G04's report once it exists.

Rules: no marketing words. Every document carries 'What this is not' at the top. Nothing says 'compliant', 'certified' or 'secure by design'.

Tests: every file path cited in the whitepaper and the self-mapping exists; the crypto inventory matches a scan of src/server for createCipheriv, scryptSync, createHmac and hkdf (a new primitive in the code fails the test until it is documented); the sbom script runs and lists pdf-lib; the G01 claims scanner passes on docs/.

Settings: SECURITY_CONTACT.
