batches.title: Accessibility conformance: WCAG 2.2 AA and EN 301 549, tested, fixed, with an honest conformance report and accessibility statement
batches.needs_from_operator: A budget decision on a third-party audit (decision 13). Assistive-technology testers (screen reader users) for the manual pass, if possible.
batches.brief:
Goal: public procurement in the EU (EN 301 549, the Web Accessibility Directive), the US (Section 508) and Canada requires accessibility evidence. Test, fix what fails, and publish a report that says exactly what was tested and how.

Build:
1. tests/a11y.e2e.mjs on the existing Playwright setup (see tests/e2e.mjs). Run axe-core (MPL-2.0, devDependency) with the WCAG 2.2 A and AA tags on every public page, the signing page in each state (consent, fields, adopt dialog, review, done, declined, code check, witness statement), the editor's three steps, the envelope page, templates, settings, /verify, /check and /help, at 390x844, 1280x800 and 320 CSS px wide (reflow, 1.4.10). Fail on any violation unless it is listed in a known-issues file with a reason and an owner.
2. A keyboard-only script: send an envelope and sign it with Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space and the arrow keys only, never the mouse. Check visible focus everywhere and focus not obscured by the sticky bars (2.4.11), dialogs that trap and return focus, and Escape. Check WCAG 2.2's new criteria: target size 24x24 minimum (2.5.8; the editor already has 44 px), dragging alternatives (2.5.7; nudge with arrows exists, so confirm it is reachable and announced), accessible authentication (3.3.8: codes can be pasted and autocomplete is not blocked on passwords), redundant entry (3.3.7), consistent help (3.2.6).
3. Fix what fails, in CSS tokens first (contrast at 4.5:1 and 3:1 for UI parts in light and dark), then in components. Each fix is a small commit naming the criterion.
4. The signature itself: a signer who cannot draw must be able to sign. Type is offered already, so confirm it is reachable by keyboard and screen reader and say so in the report.
5. Documents (EN 301 549 clause 10): uploaded PDFs are the sender's. The certificate of completion is ours. Try to produce it as a tagged PDF (structure tree, reading order, language, alt text for signature images) with pdf-lib's low-level objects. If that cannot be done well in the time, say so in the report and add the evidence pack's text audit trail as the accessible alternative. Never claim a tagged certificate that a checker (veraPDF PDF/UA, or PAC if available) has not passed.
6. docs/procurement/accessibility-conformance-report.md in the ITI VPAT 2.5 INT layout (WCAG 2.2, EN 301 549 and Section 508 tables). Each criterion is 'Supports', 'Partially supports', 'Does not support' or 'Not evaluated', with remarks that name the screen. The top says: 'Self-assessed on <date> with axe-core <version>, keyboard and <screen readers actually used>. Not audited by a third party.' Name the browsers and screen readers used (for example NVDA with Firefox, VoiceOver with iOS Safari). Write 'Not evaluated' where none was used.
7. /accessibility: an accessibility statement in the EU model-statement shape (conformance status from the report, known issues, how to report a barrier, which reaches the existing help form under a new topic 'Accessibility barrier', and the date).

Rules: the report is generated from what the tests and the manual pass found, not from what the code is meant to do. An unknown is 'Not evaluated'.

Honesty limits: never 'fully compliant' or 'WCAG certified'. Add a G01 registry entry 'third-party accessibility audit: not_held'.

Tests: the a11y run itself in CI; a unit test that the known-issues file names only existing pages.

Leave out: translating (G15), the sender app on phones beyond what fails.

batches.title: PAdES seal of the operator (B-B and B-T) with a key in a file or an HSM, and RFC 3161 timestamps
files_touched: src/server/pdf.ts (one call at the end of building the final PDF)
batches.needs_from_operator: A seal certificate. For testing, a self-made test CA. For real use, an organisation certificate from a CA, a qualified seal certificate from a QTSP if a qualified seal is wanted (not software), and a TSA (a QTSP's qualified TSA, or the deployment's own).
batches.brief:
Goal: every completed PDF carries a standard PAdES signature (an electronic seal) of whoever runs the server, timestamped, which any PDF reader or the EU DSS can check offline. This is the first step from 'a stored hash' to a standards-based file. It is a seal of the operator, not a signature of the signers: G16 adds the signers' own certificates.

Build:
1. Dependencies: pkijs and asn1js (both BSD-3-Clause, pure JavaScript) for CMS SignedData and RFC 3161. No native code in this batch.
2. src/server/pades/keys.ts: the seal key and certificate chain from SEAL_P12 (path) with SEAL_P12_PASSWORD, or, behind an interface G21 fills in, from a PKCS#11 HSM. Expose sign(digest) and chain() so the key never leaves keys.ts. Refuse to start sealing (log, file an operator alert, keep making unsealed PDFs exactly as today) when the certificate has expired, its key usage does not allow digitalSignature or nonRepudiation, or the chain does not build.
3. src/server/pades/incremental.ts: append a signature as an incremental update (a new xref section after the existing bytes), with a /Sig dictionary (SubFilter ETSI.CAdES.detached), a ByteRange covering everything except the Contents placeholder, and an invisible signature field. pdf-lib rewrites whole files, so write the incremental part yourself; pdf-lib may be used only to read. Reserve 32 KB for Contents (enough for chain plus timestamp).
4. src/server/pades/cms.ts: CAdES-BES detached SignedData: SHA-256, RSA-PSS or ECDSA P-256 per the key, signed attributes contentType, messageDigest and signing-certificate-v2 (ESSCertIDv2), and no signingTime (PAdES puts the time in /M). This is PAdES B-B per ETSI EN 319 142-1.
5. src/server/pades/tsa.ts: an RFC 3161 request for the signature value (signature-time-stamp unsigned attribute), which makes B-T. TSA_URLS is a comma-separated list tried in order, with optional HTTP Basic credentials, a 10 second timeout, and the outbound allowlist from G02. The response must verify (status, imprint, nonce, TSA certificate chain to TSA_TRUST). Without a TSA, the seal is B-B and the certificate says so.
6. src/server/pades/seal.ts: sealFinal(pdfBytes) is called once at the end of building the final PDF in src/server/pdf.ts. final_sha256 and /verify then use the sealed bytes, so '/verify matches' keeps meaning 'this exact file'. A sealing failure (TSA down) never loses the PDF: the build retries through the existing finalretry timer, and after the retry limit the PDF goes out at B-B with that recorded in the audit trail.
7. The certificate of completion and /security/certificate gain lines from one constant SEAL_TRUTH in src/lib/evidence.ts: 'This file is sealed with the certificate of <subject of the seal certificate>, issued by <issuer>, at level PAdES B-T on <time from the timestamp>. The seal shows that the file has not changed since it was sealed and who sealed it. It is not a signature of the people who signed: their signatures here are simple electronic signatures with the audit trail above.' The word 'qualified' appears only when the G01 registry says 'qualified seal: held' and the certificate carries the QcCompliance and QcSSCD statements (check them in the certificate, and both must be true).
8. Existing signatures in an uploaded PDF are still destroyed by flatPages() today. Do not fix that here (G07 does), but stop pretending: when an uploaded PDF contains a /Sig field, the editor and the API warn that its existing signatures will not survive. That is one check at upload, in a new function in src/server/pades/seal.ts that G07 will reuse.

Rules: one seal per final PDF, applied last. The seal never changes a byte of what was signed before it (incremental only). Voided, declined and expired copies are not sealed (they are not agreements), and the notice page says so.

Tests (tests/pades.test.ts, no network): make a test CA, seal certificate and TSA in the test, with a TSA answering through a fetch stub. Seal a final PDF. Check the ByteRange covers the file except Contents, the CMS verifies against the chain, the messageDigest matches, the timestamp imprint matches the signature value, and appending a byte afterwards breaks verification. Check pdf.js still opens it. Cover an expired certificate, wrong key usage, the TSA down (B-B then retry), and a key that does not match the certificate. Check /verify matches the sealed bytes. If a pdfsig (poppler-utils) or qpdf --check binary is available, call it in an optional test and skip it otherwise.

Settings: SEAL_P12, SEAL_P12_PASSWORD, TSA_URLS, TSA_USER, TSA_PASSWORD, TSA_TRUST (PEM bundle path). Add them to .env.example and the README.

Leave out: B-LT and B-LTA (G06), validation of incoming files (G07), signers' own certificates (G16), HSM (G21), XAdES, CAdES and ASiC (later, only if a target country needs them: Estonia's ASiC-E is G25's).

batches.title: Long-term validity: PAdES B-LT and B-LTA, re-timestamping on a schedule, PDF/A-3 with the audit trail embedded
batches.needs_from_operator: A decision on Ghostscript as an optional converter for uploaded files (decision 11: it is AGPL and runs as a separate container if used).
batches.brief:
Goal: a signed file stays verifiable for decades, after the seal and TSA certificates expire, as archives and EU public bodies require (B-LTA), and is produced as PDF/A so archives accept it.

Build:
1. src/server/pades/ltv.ts, which makes B-LT: after sealing, fetch OCSP responses (preferred) or CRLs for every certificate in the seal and timestamp chains, through the G02 outbound allowlist. In an air-gapped deployment, read them from a folder the operator fills (REVOCATION_DIR). Then write a DSS dictionary (Certs, OCSPs, CRLs, and VRI entries keyed by the signature hash) in a further incremental update. Revocation data that cannot be got leaves the file at B-T, and the audit trail and certificate say which level was reached.
2. B-LTA: add a document timestamp (/Type /DocTimeStamp, SubFilter ETSI.RFC3161) over the file including the DSS.
3. src/server/pades/archive.ts and a timer job in src/server/cron.ts: each sealed file records its seal_level and the expiry of the newest timestamp's TSA certificate. 180 days before that expiry (ARCHIVE_RETIMESTAMP_DAYS), add fresh validation data for the previous timestamp and a new document timestamp, as an incremental update. Each re-timestamp makes a new file version: the stored file is replaced, the previous version is kept (the original sealed version is never deleted while the envelope exists), and /verify recognises every version of the same envelope and says which one it is. Say plainly on /verify that a re-timestamped file has a new fingerprint and that both are genuine. Write an audit line for each re-timestamp.
4. src/server/pades/pdfa.ts, for PDF/A-3b on what we generate: the certificate pages and notice pages get embedded fonts (already the case), an sRGB OutputIntent (ship the ICC profile under assets/, with its licence), XMP metadata with the pdfaid part 3 and conformance B, no encryption, and no JavaScript. Attach the audit trail JSON (the same one as the evidence pack) as an associated file with AFRelationship /Data. For uploaded documents: if the source declares PDF/A, keep that. Otherwise the final file cannot honestly claim PDF/A. Then record 'PDF/A: no, the uploaded file is not PDF/A' unless the optional converter (PDFA_CONVERTER_URL, a separate container the operator runs, for example Ghostscript, chosen in decision 11) converted it at upload, in which case the converted copy is what gets signed and the original is kept beside it. The signing page and the certificate say the document was converted.
5. Validation in CI: run veraPDF (GPL/MPL, as a Docker image in CI, never shipped in the product image) on sample outputs. Record the veraPDF result per file only when veraPDF ran (VERAPDF_URL optional). Otherwise the product states what it wrote, never 'validated PDF/A'.
6. NARA: document in docs/procurement that the export holds PDF/A where achieved, plus CSV and JSON, and name the NARA format guidance it follows. Make no acceptance claim beyond that.

Rules: every upgrade is incremental and never touches earlier bytes. The level reached is always printed and never assumed.

Tests (tests/ltv.test.ts): a test CA with an OCSP responder stub; B-LT with the DSS present and VRI correct; B-LTA document timestamp; the re-timestamp job, with the fake clock jumping toward expiry, adds a timestamp and keeps the earlier version; /verify recognises both versions; the revocation folder in air-gapped mode; a missing OCSP stays at B-T and says so; the PDF/A XMP and OutputIntent are present on the certificate pages; the associated audit JSON parses and recomputes the chain.

Settings: REVOCATION_DIR, ARCHIVE_RETIMESTAMP_DAYS (180), PDFA_CONVERTER_URL, VERAPDF_URL.

Leave out: qualified preservation services (a certification, not software), XAdES and ASiC.

batches.title: Validate signed PDFs and keep signatures already in uploaded files
batches.needs_from_operator: Optionally run the European Commission's DSS demonstration web app (LGPL-2.1, Java) as a separate container for EU Trusted List validation.
batches.brief:
Goal: a public body receives signed PDFs from many senders. It must be able to check them, and the product must never break a signature someone else made.

Build:
1. src/server/pades/validate.ts, a built-in basic validator with no network. For every /Sig and /DocTimeStamp in a PDF: whether the ByteRange covers the whole file except Contents (and whether later incremental updates exist, listing what each changed: form fields, annotations, pages), integrity (the CMS messageDigest against the ByteRange hash, and the signature over the signed attributes), signer certificate subject, issuer, serial, validity and key usage, timestamp time and TSA, embedded revocation data, the detected PAdES level (B-B, B-T, B-LT, B-LTA), and whether the chain reaches a trust anchor in TRUST_ANCHORS_DIR (PEM files the operator chooses). The result is one of 'intact and chained to a trusted anchor', 'intact, signer not trusted here', 'intact, could not check revocation' or 'broken', always with the reason.
2. src/server/pades/dss.ts, optional: when DSS_URL is set, send the file to the DSS REST validation service (validateSignature, the default policy or DSS_POLICY) and show its indication (TOTAL_PASSED, INDETERMINATE, TOTAL_FAILED) with sub-indications and the ETSI validation report for download. Say on the page that the result is the DSS's, run against the EU Trusted Lists the DSS instance loaded, on <date>. Without DSS_URL, the page says EU Trusted List checks are not set up on this server.
3. /verify gains 'Check the signatures in a PDF' next to the existing byte-for-byte check. It works for any PDF, also one never signed here. It keeps nothing: the file is checked in memory and dropped, and the page says so. Rate limit as for /verify now.
4. Keep signatures in uploaded files: at upload, detect /Sig fields (the function from G05) and validate them. If the sender only needs the recipients to approve or view, or asks to 'keep the existing signatures', do not flatten: the envelope's own fields and the seal are added as incremental updates after the existing bytes (G05's writer), and each existing signature is re-validated in the final file to prove it still holds. If fields must be stamped onto pages, which changes page content and breaks the earlier signature by design, the editor says so before sending, and the original signed file is attached unchanged to the final PDF as an embedded file and to the evidence pack.
5. Show the validation result of every uploaded signed PDF to the sender in the editor, to each signer next to the document, and in the certificate, as what the validator found.

Rules: never call a signature 'valid' without saying against which anchors and policy. 'Intact' means only that the bytes are unchanged.

Honesty limits: whether Adobe, DigiDoc4, @firma, ITI VALIDAR or Japan's platform show zero warnings depends on the certificate being in their trust lists. That needs a QTSP or AATL certificate, which is not software. The page and docs say so.

Tests: files from G05 (intact, then one byte changed), a file with two signatures and an incremental form fill between them, a signature from an untrusted CA, a DSS stub answering each indication, upload of a signed PDF with keep-signatures (the final file still verifies the first signature) and without it (warning, original attached), and a limit test.

Settings: TRUST_ANCHORS_DIR, DSS_URL, DSS_POLICY.

Leave out: XAdES, CAdES and ASiC validation (DSS handles them if added later), LOTL download inside our own server.

batches.title: Single sign-on for staff: any OpenID Connect provider and SAML 2.0, per tenant, enforced, with role mapping
requirements: owner brief: national eID sign-in through standard protocols
files_touched: src/server/routes-signin.ts (shared helpers only, via exported functions)
batches.needs_from_operator: An IdP to test against (Keycloak in a container is enough), and later each agency's IdP metadata.
batches.brief:
Goal: government staff sign in with their organisation's identity provider (Entra ID, ADFS, Keycloak, Shibboleth, Okta, openDesk's Keycloak, a national government IdP) through OIDC or SAML, and an agency can make that the only way in. The README lists 'Single sign-on for a whole organization (SAML...)' as not built.

Build:
1. src/server/sso/oidcGeneric.ts: any issuer through discovery (/.well-known/openid-configuration), fetched once and cached, with the JWKS refreshed when an unknown kid appears. Reuse the checks in src/server/oidc.ts (RS256, ES256 and PS256 allowed, never none, issuer, audience, expiry, nonce, PKCE S256) by moving the pure token-check helpers into an exported function both use. Do not change behaviour for Google and Microsoft. Client secret, or private_key_jwt for IdPs that require it.
2. src/server/sso/saml.ts with a maintained library (for example @node-saml/node-saml, MIT; check its current release and advisories before choosing). SP-initiated Redirect binding out and POST binding back; signed assertions required; the audience, recipient, NotOnOrAfter and InResponseTo checked; replay cache in SQLite; SP metadata at /api/sso/<id>/metadata; optional signed AuthnRequests with an SP key; encrypted assertions accepted. IdP-initiated SSO is refused by default.
3. Per tenant (account) connections in sso_connections: type, issuer or metadata XML, client details, the email domains it owns (proved with a DNS TXT record the admin adds, checked by the server), the claim or attribute for a stable id, email and name, and group to role mapping (owner never mapped, only admin and member). The login page asks for an email first. If its domain has a connection, it goes straight to that IdP.
4. Enforcement: 'Members must sign in through <IdP>' per tenant. Then password, Google and Microsoft sign-in stop working for members of that tenant (one break-glass owner account keeps a password and two-step login, and is shown as such). API keys are unaffected. Just-in-time membership for a new person with a verified domain, as a member unless mapped. Removal: a person whose IdP says they are gone (SAML has no signal, so offer SCIM later; for now, sessions end when the IdP session cannot be refreshed and an admin can remove) is handled by the existing remove-member flow.
5. Record per session how the person signed in (IdP, protocol, the authentication context or acr/amr it reported), and show it in Settings, Profile and to admins. G13 logs it.
6. Single logout is optional: front-channel logout for OIDC, and SAML SLO if the library supports it cleanly. Otherwise sign-out is local, and the screen says the IdP session stays.

Rules: a person is recognised by issuer plus stable id, never by email alone (as routes-signin.ts already does). Two-step login is skipped only when the IdP reports multi-factor (amr contains mfa or otp, or the SAML AuthnContextClassRef is in a list the admin trusts), and the admin sees that rule.

Tests (tests/sso.test.ts) with a stand-in IdP made in the test, as tests/signin.test.ts does: discovery, every token check, SAML signed and unsigned (refused), wrong audience, expired, replay, InResponseTo mismatch, XML signature wrapping (use the library's known test vectors), domain proof, enforcement, break-glass, the role mapping and that owner is never mapped. Also a manual check against Keycloak in a container, written up with the date.

Settings: SAML_SP_KEY and SAML_SP_CERT (optional). Per-tenant settings live in the database.

Leave out: SCIM provisioning (later), signer identity (G09: this batch is for staff who send).

batches.title: Signer identity through national eID (OIDC and SAML, eIDAS nodes) with assurance levels recorded per signer
files_touched: src/server/pdf.ts (certificate lines via a function from signerid.ts)
batches.needs_from_operator: Registration with each national scheme as a relying party (GOV.UK One Login, gov.br, Singpass, FranceConnect, ID Austria, an eIDAS node, MOSIP eSignet and so on). That is a contract or onboarding step per country, not software.
batches.brief:
Goal: a sender can require that a signer proves who they are with a state identity before the document opens. The product records what the identity provider said, with the assurance level, on the certificate and in the evidence. This is the workflow layer on top of the state's own credential.

Build:
1. A new check 'verify': 'eid' (next to email_code and sms_code) with an identity provider chosen from the deployment's list. Identity providers are configured by the operator (not tenants) in an identity_providers table or the file IDENTITY_PROVIDERS_FILE (JSON). Each has a protocol (OIDC, reusing G08's generic client, or SAML, reusing G08's SP), display name, country, the claims for given name, family name, date of birth, a stable personal id and email, and the assurance it delivers. The assurance is declared by the operator for that IdP and acr value: an eIDAS level (low, substantial, high) and NIST SP 800-63-4 IAL, AAL and FAL. It is never inferred by us.
2. Starter profiles in src/lib/assurance.ts for well-documented OIDC providers, filled from their public documentation with the date read and marked 'check with the scheme': GOV.UK One Login (vtr and the returned vot), FranceConnect (eidas1 and eidas2 acr), gov.br (confiabilidade levels bronze, prata, ouro via the API), Singpass (Myinfo is FAPI and needs private_key_jwt and signed and encrypted ID tokens: support JWE decryption here), MOSIP eSignet (used by several DPI countries), and a generic eIDAS node SAML profile (eIDAS SAML attribute profile v1.2 or later: PersonIdentifier, FamilyName, FirstName, DateOfBirth, and LoA in AuthnContextClassRef). Where a profile cannot be completed from public sources, ship it disabled with a note.
3. The signing page: after consent and before the document opens, 'Prove who you are with <IdP>'. It returns to the same link, and the result belongs to that recipient and that browser for 24 hours like the existing code pass. A name match rule: the sender's typed name is compared with the IdP name after normalising case, accents, order and transliteration (reuse the look-alike rules in the Fix my name code). A mismatch does not open the document. It tells the signer and the sender, and the sender can confirm with Correct.
4. The record: the audit trail and the certificate print 'Identity checked by <IdP> (<country>) on <time>: <name as given>, <date of birth if the sender chose to show it>, level <eIDAS level> as declared for this provider by the operator of this server; NIST SP 800-63-4 IAL<n>/AAL<n>/FAL<n> as declared.' The stable personal id is stored only as a keyed hash per tenant, and shown masked or not at all (the sender chooses, the default is not shown). The raw token or assertion is kept in the evidence pack only if the tenant turns that on (some schemes forbid keeping it: say so).
5. Every existing check gets its NIST record too, honestly: a link by email and email or SMS codes are 'no identity proofing (IAL1); the code shows control of a mailbox or phone'. A G08 staff sign-in records the IdP's acr. Write these sentences in src/lib/assurance.ts and quote them from CHECK_PROVES.
6. The API: recipients[].verify = 'eid', recipients[].identity_provider, and the result on the recipient object. Templates, bulk (each row's signer proves themselves) and public forms (allowed, since the visitor proves themselves; this is the citizen self-service case) carry it.

Rules: a pass is never moved to another person. Changing the recipient's name or address resets it. A declared level is printed with 'as declared'. The product does not verify a person itself.

Tests: stand-in OIDC and SAML IdPs; every starter profile parses its own documented sample; acr to level mapping; a name match with accents, a reversed order and a Cyrillic to Latin transliteration; a mismatch; reset on correction; the certificate lines; the masked id; the API; bulk and public forms.

Settings: IDENTITY_PROVIDERS_FILE.

Leave out: signing with the eID's certificate (G16, G23, G25), document-scan identity proofing (vendor partners, later), the EUDI wallet (G24).

batches.title: Jurisdiction rules engine: the minimum signature level per country and document type, enforced and recorded
batches.needs_from_operator: A lawyer in each first-wave country to review the rules. Until then every rule says 'not reviewed by a lawyer'.
batches.brief:
Goal: the product knows the signature level a kind of document needs in a country, refuses or warns before sending when it cannot reach that level, and records the level required and the level reached on the file.

Build:
1. src/lib/jurisdiction/rules.json: entries of country (ISO 3166), document type (a fixed list: general contract, employment contract, fixed-term employment contract, termination notice, lease, real estate transfer, power of attorney, will, negotiable instrument, consumer credit, public procurement bid, official act of a public body, act of a head of power, tax filing, HR internal, other), minimum level ('SES' | 'AES' | 'AdES-QC' | 'QES' | 'national:<tool id>' | 'not_electronic'), action ('block' | 'warn'), legal source with URL, date read, reviewed_by (null) and note. Seed it only from the research the owner has, for example eIDAS Art. 25, BGB s.126a (written form needs QES), Lei 14.063/2020 Art. 5 (real estate and acts of heads of powers need ICP-Brasil), and India IT Act First Schedule (wills, negotiable instruments, powers of attorney, trusts and real estate sale are excluded), with action 'warn' unless the law excludes electronic signature entirely ('not_electronic' with 'block'). The operator can change any action in RULES_OVERRIDE_FILE.
2. src/lib/jurisdiction/engine.ts: requiredLevel(country, docType) and levelAchievable(envelope), from the checks and signing methods each signer has: SES today; AES and QES once G16 or G23 is set for that signer; national tools from G25.
3. The editor's review step and the API ask for country and document type. They default from the tenant's setting and the existing paperwork.ts word check (which now suggests a document type), and the sender confirms. If the required level is not achievable: a 'block' refuses to send with the rule, its source and what would make it possible ('Each signer must sign with a qualified certificate. Set up remote signing under Settings.'); a 'warn' shows that and asks for confirmation, recorded in the audit trail.
4. The certificate and evidence pack print 'Level required for <type> in <country> by the rules on this server: <level> (source, date, not reviewed by a lawyer | reviewed by <name> on <date>). Level reached: <per signer>.'
5. /help#outside-us is generated from rules.json, so the notes and the engine cannot disagree.

Rules: the engine decides only from rules.json and the override. It never claims a document is valid. Nothing is blocked by default except 'not_electronic' entries.

Tests: every rule has a source and a date; the override; block and warn by API and editor; the audit and certificate lines; a level reached from a mocked G16 signer; the help page built from the file.

Settings: RULES_OVERRIDE_FILE, DEFAULT_COUNTRY (per tenant in Settings).

Leave out: writing legal content beyond the research, automatic country detection from IP addresses.

batches.title: Records: retention schedules, legal hold, disposition with a record of destruction, archive export
files_touched: src/server/routes-trust.ts (purge paths call the hold check)
batches.needs_from_operator: The agency's own records schedule (for example from NARA General Records Schedules or a national archive).
batches.brief:
Goal: a public body must keep each record for a set time, keep anything under litigation, destroy on schedule with proof, and hand records to its archive. Today deletion follows account closing and sender actions only.

Build:
1. Retention schedules per tenant: name, code (for example GRS 2.1 item 050), applies to (document type from G10, template, folder or tag), keep for N years after completion, void or decline, then 'destroy' | 'transfer to archive' | 'review'. A default schedule per tenant. An envelope gets its schedule at completion, printed in the evidence pack, and a change of schedule later is logged.
2. Legal hold: an admin places a hold on envelopes (by search, folder, person or date range) with a reason and a matter reference. A held envelope cannot be deleted by anyone: not by the sender, not by account closing, not by purgeUser, not by the operator, not by disposition. Every deletion path checks one function isHeld(envelopeIds) in src/server/records.ts. Account closing with holds is refused with the list of holds. Lifting a hold needs the admin and a reason, both logged.
3. Disposition: the timer finds records past their date. 'destroy' removes them (as deleting does today) after a 30-day notice to the tenant's records officers, unless held. 'review' puts them in a queue. 'transfer' marks them for export. Every destruction writes a disposition_log line (envelope id, schedule, date, who approved, SHA-256 of the destroyed final file), which is kept and exportable as a certificate of destruction (PDF and CSV).
4. Archive export: an export in BagIt (RFC 8493) layout per batch, with each envelope's final PDF (PDF/A where G06 reached it), the audit trail JSON, the evidence pack, metadata JSON (schema from G19), and a manifest with SHA-256 sums. 'Transferred' records can then be destroyed only after the tenant confirms the archive received them.
5. A Records page for admins and a new role 'records officer' (can see schedules, holds and logs, not documents).

Rules: holds beat everything. What KEPT_AFTER_DELETION in src/lib/policy.ts lists stays true; update it to name the disposition log.

Tests: each deletion path refused under a hold (sender delete, account close, purgeUser, operator, disposition); hold and lift logged; disposition with the fake clock: notice, destroy, log; transfer then confirm; BagIt validates (check bag-info and manifests by hand-written code); the role sees no document.

Leave out: integrations with records systems (export files are the interface), legal advice on schedules.

batches.title: Security event log and export to a SIEM (syslog, HTTPS JSON lines, pull API)
files_touched: call sites in auth.ts, routes-account.ts, routes-signin.ts, routes-twostep.ts, api keys, members, exports, operator actions (one line each)
batches.needs_from_operator: The agency's SIEM endpoint (Splunk HEC, Elastic, Sentinel through syslog, a syslog collector).
batches.brief:
Goal: security teams need every sign-in, privilege change and data export in their own SIEM, in near real time, and without document contents.

Build:
1. src/server/seclog.ts: an append-only security_events table: seq, at, tenant (account id, or null for deployment-level), actor (user id, key id, operator or system), event type from a fixed list (sign-in success and failure with method, two-step events, SSO assertions, session ended, password and email changes, API key created, used for the first time from a new address, and revoked, member added, removed and role changed, settings changed with field names not values, export, evidence pack download, legal hold, disposition, operator pause, trust, unpause, webhook added or changed, rate limit hit, account closed), source IP and user agent, outcome, and a hash chain like the audit trail. No document content, no field values, no signing links, no codes. Email addresses are included only if the tenant turns that on (default: user id only).
2. Delivery, all optional, configured per tenant by admins and per deployment by the operator: (a) syslog RFC 5424 over TLS (node:tls) to host:port with an optional client certificate; (b) HTTPS POST of JSON lines in batches (works with Splunk HEC and Elastic, with a header token); (c) GET /api/security-events?after=<seq> for pull, with an admin-scope API key. Events are queued and retried with backoff, and a deliverer that keeps failing alerts the admins. The G02 outbound allowlist applies.
3. Envelope audit events can be streamed through the same deliverers as an opt-in second stream (action, envelope id, time; no detail text unless chosen).
4. Schema: a documented JSON shape, with an optional mapping to OCSF Authentication and Account Change classes, in docs/procurement.
5. Retention of the table per tenant (default 400 days). The chain head is exported daily to the deliverers so tampering shows.
6. Simple anomaly alerts to admins: many failed sign-ins for one person or address, a new API key used from a new country, an unusually large export, and bulk sends far above the tenant's 30-day pattern. Each alert names the rule, and the thresholds are in src/lib/policy.ts.

Tests: every event type written from its call site; nothing sensitive in any event (scan for the test's signing link, code and field value); syslog framing (RFC 5424, octet counting over TLS) against a local TLS server in the test; HEC batches; pull with paging; retry and alert; chain; retention.

Leave out: a SIEM product, notification to authorities (an organisational duty, see L07).

batches.title: Multi-agency tenancy: a government above its agencies, delegated admin, inherited policies
requirements: owner brief: multi-agency tenancy with delegated admin
batches.needs_from_operator: Nothing beyond configuration.
batches.brief:
Goal: one deployment serves a whole government: ministries and agencies each have their own workspace (account), and a central team sets policies and sees health without reading anyone's documents.

Build:
1. An organisation above accounts: orgs (name, parent org for nesting, for example government, then ministry, then agency), accounts.org_id, and org_admins (people with rights over an org and everything below it). The deployment's operator creates top-level orgs. Org admins create agencies (accounts) below them and name each agency's first owner.
2. Policies set at org level and inherited, which an agency may tighten but never loosen: SSO required and which connection (G08), minimum two-step, the signature levels allowed and the default country and document types (G10), retention defaults (G11), impact display and the AI helper (G01 switches), white label and verified domains (G17), allowed outside services (SMS on or off, webhooks host list), the security log destination (G12), and session length. tenantPolicy() from G01 now resolves through the chain, and each screen shows where a value comes from ('set by Ministry of X').
3. Delegated admin: org admins can manage agency owners and admins, see members, reset two-step (with the existing rules) and switch sending off for an agency. They cannot read envelopes, documents, comments or field values. A 'break-glass' document access for an org admin exists only if the org turns it on: it needs a reason, notifies the agency owners at once, and is in the security log.
4. Shared libraries: an org template library that agencies can use (with the existing template permission and lock rules) and an org-wide group directory. Cross-agency sending works as now (an agency sends to people in another agency like anyone), and an internal directory of verified staff emails per org makes suggestions.
5. Reports at org level: counts per agency (sent, completed, average time, levels reached), with no titles or names.
6. The operator page stays deployment-wide. In a government deployment the operator is the government's own IT team, and /security says who the operator is (already from OPERATOR_NAME).

Rules: no path from an org role to document content except break-glass. Every org action goes into the security log.

Tests: inheritance and tightening; a loosening attempt refused; an org admin denied every document route (list them from the router and assert 403 for each); break-glass with notification and log; nested orgs; moving an agency between orgs (operator only); templates from the library under locks.

Leave out: billing across agencies (G14 handles the deployment billing mode), cross-tenant search.

batches.title: Government billing mode, a public price list per deployment, the tree commitment, and a total-cost calculator
files_touched: one guarded call in src/server/credits.ts, agreed with its owner
batches.needs_from_operator: Owner decisions 7 (prices, bands and the tree commitment) and 2 (first countries, for the currencies). Contract terms from a lawyer.
batches.brief:
Goal: governments buy per deployment with a fixed annual fee, unlimited senders and envelopes, no overage, nothing charged to citizens, and still plant trees, in a way that procurement and green-claims rules can accept.

Wait for: the expiry batch (credits.ts, routes-billing.ts) to land, and agree one guarded call with its owner. Do not edit their code otherwise.

Build:
1. BILLING_MODE=deployment in src/server/billingmode.ts: no signature counting, no holds, no expiry, no Stripe calls, no plan page (Settings shows 'This service is provided under <LICENSE_HOLDER>'s agreement <AGREEMENT_REF>, valid until <date>'). Every place that would hold or use a signature asks billingMode() first: one call inside credits.ts's entry points, written by or with its owner. The default stays 'signatures', which is the consumer product with monthly expiry as decided.
2. src/lib/govpricing.ts: one table with bands by expected signatures a year (for example up to 100k, 1M, 10M, more), the fixed annual fee for support and updates per band for self-hosted, a separate fee for hosting by us or a partner where that exists, what is included (support hours, response times, updates, security fixes), and the price-hold and rise rules (a cap at CPI, 90 days' notice, multi-year holds, no renewal at a new price without written acceptance, annual invoicing, termination for convenience). Self-hosting under the open licence is always free. The page states that.
3. Trees: the commitment is per contract, not per signature: '<N>% of each government contract fee funds mangrove planting with Treegens: <trees per year> trees for this band.' It is never conditional on use, never presented as a gift to an official or the body, and is reported once a year in a planting statement (sites, dates, species, counts, and the evidence Treegens provides: geotagged photos and partner reports), linked from /impact. A deployment can show its own commitment on its signing pages only if the tenant turns impact display on (G01). Per-signature tree lines from the impact batch are off in deployment mode, because nothing is paid per signature.
4. /pricing/government: the public price list from govpricing.ts in the currencies the owner chooses, with what is included and the contract rules in plain words, and a link to the TCO calculator. Consumer monthly-expiring credits are never mentioned there except to say they do not apply.

The output is the annual total, cost per signature, and a line 'Licence cost per signature: 0'. Each assumption is shown and editable, and none is ours unless measured. A printable view. A comparison line for per-envelope pricing takes the user's own number, with no competitor price printed by us.

Rules: no claim 'cheaper than X' anywhere. Numbers come from one file. Citizens never pay in any mode.

Tests: deployment mode never touches credits (spy), never calls Stripe, the plan routes 404, sending is unlimited; the price page is built from govpricing.ts; the TCO arithmetic for the three sizes with fixed inputs; the tree statement page lists only commitments marked as signed contracts (a table filled by the operator).

Settings: BILLING_MODE, LICENSE_HOLDER, AGREEMENT_REF, AGREEMENT_UNTIL.

Leave out: invoicing software (governments invoice through their own systems), procurement vehicle listings.

files_touched: src/server/mail.ts (signer emails only; coordinate with others editing it)
batches.needs_from_operator: Professional translators and a lawyer for the consent text and certificate labels in each language. Canada needs equal quality in French, which is a translation contract, not software.
batches.brief:
Goal: signers read the signing page, the emails sent to them, the consent text and the certificate in their language. This is a hard requirement in Canada (English and French) and in multilingual EU states. Start with the signer side, where citizens are.

Build:
1. src/lib/i18n: a small catalogue with ICU-style plurals and placeholders, written here (no runtime dependency) or with @formatjs/intl-messageformat if it fits the bundle. Keys are stable ids, and English is the source. A missing key falls back to English and is logged in development. Dates and numbers keep using src/lib/dates.ts and numbers.ts, now passed the locale.
2. Language choice: per recipient, chosen by the sender (editor and API recipients[].language), defaulting to the tenant's default language, then the signer's browser (Accept-Language) for public forms. The signer can switch language on the page; the switch is recorded, and the agreed consent text is the one shown at that moment.

The owner decides when a language is switched on for real.

batches.title: Signers sign with their own certificate: remote signing through the Cloud Signature Consortium API (QTSP), giving AdES or QES
batches.needs_from_operator: A contract with at least one QTSP that offers the CSC API (decision 4). Test access to its sandbox.
batches.brief:
Goal: the state or a licensed provider issues the signer's certificate, and we orchestrate. With a QTSP's remote QSCD this gives a qualified electronic signature (QES) in the EU. With any CA it gives an advanced signature on a certificate (AdES).

Depends on: G05 (incremental writer, CMS, TSA), G06 (LTV), G07 (validation).

Build:
1. src/server/pades/csc.ts, a CSC API v2 client: OAuth 2.0 authorisation code with the service scope for sign-in and the credential scope for each signature (SCAL2: the signer authorises the exact hash, through hashes and numSignatures in the authorization details), credentials/list, credentials/info (the certificate chain, key algorithm, auth mode), and signatures/signHash. Signing services are configured by the operator in signing_services: base URL, client id and secret, the OAuth endpoints from /info, and the trust level the operator declares ('qualified' only when the provider is a QTSP on an EU Trusted List for qualified certificates for electronic signatures. The G07 DSS check confirms it at the first signature and the result is stored).
2. The signing model, kept standard and simple: for an envelope whose signers sign with certificates (chosen per recipient by the sender, or forced by G10), fields are filled as now. When the last field-filling step is done, the document is frozen: the final PDF with all values is built, without the seal. Then each certificate signer, in signing order, is asked to apply their signature to that frozen file: one incremental signature revision each, with no content change between them, and a DocMDP P=2 certification by the first signer where the profile requires it. The operator seal (G05) and LTV (G06) come last. Signers already done are not asked to sign twice. The certificate page lists what each signer signed.
3. The signing page: 'Sign with your qualified certificate from <provider>'. It redirects to the provider, which authenticates the signer (their app, SMS or eID), then comes back. We compute the ByteRange hash, call signHash, and assemble the CMS with the returned signature and the chain from credentials/info (signing-certificate-v2, the TSA from G05). The certificate's subject name is compared with the recipient name as in G09, and a mismatch stops with a clear message to signer and sender.
4. The record: the certificate and audit trail print, per signer, 'Signed with a certificate issued to <subject> by <issuer> through <provider>. Level: <QES | AdES on a qualified certificate | AdES>, as confirmed by <validation source> on <date>.' 'QES' is printed only when the validation found a qualified certificate on a QSCD from a provider on the Trusted List. Otherwise the lower level is printed. That level feeds G10's 'level reached'.
5. Free for citizens: we never charge the signer. Whether the QTSP charges the tenant is between them and is said in Settings.
6. EUDI wallet signing: wallets will sign through a QTSP's remote QSCD. When a wallet-linked QTSP exposes CSC, it is just another signing service here. Note that in the docs; G24 covers wallet identity.

Rules: the hash sent is the only thing that leaves the server, never the document (state this on /security). Each signer authorises exactly one hash per signature (SCAL2).

Tests: a CSC stand-in made in the test (OAuth, credentials/info with a test qualified-looking chain, signHash with a test key); two signers in order with no content change between them, both signatures verifying in the final file with G07; a name mismatch; the provider refusing; a timeout; the level printed as AdES when the stand-in's chain is not on the test trust list and as QES when it is; G10 block until each signer is set to a certificate.

Settings: signing services are configured in the database by the operator.

Leave out: becoming a QTSP, local smart cards (G23), national non-CSC APIs (G25).

batches.title: Signing inside the government's own portal, white label, portal-asserted identity, and verified sender domains
files_touched: next.config.mjs (frame-ancestors from settings, signing route only)
src/app/sign/[token]/ (postMessage events and verified-sender badge component)
batches.needs_from_operator: Each agency's portal origin and its public key, and DNS access for its sending domain (DKIM, SPF and DMARC are the agency's DNS work).
batches.brief:
Goal: citizens sign inside the government's own authenticated portal or app, under the government's name, not in an email link from a vendor brand that phishers copy.

Build:
1. Framing for allowed origins only: a tenant (or org, via G13) lists portal origins. The signing page then sends Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors with exactly those origins, only when the link was opened with ?embed=1 through a portal session (below), mirroring how /agree does it in next.config.mjs. Everything else keeps X-Frame-Options SAMEORIGIN. Events go to the parent by postMessage with targetOrigin set to the listed origin: loaded, consented, finished, declined, error.
2. Portal-asserted identity: the portal opens a signing session by calling POST /api/portal/sessions with a JWT it signs with its own key (registered per tenant as a JWK): issuer, the recipient id, the person's name, a stable id from the portal, the assurance level the portal declares (eIDAS or NIST, as in G09), the authentication time and a short expiry, with jti replay protection. We answer with a one-use URL valid for 5 minutes. The audit trail and certificate print 'Identity asserted by <portal name> (signed by its key <kid>) at <time>, level <level> as declared by that portal.'
3. No email at all for such recipients: they are created with link_by_sender semantics (no invitation, reminders through the portal's own channel by webhook event, the copy delivered through the portal by API). The existing 'Link shared by the sender' rules apply.
4. White label: when tenant.white_label is on (G01), the signing page, the emails the tenant still sends and the certificate use the tenant's name, logo and domain. Our product name appears only in an optional small 'Powered by GrowSigning' line, which the tenant chooses, and in /security. The certificate always names the operator of the server, because it is part of the evidence.
5. Verified sender domains: a tenant proves a domain (DNS TXT). Mail then goes From that domain through the tenant's SMTP relay (per-tenant SMTP_URL stored encrypted with APP_SECRET-derived keys) or the deployment's, and the check page shows 'Sent by <agency>, from a domain this server has verified (<domain>)'. A badge on the signing page appears only for verified domains. In a public multi-tenant deployment, government badges (.gov, .gouv.fr, .bund.de, gov.uk and others in a list in src/lib/policy.ts) need the operator's approval as well as DNS proof. At domain setup, check and show the domain's DMARC policy and recommend p=reject. We do not set DNS.
6. Know-your-business before API keys or bulk sending can be turned on in a public multi-tenant deployment: an operator approval step (who the organisation is, a contact, the reason), recorded. It is off in a self-hosted single-government deployment.

Rules: the portal's assertion is printed as the portal's, never as ours. Framing is never opened to '*' for signing pages.

Tests: frame-ancestors only for listed origins and only with a portal session; postMessage target origin; a JWT with a wrong key, expired, replayed, or for another tenant's recipient; the one-use URL; certificate lines; the white-label email and page; domain proof; the badge only when verified and approved; the KYB gate for keys and bulk in multi-tenant mode.

Leave out: native mobile SDKs, BIMI (it needs a trademark and a VMC certificate, which is the owner's business).

batches.title: Assisted signing at a counter: an official helps a citizen sign, with the identity check and accommodations recorded
requirements: owner brief: assisted signing at a counter
batches.needs_from_operator: The agency's own rules for checking ID at a counter and for people who cannot sign. Those are policy, not software.
batches.brief:
Goal: many citizens sign at a service counter with an official, not at home. The product must support that, building on 'sign in person on your device', the shared-device lock and the witness feature, and record exactly what the official did.

Build:
1. A Counter page for staff with the 'counter' permission: a queue of the day's in-person envelopes (from templates the agency marks 'counter'), start one for the person in front of them, and a second-screen mode. The citizen signs on a customer-facing screen or tablet opened by a short code or QR code (the existing QR code module), with the official's screen showing progress and no field values the citizen types unless the template allows it.
2. Identity check by the official: before the document opens, the official records the method (identity document seen, its type, the last 4 characters of its number, the issuing country, or 'known to me', or 'eID checked', which uses G09 on the counter device). No scan or photo is stored unless the tenant turns that on, and then it is stored encrypted and listed in the evidence pack. The official attests with their own session ('I checked this person's identity as recorded above'), and that is in the audit trail and the certificate as the official's statement.
3. Accommodations, each recorded in words on the certificate: signing by a mark (an X or any mark) with a witness (the existing witness role, and the official may not be the witness where the agency's rules say so); signing on behalf of a person who cannot sign, with their spoken consent recorded by two officials (both attest); the document read aloud (the official attests that it was read in <language>); an interpreter (name and language, attests).
4. A printed receipt after Finish: the envelope id, the fingerprint, how to get the copy (email, or /verify with the id), and the agency's contact, printable at 80 mm thermal width and A4.
5. Signature pads: pen input from a USB pad that presents as a pointer device in the browser works through the existing pad (pointer type 'pen'). Test with pointer events. Vendor SDKs (biometric pressure data) are out of scope, and the page says the product records the drawn image only.
6. The counter device is locked between citizens: the existing hand-over lock, plus 'next person' that clears everything, as the shared-device forms do.

Rules: the official's statements are theirs and are printed as such. The software cannot check an identity document, and every screen says so.

Tests: the queue and permission; second-screen pairing by code (one use, 10 minutes); each identity method; each accommodation and its certificate lines; the witness rule; the receipt; the lock between citizens; pen pointer events on the pad.

Leave out: document scanners and OCR, biometric signature capture.

batches.title: Full export with a published schema, round-trip import, and import from DocuSign
files_touched: src/server/routes-trust.ts (only to link the new export from /export)
src/app/app/settings/ (an Export and import tab file)
batches.needs_from_operator: Sample DocuSign exports from a real (test) account to check the importer against.
batches.brief:
Goal: no lock-in. One click gets everything out in open formats (the EU Data Act and the UK exit plan require it), and an agency can bring its archive in from DocuSign.

Build:
1. docs/schema: JSON Schema (2020-12) for the tenant export: account and settings (no secrets), members and roles, templates (fields, roles, rules, locks), contacts, signing groups, folders, webhooks (without secrets), click-to-agree terms and acceptances, retention schedules and holds (G11), envelopes (metadata, recipients, fields and values, audit trail with chain values, comments), and the files by SHA-256. Versioned. Published on /developers.
2. src/server/exportfull.ts: GET /api/export/full for owners and admins (an admin key may call it too), streamed as a ZIP: data JSON validated against the schema, all files, final PDFs (PDF/A and PAdES where reached), evidence packs, a README, and the SHA-256 manifest. Free, and it works when the account is closing, paused or unpaid (as the existing export does). Large tenants are exported in the background with an email when ready, the link valid 7 days.
3. src/server/importer.ts: importing our own full export into a new tenant (moving between deployments). Templates, contacts, groups, settings and completed envelopes come in as archived records. Out-for-signature envelopes are refused with a list (they must finish where they started). Every audit chain is re-verified on import, and imported records carry 'imported from <deployment> on <date>; chain verified | not verified'.
4. src/server/importers/docusign.ts: from what DocuSign lets customers download (the per-envelope 'combined documents with certificate' PDFs, the envelope CSV or report exports, and template JSON where available). Envelopes come in as archived records only: the PDF, DocuSign's certificate as part of it, the metadata, and a banner on the record: 'Imported from DocuSign on <date>. Signed there, not here. Its evidence is DocuSign's certificate inside the file.' They are never counted as signed here and never on /verify as completed here. Templates are mapped to our fields where there is a match, and the rest is listed as not imported.
5. Webhooks and API are documented as the live path. Add an 'export.ready' webhook.

Rules: an import never invents evidence. Imported things are always marked.

Tests: export validates against the schema; a round trip into a fresh tenant gives equal data (except ids, mapped and listed); out-for-signature refused; chain verification on import; the DocuSign importer against fixture files made from the documented layouts (marked as fixtures, not real exports, until the owner provides real samples); the banner and the /verify behaviour for imported files.

Leave out: importing from other vendors, live sync.

batches.title: AI helper in government mode: self-hosted open-weight model inside the boundary, switchable per tenant, nothing kept
files_touched: the chat module the 'chat' batch creates (one settings function)
batches.needs_from_operator: GPU hardware or an in-boundary host for an open-weight model (decision 10), if the agency wants model answers at all.
batches.brief:
Goal: a government tenant can have the AI helper answer from a model running inside its own boundary, or turn it off, with no prompts or logs leaving and no use for training.

Wait for: the 'chat' batch to land. Then build on its provider settings. Do not rewrite it.

Build:
1. In SOVEREIGN_MODE (G02), or when DEPLOYMENT_PROFILE=government, the hosted defaults (OpenRouter, Moonshot) are never used. Only SUPPORT_CHAT_BASE_URL counts, which must be on OUTBOUND_ALLOW or a private address (allow private addresses for this setting only). Without it, the helper gives the built-in answers only and says so.
2. Document running an open-weight model behind an OpenAI-compatible server inside the boundary (vLLM, llama.cpp server or Ollama). Kimi K3 (the model treegens.app uses) has open weights but needs a multi-GPU server. A smaller open-weight model can be configured with SUPPORT_CHAT_MODEL, and the grounding (answers only from policy.ts and the help pages) makes a smaller model workable. Test with a small model in a container if hardware allows, and write down what was tested.

4. Logs: the chat route keeps nothing but the limit counters and what a person chooses to attach to a help request (as the chat brief says). Add a test that no other table grows. /security and /security/processing name the model host the deployment configured, and say 'nothing typed here is stored, and nothing is sent to train a model'. The DPA template (G03) gets the same clause.
5. A 'model card' line on the chat panel: which model and host answer here, read from settings.
