batches.title: FIPS crypto mode and HSM keys through PKCS#11
batches.needs_from_operator: A base image or OS with an OpenSSL FIPS provider that has an active CMVP certificate (decision 3 covers whether to pursue this market), and an HSM with an active FIPS 140-3 Level 3 certificate for real keys.
batches.brief:
Goal: US federal and Canadian buyers require FIPS 140-3 validated cryptography and keys in validated HSMs. The product cannot be 'FIPS validated' itself. It can run only approved algorithms on a validated module and say exactly which module that is.

Build:
1. FIPS_MODE=1: at start, crypto.setFips(true), or check crypto.getFips() when Node was started with --enable-fips. Refuse to start with a clear message if the OpenSSL FIPS provider is not available. Print the provider name and version as OpenSSL reports them, on /security and in the log.
2. Inventory every primitive (G03's crypto inventory) and make each approved in FIPS mode. scrypt is not approved: in FIPS mode new password hashes use PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with at least 600,000 iterations (OWASP's current figure; check it). Existing scrypt hashes are verified once without FIPS (the only non-FIPS call, isolated and logged; or, if the provider forbids even that, force a password reset by email) and rehashed on the next sign-in. TOTP with HMAC-SHA1 is allowed, HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM, HMAC-SHA256 and SHA-256 are approved, and crypto.randomInt draws from the provider's DRBG. A test calls every path with FIPS on in a FIPS-enabled Node build and fails on any unapproved call.
3. Dockerfile.fips: the same image on a base whose OpenSSL FIPS provider holds a CMVP certificate (the operator picks the vendor; record the certificate number in the G01 registry only after checking it on the CMVP site and that it is active, not historical).
4. PKCS#11 for keys (pkcs11js, MIT, native: built into the image, so it still works offline): the seal key (G05) and optionally the file encryption key-encryption key (G22) live in an HSM. Config PKCS11_MODULE, PKCS11_SLOT, PKCS11_PIN (from a file), and key labels. Signing goes through C_Sign with the mechanism matching the key (RSA-PSS or ECDSA). Test with SoftHSM2 in CI, and say that SoftHSM is not validated.
5. /security prints: 'FIPS mode: on. Cryptography runs in <provider> <version>. Whether that module holds an active CMVP certificate is listed on /security/certifications.' Never 'FIPS 140-3 compliant' or 'validated' anywhere else.

Tests: startup refusal without a provider; the PBKDF2 path; rehash on sign-in; the algorithm sweep in a FIPS build (CI job using the FIPS image); SoftHSM signing for the seal; a PIN read from a file, never from the environment in logs.

Settings: FIPS_MODE, PKCS11_MODULE, PKCS11_SLOT, PKCS11_PIN_FILE, PKCS11_SEAL_KEY_LABEL.

Leave out: the CMVP process (impossible for an application anyway), FIPS for the browser side.

batches.title: Customer-held keys: a per-tenant key hierarchy in the customer's KMS or HSM, and database field encryption
files_touched: src/server/kms/*.ts (new: pkcs11, vault transit, kmip or http adapters)
src/app/security/ (what is and is not protected)
batches.needs_from_operator: Each tenant's KMS or HSM endpoint if they hold their own key.
batches.brief:
Goal: answer the sovereignty test as far as software honestly can. Each tenant's documents and personal data are encrypted under keys the tenant controls, revocable at any time, so a copy of the disk or a demand served on the operator yields nothing without the tenant's key service.

Say first, in the README and on /security: while a document is being signed, the server must read it to show it and to stamp the signed PDF, so whoever runs the server can see plaintext while it works. The full answer for sensitive data is the public body running the server itself (G02). This batch protects data at rest and makes revocation real.

Build:
1. src/server/keyring.ts: a key hierarchy. A tenant key-encryption key (KEK) lives in the tenant's KMS or HSM, or, by default, is derived from FILE_ENCRYPTION_KEY as today. A data key per tenant, rotated yearly, is stored only wrapped by the KEK. Unwrapped data keys are held in memory for at most 15 minutes and wiped on revocation.
2. Adapters in src/server/kms/: PKCS#11 (G21's module), the HashiCorp or OpenBao Vault Transit API over HTTPS, and a generic HTTP wrap/unwrap with mTLS (for cloud KMS or national HSM services). KMIP only if a maintained library exists; otherwise document it as not done.
3. Files: filestore.ts asks keyring for the tenant's data key instead of the server key. The file format header already carries a key id, so extend it to tenant plus version. Older files keep working. scripts/encrypt-files.mjs gains a per-tenant migration.
4. Database fields: src/server/fieldcrypt.ts encrypts the personal and content columns (recipient names, emails and phones, field values, signature images, comments, subjects, messages, document names, contacts, stored email copies) with AES-256-GCM under the tenant data key, with a deterministic keyed index (HMAC) where the code searches or matches by value (emails). Go table by table behind a flag, with a migration and a reverse path, and list every column that stays plain (ids, times, statuses, counts) on /security.
5. Revocation: the tenant disables its KEK. Its data is then unreadable: the app shows 'This workspace's key is not available' and sends nothing. Re-enabling restores it. Crypto-shredding (destroying the KEK) is the tenant's choice for final deletion and is logged in the security log (G12).
6. Audit: every unwrap is logged per tenant (count per hour, not per call) to the security log, so a tenant sees when its key was used.

Rules: no key material in logs, errors or exports. The export (G19) decrypts for the tenant's own admins only.

Tests: wrap and unwrap with each adapter against stand-ins (SoftHSM, a Vault dev server stub); revocation stops reads and sends; rotation; field encryption for every listed column with search still working by email; migration both ways; the security page list matches the schema (a test reads the column list).

Settings: per-tenant KMS settings in the database (the secrets encrypted with APP_SECRET-derived keys), KEYRING_CACHE_SECONDS.

Leave out: client-side end-to-end encryption of documents (incompatible with server-side stamping; revisit only as a separate 'sealed attachment' feature).

batches.title: Smart cards: PIV and CAC sign-in through the browser, and signing with a national eID or PIV card through Web eID
files_touched: deploy/ (reverse proxy examples for client certificates)
assets/trust/ (Federal Common Policy root bundle, with source and date)
batches.needs_from_operator: Cards and readers for testing (a PIV test card, an Estonian or Belgian card), and an agency reverse proxy that requests client certificates.
batches.brief:
Goal: US federal staff sign in with PIV or CAC, and staff and citizens with eID cards sign with the card's own key, using what browsers can actually do. Be exact about the limit: a web page cannot use a smart card key to sign arbitrary data by itself. Browsers can present a client certificate in TLS (sign-in), and signing needs a small native helper (Web eID).

Build:
1. Sign-in with PIV or CAC through mutual TLS: the agency's reverse proxy (nginx, Apache or HAProxy examples in deploy/) requests a client certificate on a dedicated host name and forwards the verified certificate in a header that the app accepts only from TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS proxies and only on that host. src/server/fpki.ts validates the path to the Federal Common Policy CA G2 (bundled with its source and date, replaceable), through the Federal Bridge where needed, checks revocation (OCSP through the G02 allowlist, or CRLs from a folder), and maps the identity by FASC-N, UUID or UPN SAN to a login (set up by an admin or by SSO). The session records 'PIV authentication certificate, AAL3 as the agency declares' (G09's assurance module).
2. Signing with a card through Web eID (open-source browser extension and native app, MIT): src/server/pades/webeid.ts uses the Web eID JavaScript library on the signing page to get the signing certificate, sends the hash computed over the frozen document's ByteRange (G16's model), receives the signature and assembles the CMS. Web eID supports several national eID cards (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Finland, Belgium, Croatia and others: check its current list) and, in some versions, other PKCS#11 tokens. Check whether PIV signing keys work through it today. If they do not, say so and list the options (a PKCS#11-capable helper such as the DSS NexU-style approach) as later work.
3. Federal Register and other XAdES needs: out of scope here. Note that XAdES output is not built.
4. The record: the certificate prints the card certificate subject and issuer and the level from validation (G07). PIV-signed PAdES is 'AdES on a Federal PKI certificate'. A qualified eID card signature can be QES when validation says so.
5. The signing page explains what to install (the Web eID extension and app), with links, detects whether it is missing, and offers the other ways the sender allowed.

Rules: the mTLS header is trusted only from configured proxies on the configured host. Never infer AAL3 without the PIV authentication certificate policy OID.

Tests: path validation with a test hierarchy shaped like Federal PKI (test roots made in the test); a forged header from an untrusted hop refused; FASC-N and UUID mapping; revocation; the Web eID flow with its library's test mode or a stub, and CMS assembly verified with G07; a manual test with a real card, written up with the date and card type.

Settings: MTLS_HOST, FPKI_TRUST_BUNDLE, PIV_REQUIRED (per org via G13).

Leave out: native apps, XAdES, the derived PIV credential.

batches.title: EUDI Wallet relying party pilot: identity through OpenID4VP with PID, behind a flag
batches.needs_from_operator: Registration as a relying party in a member state's EUDI pilot or sandbox, and the relying party access certificate it issues. This is onboarding, not software.
batches.brief:
Goal: be ready for the EUDI Wallet as citizens' default from about December 2026: accept the person identification data (PID) for signer identity, and sign through a wallet-linked QTSP (that part comes through G16's CSC client).

Build, behind WALLET_PILOT=1, against the EU reference implementation and the published architecture and reference framework (check the versions current when you start, and write them in the code):
1. src/server/openid4vp.ts: OpenID for Verifiable Presentations as profiled by the EUDI ARF (the HAIP profile): an authorization request with a DCQL query (or presentation_definition, if the targeted wallet version needs it) for PID claims (family_name, given_name, birth_date, and the stable identifier where available), request_uri by reference, signed request objects with the relying party access certificate (x509_san_dns client id scheme), response mode direct_post.jwt with an encrypted response, a nonce and state, and same-device and cross-device (QR code from the existing qr module) flows.
2. src/server/sdjwt.ts: verify SD-JWT VC: the issuer signature against the PID provider trust list (load the list the pilot publishes; air-gapped: from a file), disclosures hashed, key binding JWT with nonce and audience, status list (revocation) check. src/server/mdoc.ts for ISO 18013-5 mdoc only if time allows; otherwise list it as not done.
3. It becomes an identity provider type in G09 ('eudi_wallet'), with the assurance 'eIDAS high as specified for PID'. Print that the pilot is a pilot.
4. Data minimisation: request only the claims the sender's check needs, show the signer what is asked and why before they open the wallet, and store only the result (G09's rules: the identifier hashed).

Rules: off by default. The page says 'EU Digital Identity Wallet (pilot)'. Make no claim of certification or conformance.

Tests: requests built and signed; responses from a test issuer made in the test (SD-JWT with disclosures and key binding); a tampered disclosure, a wrong nonce, wrong audience, a revoked status, an unknown issuer; same-device and QR flows; minimisation (only the requested claims accepted).

Settings: WALLET_PILOT, WALLET_RP_CERT, WALLET_RP_KEY, WALLET_TRUST_LIST.

Leave out: issuing credentials, wallet signing outside CSC, mdoc unless time allows.

batches.title: National signing connectors: a connector framework and the first connector for the owner's first country
batches.needs_from_operator: Decision 2 (first countries) and the scheme contract for that country (for example SK ID Solutions for Smart-ID, an ESP agreement for Aadhaar eSign, a public-body partnership for gov.br signing).
batches.brief:
Goal: in most large states the signature itself is the state's or a licensed provider's. One connector per scheme, on one interface, so each country is a contained batch.

Build:
1. src/server/connectors/index.ts: an interface { id, country, identify?(recipient) -> identity per G09, sign?(hash, signer) -> CMS or signature value plus chain, formats: PAdES | ASiC-E | XAdES | CAdES, levelDeclared, needsContract }. Signing services from G16 and Web eID from G23 are wrapped to fit, so G10 sees one list of methods.
2. The first connector, chosen by the owner. The candidates, with what each needs:
   - Estonia, Smart-ID and Mobile-ID (SK ID Solutions REST APIs; the demo environment is public). Signing returns a signature over our hash. Output PAdES, and ASiC-E (src/server/pades/asice.ts: XAdES baseline inside an ASiC-E container) because DigiDoc users expect it.
   - Brazil, gov.br signature (the ITI API for public bodies: OAuth with the citizen's gov.br account, signing a hash, returning PKCS#7). Free for citizens. It needs a public-body partnership, so a government customer brings it.
   - India, Aadhaar eSign through an empanelled ESP (the ESP's XML API with OTP or biometric). Needs an ESP agreement. Output PAdES on the ESP's certificate. India's First Schedule exclusions come from G10.
   - Singapore, Sign with Singpass (needs onboarding as a signing partner).
   - Mexico, SAT e.firma: the signer's own .cer and .key, which must never be uploaded. Signing happens in the browser with WebCrypto after the user opens the key file locally with its password. The hash goes in and the signature comes out. Say clearly that the key never leaves their device, and test that no key bytes reach the server.
3. Each connector: a stand-in in tests made from the scheme's published documentation and samples, then one live test in the scheme's sandbox, written up with the date. A connector that has only passed the stand-in is shown to operators as 'not tried against <scheme>'.

Rules: nothing is claimed for a scheme until its contract exists. The connector is hidden unless the operator configured it.

Tests: per connector, as above, plus G07 validation of the output and G10's level reached.

Leave out: more than one connector per batch.

batches.title: Scale proof and high availability on SQLite, object storage for files, and the Postgres question answered with numbers
requirements: owner brief: Postgres as an option at national scale
files_touched: src/server/filestore.ts (an S3-compatible backend behind the existing interface)
batches.needs_from_operator: Decision 6 (stay on SQLite with replication, or fund a Postgres port).
batches.brief:
Goal: know, with measurements, how far one container on SQLite goes, make it survive a lost disk, and decide on Postgres from data. Context: the code makes about 1,147 synchronous SQL calls across 66 files through node:sqlite, so a Postgres port is a multi-week refactor to async and not one batch.

Build:
1. scripts/loadtest.mjs: drive the API on a production build with realistic mixes (create, send, open, sign, complete with PDF build, verify) at rising rates, with documents of 2, 10 and 50 pages, on a stated machine (cores, RAM, disk). Measure throughput, p50, p95 and p99 per route, PDF build time, database size per million envelopes, and blob storage per million. Write docs/procurement/capacity.md with the numbers, the machine and the date, and translate them into the signatures per year one server handles (10M a year is about 0.3 a second on average; plan for peaks of 50 times that). Feed G14's TCO calculator from this file.
2. Find and fix the top bottlenecks the test shows (likely PDF building on the main thread: move final PDF building and sealing to a worker_threads pool, so a slow PDF never blocks requests). Make sure WAL mode and busy_timeout are set.
3. Disk loss: Litestream (Apache-2.0) as an optional sidecar replicating sign.db continuously to S3-compatible storage (MinIO on premises, or the agency's object store). Document restore, test it, and record the recovery point and recovery time measured.
4. Files on object storage: an S3-compatible backend for filestore.ts (sigv4 written with node:crypto, or a small audited library), with the same encryption, the same SHA-256 names and the same damage checks. It is optional. Disk stays the default.
5. A warm standby option in the Helm chart (a second pod restoring continuously from the replica, promoted by hand), with the steps written down. Active-active is not offered, and the docs say why.
6. The Postgres decision write-up for the owner: what the measurements say, what a port costs (the call sites, the transaction helper tx(), the triggers used, the tests), and the recommended trigger point (for example, when a single tenant needs more than the measured capacity, or a buyer requires managed Postgres).

Tests: the blob backend against a local S3 stand-in written in the test (put, get, damage, missing); the worker pool builds identical PDFs to the main-thread path (byte comparison with a fixed clock); the restore drill script.

Settings: BLOB_BACKEND (disk | s3), S3_ENDPOINT, S3_BUCKET, S3_REGION, S3_ACCESS_KEY_FILE, S3_SECRET_KEY_FILE, PDF_WORKERS.

Leave out: the Postgres port itself (owner decision 6).

owner_decisions: 1. Licence (blocks open-source adoption, catalogue listings and the Digital Public Goods application). Options: EUPL-1.2 (recommended: OSI-approved, written for public administrations, available in all EU languages, and compatible by its own appendix with GPL, AGPL, MPL and others), AGPL-3.0 (strongest copyleft for network use, well understood in the US), or Apache-2.0 (permissive; maximises reuse but lets anyone close a fork). The research (L01) points to a copyleft licence with no reserved rights. Also decide whether to require a contributor agreement, which is needed only if you want to dual-license later. Note: once the repository is public, the free code GROWalition in the source is public too.

2. Which countries and segments first. The research says to avoid attacking US civilian agencies head-on, where DocuSign holds OneGov, FedRAMP and IL4, and to go where DocuSign is structurally blocked. The cheapest first wave in software and certification is (a) public bodies that self-host on their own infrastructure, so it inherits their authorisation: EU municipalities, German Laender and openDesk users, who need G02, G05-G08 and German or French; (b) donor-funded DPI programmes, which need the licence, the DPG application, G09 with MOSIP eSignet or national OIDC, and G25. Pick at most two to three countries, because each needs its own connector, language and legal review.

3. Whether to pursue any certification now, and which one first. Recommended: none for SaaS yet. Lead with self-hosting, where the agency's own accreditation covers the deployment. If you will host for governments, start with ISO/IEC 27001 plus SOC 2 Type II (6 to 12 months, auditor fees), then the national scheme of the first country (C5, ENS, IRAP and so on). FedRAMP only through a partner, and only if the US becomes a target.

4. Qualified signatures: become a QTSP yourself (conformity assessment, liability insurance, years) or partner with QTSPs through the CSC API (G16). Recommended: partner, and pick the first QTSP in the first EU country.

5. Hosting and the legal entity: offer hosted service to governments at all, or self-host only plus local sovereign hosting partners? A hosted EU offer needs an EU entity with no non-EU control (O01, SecNumCloud caps) and a legal opinion on CLOUD Act exposure, which depends on where Treegens and its owners are incorporated.

6. Database: stay on SQLite with replication and a warm standby (recommended until G26's measurements show a limit), or fund a multi-week port to Postgres (about 1,150 synchronous SQL call sites in 66 files).

7. Government prices and the tree commitment: fixed annual fees per band, currencies, what support includes, and how much of each contract funds planting (for example the same 10 mangroves per dollar of fee, reported yearly with planting evidence). Also confirm that the monthly-expiring credits you decided for the consumer plan do NOT apply to the government tier: the research found that fixed public budgets do not fit them.

8. Trees on the certificate: take the paper, water, CO2e and mangrove lines off every certificate of completion (recommended, since a signed record should hold only the agreement and its evidence), or only off government tenants' certificates. Either way they stay on screens, in emails and on /impact where the tenant allows.

9. Name and white label: confirm GrowSigning as the product name in code and docs (the code still says Sign&Grow), and whether white-labelled government tenants may hide 'Powered by GrowSigning' entirely.

10. AI helper for governments: allow it only with a self-hosted open-weight model inside the agency's boundary (recommended). Decide whether you will support a smaller open-weight model on premises, since Kimi K3 needs a multi-GPU server, or leave the helper off by default for government tenants.
11. PDF/A conversion of uploaded files: allow Ghostscript (AGPL) as an optional separate converter container, or accept that only documents already uploaded as PDF/A come out as PDF/A.

wrong.claim: Reason 6 and L01: the Interoperable Europe Act Art. 4 (in force 11 April 2024) requires sharing interoperability solutions, which a third-party IP product cannot satisfy.
wrong.really: Overstated. Art. 4 obliges a public sector body to share interoperability solutions it holds when another public body asks. It carves out solutions where third parties hold intellectual property rights that do not allow sharing, plus some security-related cases. Buying a proprietary product therefore does not breach the Act. It is a duty to share, not a preference against proprietary purchases. It entered into force on 11 April 2024 and applies from 12 July 2024. Confidence medium-high, from my own knowledge of Reg. 2024/903; not re-fetched in this pass.

wrong.claim: Reason 2, S01 and G10: German written form (BGB s.126a) ties formal acts to a QES, so the rules engine should force QES for German written form.
wrong.really: Incomplete in a way that would produce wrong rules. Under BGB s.126(3), electronic form (s.126a, a QES) replaces written form only where the law does not say otherwise. Several provisions exclude electronic form outright: s.623 (termination of employment and separation agreements), s.766 (guarantee) and ss.780-781 (promise and acknowledgement of debt). For these a QES does not help, and the rule must be 'not_electronic' with 'block'. Separately, the Bürokratieentlastungsgesetz IV moved some requirements to text form from 1 January 2025, for example commercial leases (s.578), so 'long lease needs QES' is wrong for those. The product's own dated Germany note already says a termination needs ink on paper, so it is more accurate than the synthesis. Confidence high on s.623, medium on the BEG IV details; not re-fetched.

wrong.claim: Reason 2 and S01: in Brazil only ICP-Brasil signatures carry a presumption of truth, and Lei 14.063/2020 makes them mandatory for acts of heads of Powers and for real estate.
wrong.really: Overstated, and the source is misattributed. Lei 14.063/2020 governs signatures in dealings with and between public entities. Art. 5 requires the qualified signature for acts of heads of Powers and for transfers and registration of real estate. However, Lei 14.620/2023 added Art. 17-A, which allows advanced signatures for property-credit instruments that financial institutions may sign with the force of a public deed, so 'mandatory for real estate' is no longer a blanket rule. The presumption of truth comes from MP 2.200-2/2001 Art. 10 s.1. Its s.2 also lets parties accept other means, which the product's Brazil note already relies on. Confidence medium; the saved research notes flag the same Art. 17-A point as unconfirmed.

wrong.claim: Reason 2: India recognises only Second Schedule methods from CCA-licensed providers. S01 and G10: the First Schedule excludes wills, negotiable instruments, powers of attorney, trusts and real estate sales.
wrong.really: Overstated. IT Act s.10A makes contracts formed electronically valid, and simple e-signatures (click, typed, OTP) are widely used and admissible. Second Schedule methods (Aadhaar eSign, DSC) are needed where a law itself requires a signature (ss.3, 3A, 5), and they carry the statutory presumptions. The First Schedule was amended by S.O. 4720(E) in 2022. The product's sourced note confirms only wills and trusts after that amendment. Check the research's longer list against the current Schedule before G10 hard-codes any block. Confidence medium-high; not re-fetched.

wrong.claim: Reason 2: Canada requires Treasury Board-recognised CAs.
wrong.really: Too broad. SOR/2005-30 defines a 'secure electronic signature' under PIPEDA Part 2, which is needed only where a federal statute specifically calls for one (for example originals, seals and statements made under oath). Treasury Board guidance lets departments choose other electronic signatures by risk assessment for most transactions. Confidence medium; not re-fetched.

wrong.claim: S07: Reg. 2024/1183 makes free wallet QES the default citizen path from about December 2026.
wrong.really: Overstated. The Regulation sets a deadline: a wallet in each Member State within 24 months of the first implementing acts, so around the end of 2026. Art. 5a(5)(g) makes wallet QES free for natural persons, and states may limit that to non-professional use. Using the wallet is voluntary and must not disadvantage people who do not use it (Art. 5a(15)). National rollouts are uneven and several are late. Plan S07 and the EUDI batch for staggered availability, and keep non-wallet routes. Confidence medium-high.

wrong.claim: Reason 6 (procurement law prefers reuse and open source) is rated 'strong'.
wrong.really: The evidence is moderate. Only Italy and Spain impose a procedural duty. Italy's CAD Art. 68 comma 1-ter still allows proprietary licences after a reasoned comparison, and it lists cloud services as an option ahead of proprietary licences, which is the route SaaS such as DocuSign is bought by. Spain's duty is Ley 40/2015 Art. 157. France's 2016 law Art. 16 only 'encourages' free software. Germany's open-source-by-default is a coalition commitment, not a statute. M-16-21 covers custom-developed code. The Interoperable Europe Act exempts third-party IP. The pressure is real, but it does not explain DocuSign's absence where it is absent; state credentials and sovereignty do.

wrong.claim: Reason 3 and S12: HM Land Registry built Sign your mortgage deed on GOV.UK One Login, so the product should integrate One Login.
wrong.really: Not confirmed. To my knowledge the service launched on GOV.UK Verify and later relied on the conveyancer's identity check plus a code by text message. More important: GOV.UK One Login is offered to central government services only, so a vendor cannot become a relying party on its own. The integration has to run under a department's own One Login onboarding, with that tenant's client credentials. Confidence low on the history, medium-high on the access rule.

wrong.claim: S09: Federal Register submissions require PIV-based XAdES.
wrong.really: Not confirmed, and the format looks doubtful. The Office of the Federal Register accepts digitally signed submissions signed with an agency PIV or CAC certificate, but I know of no XAdES requirement. Check the Document Drafting Handbook before S09 names a format. Confidence low.

wrong.claim: Reason 8 and L05: fixed public budgets cannot absorb expiring credits, so monthly-expiring credits must stay out of the government tier.
wrong.really: An inference the evidence does not support. Public buyers routinely buy annual envelope allowances that lapse at the end of the term; enterprise e-signature plans, DocuSign's included, are sold that way. Many budgets are also use-it-or-lose-it by fiscal year. What the evidence shows is overage, unconsented increases and unpredictability, not expiry. A government tier can keep the owner's expiry decision: a yearly pool aligned to the buyer's fiscal year, a hard cap instead of overage, and a fixed price. Confidence medium.

wrong.claim: Reason 9: DocuSign is one of the most impersonated brands in phishing.
wrong.really: Unsourced as written. The only source is the research.checkpoint.com home page, not a dated brand-phishing report. The 2017 breach of a non-core system and the November 2024 Envelopes API abuse are well documented; keep those, and either cite a specific report for the ranking or drop it.

wrong.claim: Reason 1 and S11: DocuSign lacks native Aadhaar eSign support.
wrong.really: Internally inconsistent and thinly sourced. Reason 1 says DocuSign plugs into these schemes through eMudhra, a CCA-licensed eSign service provider, and also says it does not support Aadhaar, citing only a developer-forum feature request. The claim is unproven either way and should stay out of comparisons.

wrong.claim: D04, Reason 5 and C03: DocuSign's HSM validations are historical, its interim FIPS 140-3 certificate (CMVP 4782) passed its sunset on 27 August 2026, it has no UK data region, and no ISMAP, CSAP or SecNumCloud status.
wrong.really: None of these could be confirmed in this pass, and the synthesis lists several as unchecked itself. Wrong comparative claims about a named competitor's certifications carry false-advertising risk: Lanham Act s.43(a) in the US and Directive 2006/114/EC in the EU. Keep them out of every page, deck and tender answer until each has been read on the CMVP, FedRAMP Marketplace, ISMAP, KISA and EU Trusted List registries and on DocuSign's data-residency page.

wrong.claim: Reason 5: Korea requires CSAP, which Modusign holds and DocuSign was not found to.
wrong.really: Needs nuance. Korea reformed CSAP in 2023 into high, medium and low tiers. The low tier allows logically separated cloud services, including foreign ones. CSAP gates public cloud purchases, but which gate applies depends on the tier of the data. Confidence medium.

Accessibility is missing from the synthesis's requirements, even though one research angle covered it. A buyer asks for it on day one. In the EU, EN 301 549 applies through the procurement directives and the Web Accessibility Directive. G04 exists only because the owner brief asked for it.

Availability and support. Buyers ask on day one for an uptime SLA, RTO and RPO, disaster recovery, maintenance windows, support hours, on-call cover and escalation. Security evidence. The research leaves out four day-one asks: (1) An independent penetration-test report. G03 leaves pen testing out. FIPS-validated cryptography is needed for all cryptography, not only the HSM (FedRAMP SC-13). Node's bundled OpenSSL is not a validated module, and scrypt password hashing (/home/user/treegens-app/sign-and-grow/src/server/auth.ts) is not an approved algorithm. A FIPS mode needs a validated OpenSSL 3 provider and PBKDF2. Also, node:sqlite still prints an ExperimentalWarning on Node 22 (checked here on v22.23.5), and Node 22 reaches end of life on 30 April 2027.

Vendor viability and contract terms: the legal entity and its beneficial owners, financial statements, cyber and professional-indemnity insurance, liability caps, IP indemnity, and registration (SAM.gov UEI and CAGE code in the US, the ESPD in EU tenders). The economics also need an answer. package.json says 100% of subscription revenue funds tree planting, which leaves nothing for audits (FedRAMP alone typically costs six to seven figures), staff, on-call support and insurance. Buyers will ask about Microsoft 365 GCC, SharePoint, Teams, Salesforce Government Cloud, ServiceNow and SAP, and the README says no ready-made integrations exist.

Assisted digital and inclusion. Governments must serve people without email, a phone or a national eID; signing at a counter; signing by a legal representative or proxy (power of attorney, guardian); a paper fallback; and foreigners without the local eID (gov.br needs a CPF). eIDAS 2 makes wallet use voluntary. G09's eID gate needs a fallback the sender chooses.

Public records and classification: FOIA and public-records requests, eDiscovery export, and redaction. Buyers also ask which data classification the product may hold: UK OFFICIAL or OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE, Australian PROTECTED, US CUI, and CMMC or DFARS 252.204-7012 for defence contractors handling CUI.
Logging: the log types and retention in US OMB M-21-31 (12 months active, 18 months cold storage), export to a SIEM, and a trusted time source for the audit trail.

AI helper. (1) EU AI Act Art. 50(1) disclosure applies from 2 August 2026; the chat brief already says the helper states it is an AI. Check the outcome of the digital omnibus. (2) US OMB M-25-21 governs federal AI use. (3) Model provenance: Kimi is from Moonshot AI in Beijing. In 2025 several governments barred DeepSeek on official devices (Australia, Italy's data protection authority, South Korean ministries, the US Navy and NASA), so expect the same question about Kimi. Multi-agency tenancy. Many agencies share one email domain, and buyers will also ask about delegated admin, envelopes across agencies and central billing. The research has no requirement for these.

Without assistive-technology testers, the conformance report will mostly read 'Not evaluated', which is honest but weak for US federal and Canadian buyers. The new UI from the other briefs (the impact animation and the chat widget) is not in the test list.

batch_concerns.concern: (1) The seal belongs to 'whoever runs the server'. In multi-tenant SaaS that is the vendor, so every agency document would carry the vendor's organisation seal, which agencies will not accept as their own. (2) Adobe shows a sealed file as 'Signed by <operator>' with a valid-signature banner, which readers take to mean the parties signed with PKI, even though the certificate text says otherwise. (3) src/server/pdf.ts calls doc.save() with defaults, and pdf-lib then writes object streams and a cross-reference stream. A hand-written incremental update that appends a classic xref table to such a file is a known way to break it. pdf-lib has been unmaintained since 1.17.1 (2021).
batch_concerns.fix: Give each tenant its own seal key and certificate (from its own CA or a QTSP), with the operator's seal only as a fallback. Set the signature field name, /Name and /Reason to 'Integrity seal by <operator>; not a signature of the signers'. Make the incremental writer emit an xref stream whenever the base file uses one, or save with useObjectStreams: false before sealing. Test against Adobe, pdfsig and DSS, or let DSS write the signature.

batch_concerns.concern: (1) PDF/A identification applies to the whole document. Writing pdfaid part 3 into the XMP for 'the certificate pages' marks the entire merged file as PDF/A, which is false whenever the uploaded pages are not PDF/A. That is exactly the overclaim the honesty rules forbid. (2) Embedding the full audit JSON in the file sent to every party hands every signer's email, IP address and device data to all of them, which may go beyond what each party may see under GDPR data minimisation. (3) Re-timestamping changes the fingerprints already sent by email.
batch_concerns.fix: Write PDF/A metadata only when the entire final file was produced or converted as PDF/A, and validated where VERAPDF_URL is set; otherwise write none. Alternatively, ship the certificate as a separate PDF/A file in the package. Embed only the audit view each party already sees, and keep the full JSON in the sender's evidence pack. Keep the plain wording on /verify about version fingerprints.

batch_concerns.concern: (1) /verify would parse arbitrary PDFs and ASN.1 from anonymous visitors inside the process that holds tenant data and keys. (2) Correct PKIX path validation in 4 days of TypeScript is unrealistic: validity at the timestamped time, key usage, policies, name constraints and revocation, plus PAdES level detection. A wrong 'intact and chained to a trusted anchor' verdict is worse than none. (3) The keep-existing-signatures path ignores DocMDP and FieldMDP. Adding fields, annotations or a seal after a certification signature with P=1 (no changes) or P=2 (no annotations) invalidates that signature.
batch_concerns.fix: Parse in a separate worker or container with memory, CPU-time and size limits. Have the built-in checker report only byte integrity and the CMS checks, and take any 'trusted' verdict from DSS. Read /Perms DocMDP and the FieldMDP locks, refuse the changes they forbid, and fall back to attaching the original unchanged.

batch_concerns.concern: (1) SAML in Node has had critical signature-bypass flaws recently: xml-crypto CVE-2025-29774 and CVE-2025-29775 (March 2025) and samlify CVE-2025-47949 (May 2025). Hand-integrating SAML plus generic OIDC, domain proof, enforcement, just-in-time membership and role mapping in 5 days is unsafe. (2) 'An email domain belongs to one tenant' fails in governments where many agencies share one domain. (3) The break-glass owner signs in with a password plus TOTP, which is not phishing-resistant.
batch_concerns.fix: Put an identity broker (Keycloak, Apache-2.0) in front for SAML and national IdPs, and keep the app OIDC-only. Let a domain map to several tenants, with an IdP claim that picks the tenant. Require WebAuthn for the break-glass account.

batch_concerns.concern: (1) Most national schemes will not accept an arbitrary SaaS vendor as a relying party. GOV.UK One Login is for central government services, FranceConnect for public services and approved partners, Singpass and Myinfo for approved Singapore entities, and many eIDAS nodes for public-sector services only. Identity providers configured by the operator are therefore the wrong shape. (2) Six profiles, FAPI with JWE, eIDAS SAML and transliterated name matching in 4 days is unrealistic. (3) Blocking on a fuzzy, transliterated name match produces both false rejections and false matches. (4) Storing dates of birth and national identifiers is restricted in places: Aadhaar numbers may not be stored outside the vaults the Aadhaar rules allow. (5) Signers without that country's eID have no route.
batch_concerns.fix: Register IdPs per tenant, with each agency's own client registration. Ship one profile end to end first (the tenant's own OIDC or one eIDAS node). Let the sender give an expected identifier, or require an explicit sender confirmation, instead of deciding automatically by name. Never store Aadhaar numbers. Always offer a fallback check that the sender chooses.

batch_concerns.concern: (1) The seed list carries the research errors above: s.623 BGB excludes electronic form entirely, BEG IV moved commercial leases to text form, Lei 14.620/2023 Art. 17-A allows advanced signatures for some property instruments, and India's Schedule changed in 2022. (2) Printing 'Level required for <type> in <country> by the rules on this server' on the certificate of completion puts an unreviewed legal opinion into the legal record. The sender picks the document type, so a wrong choice gets an official-looking stamp.
batch_concerns.fix: Seed only the rules the product's own dated, sourced notes already carry, and mark everything else 'warn'. Record the result in the audit trail as 'sender chose X; server rule said Y; word check suggested Z', not as a statement of law on the certificate. Require a lawyer's review before any rule can 'block'.

batch_concerns.concern: 'A held envelope cannot be deleted by anyone ... not by the operator' claims more than software can guarantee. Anyone with access to the database, disk or backups can delete. A hold also has to give way to a court order or the operator's own legal duty.
batch_concerns.fix: Word it as 'the software refuses every deletion path while a hold is on and records any attempt'. Add an operator override that needs two people and writes an audit line. Keep held items out of backup rotation and say so.

batch_concerns.concern: G01 only adds a per-tenant on/off switch for the helper. The helper still defaults to hosted Kimi K3 through OpenRouter or Moonshot (research/briefs.json 'chat'; the treegens.app reference route.ts). For government tenants that sends chat text to a third party, and for Moonshot to a PRC company, against S20's self-hosting requirement and the DPA in G03.
batch_concerns.fix: For DEPLOYMENT_PROFILE=government, refuse any provider URL outside OUTBOUND_ALLOW. Document a self-hosted OpenAI-compatible endpoint (vLLM or llama.cpp serving the open weights). Let each tenant choose a model, including an open-weight model from a non-PRC developer. Keep the consumer default the owner asked for.
